definition: (of clothing) very short.
example: An abbreviated swimsuit.

definition: A shortened form of a word or phrase.
example: Hants is an abbreviation of Hampshire.
etymology: First attested 1400–50. From Middle English abbreviacioun, from Middle French abreviation, from Ecclesiastical Latin abbreviātiō, from Latin ad + breviō (“shorten”), from brevis (“short”).

definition: A seaman in the merchant marine; trained in special skills.
In an abnormal manner.
example: They were behaving abnormally.
etymology: From abnormal + -ly.

definition: Any address at which you dwell more than temporarily.
example: Of no fixed abode.
etymology: From Middle English abod, abad, from Old English *ābād, related to ābīdan (“to abide”); see abide. Cognate with Scots abade, abaid (“abode”). For the change of nouns, compare abode, preterite of abide.

definition: A person who is loathsome or disgusting.
etymology: From Middle English abominacioun, from Middle French abomination (“horror, disgust”), from Late Latin abōminātiō, abōminātiōnem (“abomination”) Doublet of abominatio.

definition: Causing abrasion.
example: An abrasive person can grate on one's sensibilities.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin abrāsīvus.

definition: A substance that abrades or wears down.
(used of texts) shortened by condensing or rewriting.
example: An abridged version.
etymology: From abridge + -ed.

definition: One that is absent or not in residence.
example: At roll-call there were three absentees.
etymology: From absent + -ee.

definition: (election) a ballot that is cast while absent (usually mailed in prior to election day).
The percentage of workers who do not report to work.
A measure of the resistance to flow of a fluid under an applied force.

A measure of the rate of decrease in the intensity of electromagnetic radiation (as light) as it passes through a given substance; the fraction of incident radiant energy absorbed per unit mass or thickness of an absorber.
example: Absorptance equals 1 minus transmittance.

definition: Refrain from voting.
example: In order to improve his health, Rob decided to abstain from smoking.
etymology: First attested around 1380. From Middle English absteynen, absteinen, abstenen, from Old French astenir, abstenir, from Latin abstineō (“to hold oneself back”) from abs- (“from”) + teneō (“to hold”). See also tenable.

definition: The trait of abstaining (especially from alcohol).
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:abstinence.
etymology: From Middle English abstinence, from Old French abstinence, from Latin abstinentia, from abstinēns, present participle of abstineō (“to withhold”). Equivalent to abstain + -ence.

definition: A message whose content is at variance with reason.
etymology: First attested around 1472. From Middle English absurdite, then from either Middle French absurdité, or from Late Latin absurditas (“dissonance, incongruity”), from Latin absurdus + -itas (“quality, state, degree”).

definition: In an abundant manner.
example: They were abundantly supplied with food.
etymology: From Middle English abundantly, abundauntli, habundantly, habundauntliche, equivalent to abundant + -ly.

definition: Someone who abuses.
Any of various spiny trees or shrubs of the genus Acacia.
In regard to academic matters.
example: Academically, this is a good school.
etymology: From academical + -ly or academic + -ally.

definition: A pedal that controls the throttle valve.
An event or situation that happens at the same time as or in connection with another.
example: Brooks performed a saxophone solo on stage, with Robert as accompaniment on the bass.
etymology: From French accompagnement; equivalent to accompany + -ment. First attested in 1744.

definition: A person who joins with another in carrying out some plan (especially an unethical or illegal plan).
etymology: First attested in 1550. From a complice, from Middle English complice, from Old French complice (“confederate”), from Latin complicāre (“fold together”).

definition: A portable box-shaped free-reed instrument; the reeds are made to vibrate by air from the bellows controlled by the player.
etymology: First attested in 1831. Borrowed from German Akkordeon, from Akkord (“harmony”), from French accord, from Old French acorder, based on Italian accordare (“to tune”). See also accord.

definition: An interior door that opens by folding back in sections (rather than by swinging on hinges).
A continuous parallel folding in an accordion-like fashion, that is with folds alternatively made to the front and back in zig-zag folds.
The occupation of maintaining and auditing records and preparing financial reports for a business.
example: Professional accountancy.
etymology: From account + -ancy.

definition: Periodically accumulated over time.
example: Accrued interest.

definition: A salt or ester of acetic acid.
etymology: Formed from the root of Latin acētum (“vinegar”) + -ate, from aceō (“to be sour”). By surface analysis, acet- + -ate.

definition: A disk coated with cellulose acetate.
Capable of existing or taking place or proving true; possible to do.
example: Achievable goal.
etymology: From achieve + -able.

definition: The property of being acidic.
example: The acidity of lemon juice.
etymology: From French acidité, from Latin aciditātem, accusative singular of aciditās (“sourness, acidity”), from acidus (“sour, acid”). Equivalent to acid + -ity.

definition: The state or quality of being recognized or acknowledged.
example: She seems to avoid much in the way of recognition or acknowledgement of feminist work prior to her own.
etymology: From acknowledge + -ment.

definition: Fruit of the oak tree: a smooth thin-walled nut in a woody cup-shaped base.
etymology: Cognate with Scots aicorn (“acorn”), Dutch aker (“acorn”), German Ecker (“acorn”), Danish agern (“acorn”), Faroese and Icelandic akarn (“acorn”), Norwegian Nynorsk åkorn (“acorn”), Gothic 𐌰𐌺𐍂𐌰𐌽 (akran, “fruit”);

definition: Cup-shaped structure of hardened bracts at the base of an acorn.
etymology: From acorn + cup.

definition: A small vacuum tube; used at high frequencies.
etymology: From the resemblance of the glass cap to the cup of an acorn.

definition: Shaped like an acorn.
Opposition to the flow of sound through a surface; acoustic resistance is the real component of acoustic impedance and acoustic reactance is the imaginary component.
The study of the physical properties of sound.
example: The acoustics in the opera house gave the whole concert a spooky sound.
etymology: From acoustic + -s.

definition: A judgment of not guilty.
example: Criminal acquittal.
etymology: From acquit + -al.

definition: An area of ground used for some particular purpose (such as building or farming).
example: He wanted some acreage to build on.
etymology: From acre + -age.

definition: A glassy thermoplastic; can be cast and molded or used in coatings and adhesives.
One of the proteins into which actomyosin can be split; can exist in either a globular or a fibrous form.
Affording grounds for legal action.
example: Slander is an actionable offense.
etymology: From action + -able. Compare Late Latin actionabilis. See action.

definition: Treatment of pain or disease by inserting the tips of needles at specific points on the skin.
etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin acūpūnctūra, from Latin acus + pūnctūra. First attested in 1684. By surface analysis, acu- + puncture.

definition: In a keen or penetrating way.
example: She pitied her sister acutely.
etymology: From acute + -ly.

definition: Capable of adapting (of becoming or being made suitable) to a particular situation or use.
example: To succeed one must be adaptable.
etymology: From adapt + -able.

definition: (mathematics) one of a pair of numbers whose sum is zero; the additive inverse of -5 is +5.
example: The additive inverse of 12 is −12.
etymology: So-called because the sum of a number and its additive inverse is the additive identity.

definition: Abnormal union of bodily tissues; most common in the abdomen.
etymology: From French adhésion, from Latin stem of adhaesio, from past participle of adhaerare.

definition: A contract that heavily restricts one party while leaving the other free (as some standard form printed contracts); implies inequality in bargaining power.
Bandage consisting of a medical dressing of plain absorbent gauze held in place by a plastic or fabric tape coated with adhesive.
The friction between a body and the surface on which it moves (as between an automobile tire and the road).
Adhesive tape used in dressing wounds.
Can be changed to different settings.
An officer who acts as military assistant to a more senior officer.
Large Indian stork with a military gait.
A general's adjutant; chief administrative officer.
A person who backs a politician or a team etc.
example: Deven is an enthusiastic admirer of The Beatles.
etymology: From admire + -er.

definition: A rapid active commotion.
etymology: From Northern Middle English at do (“to do”), infinitive of do, don (“to do”), see do. Influenced by an Old Norse practice of marking the infinitive by using the preposition at, att (compare Danish at gå (“to go”)).

definition: Of parents and children; related by adoption.
example: Adoptive parents.
etymology: From adopt + -ive.

definition: A person who adopts a child of other parents as his or her own child.
A feeling of profound love and admiration.
example: Because of Gerald's adoration for Katie, he was blind to her flaws.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French adoration, from Latin adōrātiō, adōrātiōnem (“worship, adoration”), from adōrō (“beseech; adore, worship”), from ad (“to, towards”) + ōrō (“beg”). From adore + -ation.

definition: Make more attractive by adding ornament, colour, etc.
example: A man adorned with noble statuary and columns.
etymology: From Middle English adornen, adournen, from Latin adōrnāre; from ad- + ōrnō (“furnish, embellish”). See adore, ornate.

definition: Aimlessly drifting.
example: The team were six points adrift of their rivals.
etymology: The adjective is probably derived from the adverb, as it is attested later.

definition: A person who enjoys taking risks.
example: It's a challenging game for the inexperienced adventurer, and should even give the hardened pros a bit of a run for their money.
etymology: From adventure + -er.

definition: Kindly endorsement and guidance.
example: Under the aegis.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin aegis, from Ancient Greek αἰγίς (aigís, “goatskin; shield of Athena”), probably from αἴξ (aíx, “goat”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyǵ- (“goat”).

definition: Exercise that increases the need for oxygen.
Forces acting on airfoils in motion relative to the air (or other gaseous fluids).
The component of the aerodynamic forces acting on an airfoil that opposes gravity.
Of or pertaining to aeronautics.
etymology: From aero- + nautical.

definition: An engineer concerned with the design and construction of aircraft.
The theory and practice of navigation through air or space.
etymology: Borrowed from French aéronautique or New Latin aeronauticus. By surface analysis, aero- + nautic + -s.

definition: An aircraft that has a fixed wing and is powered by propellers or jets.
etymology: Borrowed from French aéroplane, from Ancient Greek ἀερόπλανος (aeróplanos, “wandering in air”), from ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + πλάνος (plános, “wandering”), equivalent to aero- + plane.

definition: A cloud of solid or liquid particles in a gas.
etymology: From aero- + sol (“solution”).

definition: A bomb that uses a fuel-air explosive.
A dispenser that holds a substance under pressure and that can release it as a fine spray (usually by means of a propellant gas).
In a tasteful way.
example: This building is aesthetically very pleasing.
etymology: From aesthetic + -ally.

definition: With affection.
example: He treats her affectionately.
etymology: From affectionate + -ly.

definition: Characterized by emotion.
etymology: From Medieval Latin affectivus, from Latin affectus, past participle of afficere (“to affect”). By surface analysis, affect + -ive.

definition: Establish or strengthen as with new evidence or facts.
example: She affirmed that she would go when I asked her.
etymology: From Middle English affermen, from Old French afermer, affermer, from Latin affirmare, adfirmare (“to present as fixed, aver, affirm”), from ad (“to”) + firmare (“to make firm”), from firmus (“firm”).

definition: A statement asserting the existence or the truth of something.
example: Her success was an affirmation of all her hard work.
etymology: From Old French afermacion, from Latin affirmare (“to assert”). Doublet of affirmatio.

definition: Far away from home or one's usual surroundings.
example: Looking afield for new lands to conquer.
etymology: From Middle English afeld, a-felde, o felde, on felde, from Old English on felde (“afield”, literally “in (the) field”), equivalent to a- (“on”) + field.

definition: Any culture medium that uses agar as the gelling agent.
etymology: From Malay agar (“jelly”) or agar-agar.

definition: Making worse.
example: Aggravating circumstances.

definition: Formed of separate units gathered into a mass or whole.
example: Aggregate expenses include expenses of all divisions combined for the entire year.

definition: Someone who attacks.
etymology: Derived from Latin aggressor (“attacker, assailant, aggressor”).

definition: A mental state of extreme emotional disturbance.
example: During a storm the sea is in agitation.
etymology: From French agitation, from Latin agitātiō (“movement, agitation”).

definition: Of or pertaining to an agnostic or agnosticism.
example: She left the church when she had become agnostic.
etymology: Coined by Thomas Henry Huxley in 1870. Either from Ancient Greek ἄγνωστος (ágnōstos, “ignorant, not knowing”), or from a- + Gnostic, deriving (either way) from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “I know”).

definition: Relating to farming or agriculture.
example: An agrarian (or agricultural) society.
etymology: From Middle French agrarien, from Latin agrarius (“of the land”), from stem of ager (“field”) + -arius.

definition: Conforming to your own liking or feelings or nature.
example: Is the plan agreeable to you?
etymology: From Middle English agreable, from Old French agreable. Equivalent to agree + -able.

definition: Somewhat ill or prone to illness.
example: My poor ailing grandmother.

definition: Thermometer that measures temperature by changes in the pressure of a gas kept at constant volume.
The flow of air.
example: She adjusted the fan so that the airflow was directed right at her.
etymology: From air + flow.

definition: A warm cupboard where you put newly washed clothes until they are completely dry.
A commercial airplane that carries passengers.
etymology: From air + liner.

definition: A propeller that rotates to push against air.
A duct that provides ventilation (as in mines).
etymology: From air + way.

definition: Open to or abounding in fresh air.
example: Airy rooms.
etymology: From air + -y.

definition: An animal with congenital albinism.
One who was versed in the practice of alchemy and who sought an elixir of life and a panacea and an alkahest and the philosopher's stone.
etymology: From Old French alquemiste (French alchimiste), from Medieval Latin alchemista. Equivalent to alchemy + -ist.

definition: The way two individuals relate to each other.
example: A mysterious alchemy brought them together.
etymology: From Old French alkimie, arquemie (French alchimie), from Medieval Latin alchēmia, from Arabic اَلْكِيمِيَاء (al-kīmiyāʔ), from Ancient Greek χυμείᾱ (khumeíā, “art of alloying metals”), from χύμα (khúma, “ingot, bar”).

definition: Thermometer consisting of a glass capillary tube marked with degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit and containing alcohol which rises or falls as it expands or contracts with changes in temperature.
A male member of a municipal legislative body (as a city council).
Someone whose favorite drink is beer or ale.
Of or relating to algebra.
example: Algebraic geometry.
etymology: Partly from algebra + -ic and partly from French algébraïque.

definition: An algorithmic language having statements that resemble algebraic expressions.
Root of an algebraic equation with rational coefficients.
example: The golden ratio (φ) is an algebraic number since it is a solution of the quadratic equation x²-x-1=0, whose coefficients are integers.

definition: (law) a defense by an accused person purporting to show that they could not have committed the crime in question.
example: To set up an alibi.
etymology: From the 18th century, from Latin alibī (“elsewhere, at another place”, adverb). Probably after French alibi, which has this use since the late 14th century.

definition: Arouse hostility or indifference in where there had formerly been love, affection, or friendliness.
example: She alienated her friends when she became fanatically religious.
etymology: From Middle English alienat(e) (“deranged; uncertain; sequestred, secluded”), from Latin aliēnātus, perfect passive participle of aliēnō (“to estrange, alienate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from aliēnus.

definition: Causing hostility or loss of friendliness.
example: Her sudden alienating aloofness.

definition: The feeling of being alienated from other people.
example: The alienation of that viewing demographic is a poor business decision.
etymology: From Middle English alienacioun, from Old French alienacion, from Latin aliēnātiōn(em).

definition: To come to rest, settle.
example: He alighted from his horse.
etymology: From Middle English alighten (“to descend from a place: to dismount, get off; to descend to a place: to arrive or stop (at a place); to land; to drop; to attack; of lightning: to strike; to leap on to, mount;

definition: Causing to fall into line or into position.
Court-ordered support paid by one spouse to another after they are separated.
Any of the bivalent metals of group II of the periodic table (calcium or strontium or barium or magnesium or beryllium).
Any of the monovalent metals of group I of the periodic table (lithium or sodium or potassium or rubidium or cesium or francium).
example: The hydroxides of the alkali metals are strongly alkaline.

definition: Thriving in a relatively alkaline environment; (especially of plants requiring a pH above 7).
Card games in which points are won for taking the high or low or jack or game.
example: To be on all fours.

definition: Report or maintain.
example: He alleged that he was the victim of a crime.
etymology: From Middle English alleggen, from Old French alegier, from Latin alleviāre (“lighten”), from ad + levis (“light”). Doublet of alleviate.

definition: A short moral story (often with animal characters).
etymology: The noun is derived from Late Middle English allegorie (“symbolic interpretation; symbolism;

definition: Slim short-limbed lizard having a distinctive fold on each side that permits expansion; of western North America.
A pear-shaped tropical fruit with green or blackish skin and rich yellowish pulp enclosing a single large seed.
etymology: The "alligator" is likely an alteration of Spanish aguacate, perhaps influenced by the similarity in texture between the skin of the fruit and of an alligator.

definition: A wrench with a v-shaped jaw and serrations on one side (resembles the open jaws of an alligator).
A share set aside for a specific purpose.
etymology: From Old French alotement (modern French allotement). By surface analysis, allot + -ment.

definition: The power to entice or attract through personal charm.
example: Harper's Magazine The swing, the gait, the pose, the allure of these men.
etymology: From Middle English aluren, from Old French aleurer, alurer, from a (“to, towards”) (Latin ad) + leurre (“lure”). By surface analysis, al- + lure.

definition: Highly attractive and able to arouse hope or desire.
example: An alluring prospect.
etymology: By surface analysis, allure + -ing.

definition: Your alma mater is a school you graduated from.
etymology: From Latin alma māter (literally “nourishing mother”). Derives from the full name ("Alma Mater Studiorum Università di Bologna") of the oldest European university, the University of Bologna, founded in 1088.

definition: An annual publication including weather forecasts and other miscellaneous information arranged according to the calendar of a given year.
etymology: From Middle English almenak, from Old French almanach, from Medieval Latin almanachus, from Andalusian Arabic مَنَاخ (manāḵ, “almanac, calendar”), from Arabic الْمُنَاخ (al-munāḵ, “climate”).

definition: A moth whose larvae feed on and mat together with webbing various stored products of vegetable origin.
Smelling of almond.
Succulent plants having rosettes of leaves usually with fiber like hemp and spikes of showy flowers; found chiefly in Africa.
One of many families or subfamilies into which some classification systems subdivide the Liliaceae but not widely accepted.
At or on or to the masthead or upper rigging of a ship.
example: Climbed aloft to unfurl the sail.
etymology: From Old Norse á lopti (“in the sky”); equivalent to a- + loft.

definition: An acknowledgment that can be used to say hello or goodbye (aloha is Hawaiian and ciao is Italian).
example: When I got back to Hawaii, a feeling of aloha flooded me, and my anxiety vanished.
etymology: Borrowed from Hawaiian aloha (“love”), from Proto-Polynesian *qarofa. Doublet of aroha and aropa.

definition: Any high mountain.
etymology: Late Middle English, back-formation from alps pl, via French from Latin Alpes (“high mountains, especially those of Switzerland”). Compare Old Saxon elbon (“Alps”), Old High German Alpūn (“Alps”);

definition: Any of various drugs that block alpha-adrenergic receptors; used in treating benign prostatic hyperplasia; relaxes the muscles of the prostate and bladder.
Any of various drugs that block alpha-adrenergic receptors; used in treating benign prostatic hyperplasia; relaxes the muscles of the prostate and bladder.
Relating to or expressed by a writing system that uses an alphabet.
example: Alphabetical writing system.
etymology: From Latin alphabēticus + -al. By surface analysis, alphabet + -ical.

definition: In alphabetical order.
example: The list was arranged alphabetically.
etymology: From alphabetical + -ly.

definition: European mountain clover with fragrant usually pink flowers.
Whitish hairy plant with featherlike leaves and a few stout stems each bearing an especially handsome solitary large yellow flower head; mountainous regions north central United States.
Noisy quarrel.
example: To get into an altercation over (something).
etymology: Borrowed from Latin altercātiō. Cognates * Catalan altercació * Italian altercazione * Occitan altercatio, altercassion * Portuguese altercação * Spanish altercación

definition: In an alternating sequence or position.
example: They were deglycerolized by alternately centrifuging and mixing.
etymology: From alternate + -ly.

definition: A chloride used as a wood preservative or catalyst.
A salt of aluminium and nitric acid, existing normally as a crystalline hydrate, most commonly as aluminium nitrate nonahydrate, Al(NO3)3·9H2O.
The combination of two or more commercial companies.
etymology: From Medieval Latin amalgamātiō.

definition: Affect with wonder.
example: Your ability to speak six languages amazes me!

definition: The feeling that accompanies something extremely surprising.
example: We stared in amazement at the skills on display.
etymology: From amaze + -ment.

definition: Uncertain or unable to decide about what course to follow.
example: Was ambivalent about having children.
etymology: Back-formation from ambivalence, from German Ambivalenz, from Latin ambi- (“in two ways”) + valeō (“be strong”); equivalent to ambi- + -valent. Compare ambivert.

definition: A cadence (frequently ending church music) in which the chord of the subdominant precedes the chord of the tonic.
Of a moderate purple color.
etymology: From Middle English ametist, from Old French ametiste (French améthyste), from Ancient Greek ἀμέθυστος (améthustos, “not drunk”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + μεθύω (methúō, “to be drunk”), from μέθυ (méthu, “wine”).

definition: A white crystalline double sulfate of aluminum: the ammonium double sulfate of aluminum.
The ion NH4 derived from ammonia; behaves in many respects like an alkali metal ion.
etymology: From New Latin ammōnium. Equivalent to ammonia + -ium.

definition: The ion NH4 derived from ammonia; behaves in many respects like an alkali metal ion.
Any salt containing the NH 4 + ion, formed by the neutralization of ammonium hydroxide by an acid.
Relating to or characteristic of animals of the class Amphibia.
example: An amphibious vehicle.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀμφίβιος (amphíbios), from ἀμφί (amphí) + βίος (bíos, “life”).

definition: An airplane designed to take off and land on water.
An amphibious operation attacking a land base that is carried out by troops that are landed by naval ships.
A military action of coordinated land, sea, and air forces organized for an invasion.
example: MacArthur staged a massive amphibious landing behind enemy lines.

definition: A military operation by both land and sea forces.
A flat-bottomed motor vehicle that can travel on land or water.
Addition of extra material or illustration or clarifying detail.
example: A few remarks added in amplification and defense.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin amplificātiō.

definition: Increase in size, volume or significance.
example: Amplify the loudspeaker.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English amplifiyen, borrowed from Old French amplifier, borrowed from Latin amplificāre, from amplus (“abundant, ample”) + -ficō. By surface analysis, ample + -ify.

definition: Distortion that occurs when the output signal does not have a linear relation to the input signal.
A condition of disability resulting from the loss of one or more limbs.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French amputation, borrowed from Latin amputātiō (“pruning (of a tree)”).

definition: Occupy in an agreeable, entertaining or pleasant fashion.
example: The play amused the ladies.
etymology: This would make it a cognate of Dutch musen (“to leisure”), Old High German *muoza (“careful attention, leisure, idleness”) and muozōn (“to be idle, have leisure or opportunity”), German Muße (“leisure”). More at empty.

definition: The use of algebra to study geometric properties; operates on symbols defined in a coordinate system.
An instrument that performs analyses.
etymology: From analyze + -er.

definition: A political theory favoring the abolition of governments.
etymology: From anarchy + -ism.

definition: Of or relating to the structure of the body.
example: Anatomical features.
etymology: From anatomic + -al, after -ical. By surface analysis, anatomy + -ical.

definition: An expression that relates to anatomy.
A particular complex anatomical part of a living thing and its construction and arrangement.
People who lived in times long past (especially during the historical period before the fall of the Roman Empire in western Europe).
Furnishing added support.
example: An ancillary pump.
etymology: From Latin ancillāris (“ancillary; relating to female slaves”), from ancilla (“slave-woman”).

definition: Broad-leaved evergreen Asiatic shrub with glossy leaves and drooping clusters of white flowers.
etymology: From Andromeda.

definition: Having the character of an anecdote.
example: Anecdotal evidence.
etymology: From anecdote + -al.

definition: Short account of an incident (especially a biographical one).
example: Tell an anecdote.

definition: A deficiency of red blood cells.
example: Pernicious anemia and sickle-cell anemia are two anemias.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀναιμία (anaimía), from ἀν- (an-, “not”) + αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) -ία (-ía). By surface analysis, an- + -emia.

definition: Relating to or producing insensibility.
etymology: From an- + esthetic, or Latinized form of Ancient Greek ἀναίσθητος (anaísthētos, “insensible”) + -ic, from ἀν- (an-, “un-”) + αἰσθητικός (aisthētikós, “perceptible”).

definition: A drug that causes temporary loss of bodily sensations.
A cardiovascular disease characterized by a saclike widening of an artery resulting from weakening of the artery wall.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀνεύρυσμα (aneúrusma, “a widening, a dilation”), from ἀνευρύνω (aneurúnō, “to dilate”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + εὐρύς (eurús, “wide”).

definition: Again but in a new or different way.
example: Wanted to write the story anew.
etymology: From Middle English onew, of newe, from Old English of niowe. By surface analysis, a- (“of, from”) + new.

definition: Marked by utter benignity; resembling or befitting an angel or saint.
example: Angelic beneficence.

definition: Any of various tall and stout herbs of the genus Angelica having pinnately compound leaves and small white or greenish flowers in compound umbels.
Fishing with a hook and line (and usually a pole).
Black tropical American cuckoo.
etymology: Borrowed from Portuguese ani or Spanish aní, both from Old Tupi any.

definition: A blue dye obtained from plants or made synthetically.
Magnetic personal charm.
etymology: Calque of French magnétisme animal; 18th century. The pseudoscientific sense (sense 2) predates the sense that is now the more common one.

definition: Heighten or intensify.
A living organism characterized by voluntary movement.
A living (or once living) entity.
A feeling of ill will arousing active hostility.
example: There was open animosity between the two rival teams.
etymology: From French animosité, from Latin animositas (“courage, spirit, vehemence”), from animosus, from animus (“courage, spirit, mind”); see animose, animate.

definition: Destruction by annihilating something.
example: The annihilation of a corporation.
etymology: From Middle French annihilation, from Latin annihilātiō. By surface analysis, annihilate + -ion.

definition: (Latin) year.
etymology: From Latin per annum (“yearly”), from annus (“year”).

definition: A prolonged disorder of eating due to loss of appetite.
example: Intimacy anorexia; emotional anorexia.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνορεξία (anorexía), from ἀν- (an-, “not”, alpha privativum) + ὄρεξῐς (órexĭs, “yearning”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, abstract-noun-forming suffix).

definition: Indicating opposition or resistance.
etymology: From antagonist + -ic.

definition: (physiology) a muscle that opposes the action of another.
example: The biceps and triceps are antagonistic muscles.

definition: A highly infectious animal disease (especially cattle and sheep); it can be transmitted to people.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἄνθραξ (ánthrax, “abscess, boil”).

definition: A form of anthrax infection acquired by inhalation of dust containing Bacillus anthracis; initial symptoms (chill and cough and dyspnea and rapid pulse) are followed by extreme cardiovascular collapse.
Of or concerned with the science of anthropology.
example: Anthropological studies.
etymology: From anthropology + -ical.

definition: A social scientist who specializes in anthropology.
etymology: From anthropology + -ist.

definition: Any substance (as a toxin or enzyme) that stimulates an immune response in the body (especially the production of antibodies).
etymology: From French antigène, from anti- + gène.

definition: Capable of destroying or inhibiting the growth of disease-causing microorganisms.
etymology: From anti- + microbe + -ial.

definition: So extremely old as seeming to belong to an earlier period.
etymology: From antiquate + -ed.

definition: The intense dislike for and prejudice against Jewish people.
Shunning contact with others.
example: Standoffish and antisocial.
etymology: From anti- + social.

definition: A heavy block of iron or steel on which hot metals are shaped by hammering.
example: 1794, William Blake, “The Tyger,” lines 15-16, What the anvil? what dread grasp / Dare its deadly terrors clasp?

definition: With anxiety or apprehension.
example: We watched anxiously.
etymology: From anxious + -ly.

definition: The traditional dress of Vietnamese women consisting of a tunic with long sleeves and panels front and back; the tunic is worn over trousers.
etymology: Borrowed from Vietnamese áo dài.

definition: Of or relating to the aorta.
etymology: From aorta + -ic. By surface analysis, aort- + -ic.

definition: The part of the aorta that arches and turns downward.
A semilunar valve between the left ventricle and the aorta; prevents blood from flowing from the aorta back into the heart.
To or from every one of two or more (considered individually).
example: These melons cost a dollar apiece.
etymology: Univerbation of a + piece (noun), from Late Middle English a pece. Pece is derived from Anglo-Norman pece, peece, peice, Middle French piece, and Old French pece, pice, piece (“part of a whole”) (modern French pièce);

definition: Transient cessation of respiration.
etymology: From a- + -pnea, from the New Latin apnoea, from the Ancient Greek ἄπνοια (ápnoia), formed from ἀ- (a-, “absence of”) + πνοή (pnoḗ, “breathing”).

definition: Of or relating to or deriving from the Apostles or their teachings.
example: An apostolic mission.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin apostolicus (“apostolic”), from Ancient Greek ἀποστολικός (apostolikós, “apostolic”).

definition: (Roman Catholic Church) a representative of the Holy See in a country that has no formal diplomatic relations with it.
Struck with fear, dread, or consternation.
etymology: From appall + -ed.

definition: Cause to be more favorably inclined; gain the good will of.
example: To appease the tumult of the ocean.
etymology: From Middle English apesen, from Old French apeser (“to pacify, bring to peace”).

definition: A disease of apple trees.
Feeling or expressive of gratitude.
example: Was appreciative of his efforts.
etymology: From appreciate + -ive.

definition: Get the meaning of something.
example: Officers apprehended the suspect two streets away from the bank.
etymology: From Late Middle English apprehenden (“to grasp, take hold of; to comprehend; to learn”), from Old French apprehender (modern French appréhender (“to apprehend; to catch;

definition: Fearful expectation or anticipation.
example: The student looked around the examination room with apprehension.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin apprehensio, apprehensionis, compare with French appréhension. See apprehend.

definition: Quick to understand.
example: A kind and apprehensive friend.
etymology: From Latin apprehensīvus, from apprehensus, perfect passive participle of apprehendō (“to apprehend, understand, learn”) + -īvus (“-ive”).

definition: Inherent ability.
example: She showed an early aptitude for mathematics.
etymology: From Middle French aptitude, from Medieval Latin aptitudo, from Latin aptus (“apt, fit”). By surface analysis, apt + -itude. Doublet of attitude.

definition: With competence; in a competent capable manner.
example: An aptly named hotel.
etymology: From apt + -ly.

definition: Rearing aquatic animals or cultivating aquatic plants for food.
example: Finally, sturgeon aquaculture would create a sustainable industry […].
etymology: From aqua- + culture.

definition: Ferns that grow in water.
Whales and dolphins, manatees and dugongs, walruses, seals.
Similar to or containing or dissolved in water.
example: Aqueous solutions.
etymology: Formed from Latin aqua + -ous (or from Medieval Latin aqueus), partly the analogy of Middle French aqueux (itself actually from Latin aquosus). Or based on the analogy of Latin terreus from terra.

definition: The limpid fluid within the eyeball between the cornea and the lens.
The limpid fluid within the eyeball between the cornea and the lens.
A solution in water.
In a random manner.
example: The winner was chosen arbitrarily.
etymology: From arbitrary + -ly.

definition: The inverse function of the sine; the angle that has a sine equal to a given number.
The inverse function of the tangent; the angle that has a tangent equal to a given number.
An anthropologist who studies prehistoric people and their culture.
etymology: From archaeolog(y) + -ist. By surface analysis, archaeo- + -logist.

definition: The diocese of an archbishop.
etymology: Ultimately from Medieval Latin archdiocesis, variant of archidioecēsis, from archi- (“chief, main”) + Late Latin dioecēsis, q.v., equivalent to arch- + diocese.

definition: Constructed with or in the form of an arch or arches.
example: An arched passageway.

definition: (architecture) something added to a building to improve its appearance.
A simple light plough without a mouldboard.
etymology: Borrowed from Norwegian ard (“plough”), from Old Norse arðr, from Proto-Germanic *arþrą (“plough”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érh₃trom (“plough”), whence also Latin aratrum.

definition: Strong distilled liquor or brandy.
etymology: First attested 1471, from its inflammability; see etymology section of ardent.

definition: Characterized by effort to the point of exhaustion; especially physical effort.
example: Worked their arduous way up the mining valley.
etymology: From Latin arduus (“lofty, high, steep, hard to reach, difficult, laborious”), akin to Irish ard (“high”).

definition: Large brilliantly patterned East Indian pheasant.
etymology: Special use of Argus, a many-eyed mythological figure.

definition: Having very keen vision.
A privileged class holding hereditary titles.
Belonging to or characteristic of the nobility or aristocracy.
example: An aristocratic family.
etymology: From French aristocratique, from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατικός (aristokratikós). By surface analysis, aristo- + -cratic.

definition: A large fleet.
example: An armada of insects attacked us every day at sunset.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish armada (“fleet, navy”), from Medieval Latin armāta, from the feminine past participle of Latin armō, from arma. Doublet of army.

definition: A person of liberal ideals who takes no action to realize them.
Specially hardened steel plate used to protect fortifications or vehicles from enemy fire.
South American catfish having the body covered with bony plates.
A collection of resources.
example: He dipped into his intellectual armory to find an answer.

definition: Any property detected by the olfactory system.
example: I love the aroma of cinnamon.
etymology: From Late Latin arōmata (“spices”) (or arōma (“spice”)), from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma, “seasoning, spicy and/or fragrant smell”).

definition: The act of arousing.
example: The purpose of art is the arousal of emotions.
etymology: From arouse + -al.

definition: An acid formed from arsenic pentoxide.
The univalent group derived from arsine.
A French school of art and architecture popular in the 1890s; characterized by stylized natural forms and sinuous outlines of such objects as leaves and vines and flowers.
Blood found in arteries.
example: Except for the pulmonary artery the arterial blood is rich in oxygen.

definition: A fatty deposit inside an arterial wall; characteristic of atherosclerosis.
The pressure of the circulating blood on the arteries.
example: Arterial pressure is the product of cardiac output and vascular resistance.

definition: The aspect of pronunciation that involves bringing articulatory organs together so as to shape the sounds of speech.
example: The articulation allowed the robot to move around corners.
etymology: From Middle English articulacioun, from Old French articulacion, from Medieval Latin articulatio. Equivalent to articulate + -ion.

definition: An emergency procedure whereby breathing is maintained artificially.
A superior skill that you can learn by study and practice and observation.
etymology: From artist + -ry.

definition: Travel up.
example: We ascended the mountain.
etymology: From Middle English ascenden, borrowed from Old French ascendre, from Latin ascendō (“to go up, climb up to”), from ad (“to”) + scandō (“to climb”); see scan. Unrelated to accede other than common ad prefix.

definition: The branch of the ileocolic artery that supplies the ascending colon.
The part of the large intestine that ascends from the cecum to the transverse colon.
The point at which an orbit crosses the ecliptic plane going north.
A cravat with wide square ends; secured with an ornamental pin.
Of southern Europe; similar to but smaller than the adder.
example: Sexual Offences (Scotland) Act 2009 (2009 asp 9).
etymology: From Middle English aspe, from Old French aspe, from Latin aspis, aspidis (“asp, viper”), from Ancient Greek ἀσπίς (aspís, “shield; Egyptian cobra Naja haje”); compare Middle English aspide.

definition: South American bean having very long succulent pods.
A bed in which asparagus is growing.
Sprawling European annual having a 4-winged edible pod.
Someone who attacks.
etymology: From Old French assaillant, from the verb assaillir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“to, towards”) + salīre (“to jump”). Equivalent to assail + -ant.

definition: Agreement with a statement or proposal to do something.
example: He gave his assent eagerly.
etymology: From Middle English assent (noun) and assenten (verb), from Old French assent (noun) and assentir (verb), from Latin assentiō (whence as-).

definition: Aggressively self-assured.
example: An energetic assertive boy who was always ready to argue.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin assertīvus. Synchronically analyzable as assert + -ive.

definition: Take up mentally.
example: Food is assimilated and converted into organic tissue.
etymology: First attested in the early 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; Middle English assimilaten (“to become similar;

definition: Giving confidence.
A star-shaped character * used in printing.
example: They came into the tournament highly ranked, but with a little bit of an asterisk as their last two wins had been unconvincing.
etymology: Noun sense 1.1.2 (“something which is of little importance or which is marginal”) refers to the use of an asterisk to denote a footnote or marginal note in a text;

definition: Being or relating to or resembling or emanating from stars.
example: An astral body.
etymology: From Late Latin astrālis, from Latin astrum (“star”), from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “star”).

definition: Away from the right path or direction.
example: He was led astray.
etymology: From Middle English astraien or by apheresis straien, from Old French estraier (“to stray”), from late Medieval Latin extravagari (“to wander beyond”), from Latin extra (“beyond”) + vagārī (“to wander, stray”).

definition: A physicist who studies astronomy.
etymology: From Middle English astronomer, equivalent to astronomy + -er. Displaced native Old English tungolcræftiga.

definition: Marked by practical hardheaded intelligence.
example: An astute tenant always reads the small print in a lease.
etymology: From Latin astūtus, from astus (“craft”).

definition: Characterized by asymmetry in the spatial arrangement or placement of parts or components.
example: An asymmetric shape.
etymology: From a- + symmetric, as Ancient Greek ἀσυμμετρία (asummetría, “disproportion, deformity”).

definition: Characterized by asymmetry in the spatial arrangement or placement of parts or components.
etymology: From a- + symmetrical.

definition: Compensation for a wrong.
etymology: Perhaps from atone + -ment as translation of Medieval Latin adūnāmentum; however, the noun is found earlier than the verb (atone); and in this light, the proper etymology is at + onement.

definition: Any chamber that is connected to other chambers or passageways (especially one of the two upper chambers of the heart).
example: An atrium of the infundibula of the lungs.
etymology: From Latin ātrium (“entry hall”), from Etruscan.

definition: Shockingly brutal or cruel.
example: Murder is an atrocious crime.
etymology: From Latin atrōx (“cruel, fierce, frightful”) + -ious.

definition: The quality of being shockingly cruel and inhumane.
example: To carry out / commit / perpetrate an atrocity.
etymology: From Middle French atrocité, from Latin atrōcitās, from atrōx (“terrible, cruel”) + -tās, from āter (“matte black”).

definition: Capable of being attained or accomplished.
example: Choose an attainable goal.
etymology: From attain + -able.

definition: The act of achieving an aim.
example: The attainment of independence.
etymology: From attain + -ment; compare Old French ataignement.

definition: Established as genuine.
example: The word "slæpwerig" (sleep-weary) is attested in the Exeter Book in the form "slæpwerigne".

definition: Erosion by friction.
The rate of shrinkage in size or number.
Not representative of a group, class, or type.
example: A class of atypical mosses.
etymology: From a- + typical.

definition: An acute respiratory disease marked by high fever and coughing; caused by mycoplasma; primarily affecting children and young adults.
Served in its natural juices or gravy.
example: Roast beef au jus.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French au jus (“in the juice”).

definition: An agent who conducts an auction.
etymology: From auction + -eer.

definition: The field of forensic science relating to the acquisition, analysis, and evaluation of sound recordings that may ultimately be presented as admissible evidence in a court of law or some other official venue.
example: Emergency calls can be analyzed using audio forensics if the context and situation of the caller has to be identified.

definition: An inspection of the accounting procedures and records by a trained accountant or CPA.
All of the components of the organ of hearing including the outer and middle and inner ears.
Either of the passages in the outer ear from the auricle to the tympanic membrane.
Communication that relies on hearing.
The cortical area that receives auditory information from the medial geniculate body.
A mental image that is similar to an auditory perception.
A composite sensory nerve supplying the hair cells of the vestibular organ and the hair cells of the cochlea.
The perception of sound as a meaningful phenomenon.
The subjective sensation of hearing something.
Either of the paired tubes connecting the middle ears to the nasopharynx; equalizes air pressure on the two sides of the eardrum.
Enlarge or increase.
example: The recent speech of the president augmented tensions in the Near East.
etymology: From Middle English augmenten, from Middle French augmenter, from Old French augmenter, from Late Latin augmentare (“to increase”), from Latin augmentum (“an increase, growth”), from augere (“to increase”).

definition: The amount by which something becomes greater.
etymology: From Middle English augmentation, augmentacion, augmentacioun, from Old French augmentacion, from Latin augmentātiō, verbal noun from augmentō (“increase”, verb).

definition: The sister of your father or mother; the wife of your uncle.
etymology: From aunt + -y.

definition: Kindly endorsement and guidance.
example: The tournament was held under the auspices of the city council.

definition: Auguring favorable circumstances and good luck.
example: An auspicious beginning for the campaign.
etymology: From auspice + -ious, from Latin auspicium (“augury”), from auspex (“augur”), possibly via French.

definition: Severely simple.
example: The headmistress was an austere old woman.
etymology: From Ancient Greek αὐστηρός (austērós, “bitter, harsh, astringent”), having the specific meaning “making the tongue dry” (originally used of fruits, wines), related to αὔω (aúō, “to singe”), αὖος (aûos, “dry”).

definition: A document giving an official instruction or command.
A form of government in which the ruler is an absolute dictator (not restricted by a constitution or laws or opposition etc.).
etymology: From authoritarian + -ism.

definition: The act of creating written works.
example: It was a matter of disputed authorship.
etymology: From author + -ship.

definition: Of or relating to or characteristic of an autobiographer.
example: He seldom suppressed his autobiographical tendencies.
etymology: From autobiography + -ical or auto- + biographical.

definition: Of or relating to the immune response of the body against substance normally present in the body.
etymology: From auto- + immune.

definition: Severe diabetes mellitus with an early onset; characterized by polyuria and excessive thirst and increased appetite and weight loss and episodic ketoacidosis; diet and insulin injections are required to control the disease.
Any of a large group of diseases characterized by abnormal functioning of the immune system that causes your immune system to produce antibodies against your own tissues.
Any of a large group of diseases characterized by abnormal functioning of the immune system that causes your immune system to produce antibodies against your own tissues.
Make automatic or control or operate automatically.
example: Automatize the production.

definition: A cognitive state in which you act without self-awareness.
example: She talked and he dozed and my mind went on autopilot.
etymology: From auto- + pilot.

definition: An airfield that functions in a subsidiary capacity.
Radically new or original.
example: An avant-garde theater piece.
etymology: From Middle English advaunte-garde, avauntgard, from Old French avangarde, avant-garde, avantgarde, from avant (“before; in front”) + garde (“guard”). Doublet of vanguard and vaward

definition: Someone who takes vengeance.
example: An avenger of blood.
etymology: From Middle English avengere; equivalent to avenge + -er.

definition: (usually followed by ‘to’) strongly opposed.
example: Averse to taking risks.
etymology: From Latin aversus, past participle of avertere (“to avert”).

definition: Any technique of behavior modification that uses unpleasant stimuli in a controlled fashion to alter behavior in a therapeutic way; primarily used for alcoholism or drug abuse (but with little success).
Prevent the occurrence of; prevent from happening; to protect from or to keep away anything undesirable; to ward off.
example: Avert a strike.
etymology: From Middle English averten, adverten, from Old French avertir (“turn, direct, avert; turn the attention, make aware”), from Latin āvertere, from ab + vertō (“to turn”).

definition: Pertaining to or characteristic of birds.
etymology: From Latin avis (“bird”) + -ian.

definition: A pear-shaped tropical fruit with green or blackish skin and rich yellowish pulp enclosing a single large seed.
Unskillfulness resulting from a lack of training.
etymology: From awkward + -ness.

definition: Of or relating to or resembling an axis of rotation.
example: The axial skeleton.
etymology: From axis + -al.

definition: Rotary motion of an object around its own axis.
example: Wheels in axial rotation.

definition: A skeletal muscle of the trunk or head.
Rotary motion of an object around its own axis.
example: Wheels in axial rotation.

definition: The part of the skeleton that includes the skull and spinal column and sternum and ribs.
An axial flow turbine operates in the exactly reverse of an axial flow compressor,.
Any of numerous ornamental shrubs grown for their showy flowers of various colors.
etymology: Borrowed from translingual Azalea, from Ancient Greek ἀζαλέος (azaléos, “dry”), because it grows in dry soil; from ἄζω (ázō, “to dry up”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eHs-.

definition: A person engaged to care for children when the parents are not home.
Take watchful responsibility for.
example: My daughter is babysitting for the Morgans at number ten, who are going out on a date night.
etymology: Back-formation from babysitter.

definition: The work of a baby sitter; caring for children when their parents are not home.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: A young unmarried woman who lives alone.
etymology: From bachelor + -ette. Displaced maid.

definition: An undocumented way to get access to a computer system or the data it contains.
etymology: From back + door.

definition: Someone who provides financial support for some venture.
etymology: From back + -er.

definition: An accumulation of jobs not done or materials not processed that are yet to be dealt with (especially unfilled customer orders for products or services).
example: He went to work on Saturday to try to work through the backlog of papers on his desk.
etymology: From back + log. 1680s; originally a large log at the back of a fire. Figurative sense from 1880s, meaning "something stored up for later use". Possibly influenced by logbook as well.

definition: Carrying something in a pack on the back.
example: The backpacking of oxygen is essential for astronauts.
etymology: From backpack + -ing.

definition: A secondary or inferior position or status.
example: Tennis has had to take a backseat while his work is so demanding.
etymology: From back + seat.

definition: A meddler who insists on giving unwanted advice.
The side of an object that is opposite its front.
example: The building's backside faced an alley and was covered in grime and graffiti.
etymology: From back + side.

definition: Any endotoxin or exotoxin formed in or elaborated by bacterial cells.
Socially incorrect in behavior.
example: He was extremely bad-mannered and caused offence wherever he went.

definition: A light long-handled racket used by badminton players.
Making great mental demands; hard to comprehend or solve or believe.
example: A baffling problem.

definition: Coarse fabric used for bags or sacks.
example: Baggings used to cover cotton bales.

definition: Not fitting closely; hanging loosely.
example: Baggy trousers.
etymology: From bag + -y (adjectival suffix).

definition: A large pan that is filled with hot water; smaller pans containing food can be set in the larger pan to keep food warm or to cook food slowly.
etymology: Borrowed from French bain-marie, from Medieval Latin balneum Mariae (literally “Maria's bath”).

definition: Harassment especially of a tethered animal.
Wood of a deciduous conifer of the genus Taxodium, native to North America.
A skillful maneuver in catching balls or in stealing the ball from the opposing team.
Used of a player skilled in stealing the ball or robbing a batter of a hit.
example: A ball-hawking center fielder.
etymology: From ballhawk + -ing.

definition: Any heavy material used to stabilize a ship or airship.
etymology: From Middle English bar (“bare”) + last (“load”).

definition: A female ballet dancer.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian ballerina.

definition: A physical pendulum consisting of a large mass suspended from a rod; when it is struck by a projectile its displacement is used to measure the projectile's velocity.
The trajectory of an object in free flight.
Fast-growing sturdy Japanese fern; cultivated for their attractive broad dark-green pinnate fronds.
Identified with a band especially around a leg.
example: Kept watch for the return of their banded birds.

definition: North American butterfly with blue-black wings crossed by a broad white band.
(British informal) pork sausage.
Expel from a community or group.
example: He was banished from the kingdom for his crimes.
etymology: From Middle English banishen, from Old French baniss-, extended stem of banir (“to proclaim, ban, banish”), of Germanic origin and Old English bannan, from Proto-Germanic *bannaną (“curse, forbid”). Compare French bannir.

definition: Strong wire with barbs at regular intervals used to prevent passage.
Characterized by disorderly action and disregard for rules.
example: Undisguised bare-knuckle capitalism.

definition: Electronic jamming over a wide range of frequencies simultaneously.
Render unsuitable for passage.
example: Barricade the streets.
etymology: The noun is borrowed from French barricade, or an assimilation of the earlier barricado to the French form. The verb is from the noun or French barricader.

definition: An equal exchange.
example: We had no money so we had to live by barter.
etymology: Late Middle English, from Old French barater.

definition: Trade in in a bartering transaction.
Juicy yellow pear.
A sculptural relief in which forms extend only slightly from the background; no figures are undercut.
The commonest type of solidified lava; a dense dark grey fine-grained igneous rock that is composed chiefly of plagioclase feldspar and pyroxene.
etymology: From Late Latin basaltes, a misspelling of Latin basanites, from Ancient Greek βασανίτης (basanítēs), from βάσανος (básanos, “touchstone”), from Egyptian bḫn (“a hard stone”), b-x:n-O39

definition: Without a basis in reason or fact.
example: Baseless gossip.
etymology: From base + -less.

definition: Slag produced in making steel; low in silica but having large amounts of calcium phosphate; useful as fertilizer.
Perennial herb of North America (New York to Illinois and mountains of Alaska) having aromatic leaves and clusters of yellowish-pink balls.
An early Christian church designed like a Roman basilica; or a Roman Catholic church or cathedral accorded certain privileges.
example: The church was raised to the rank of basilica.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin basilica, from Ancient Greek βᾰσῐλῐκή (băsĭlĭkḗ), from βᾰσῐλῐκὴ στοά (băsĭlĭkḕ stoá, “royal hall”), ultimately from βασιλικός (basilikós, “royal”), from βασιλεύς (basileús, “king, chief”).

definition: Tropical American fern cultivated for its finely divided greyish-green foliage; West Indies and southern Mexico to Peru and Brazil.
A large clarinet whose range is an octave below the B-flat clarinet.
A musician who play the bass viol.
etymology: From bass + -ist.

definition: East Indian shrub.
Grey sea turtle of the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts of North America.
Old World star of Bethlehem having edible young shoots.
Cleanse the entire body.
example: Bathe daily.
etymology: From Middle English bathen, from Old English baþian (“to bathe, wash”), from Proto-West Germanic *baþōn, from Proto-Germanic *baþōną (“to bathe”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₁- (“to warm”).

definition: Swimsuit worn by men while swimming.
example: His bathing trunks were ruined and he didn't have another pair.

definition: A region where a battle is being (or has been) fought.
example: They made a tour of Civil War battlefields.
etymology: From battle + ground.

definition: Large and heavily armoured warship.
etymology: From battle + ship; shortened from line-of-battle ship, attested 1794.

definition: Small lynx of North America.
A swampy arm or slow-moving outlet of a lake (term used mainly in Mississippi and Louisiana).
etymology: From Louisiana French bayou, from Choctaw bayuk (“a creek”). Doublet of bogue.

definition: Any of various units of capacity.
example: Measured in 1000-bbl units.

definition: Be in motion due to some air or water current.

Beautiful spreading fern of eastern North America and eastern Asia naturalized in western Europe; pinnately divided fronds show a slight tendency to fold when touched; pinnules enclose groups of sori in beadlike lobes.
Covered with beads of liquid.
example: A face beaded with sweat.

definition: A small short-legged smooth-coated breed of hound.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English *begel (attested in the plural begles), of uncertain origin.

definition: Cheerful and bright.
example: A beaming smile.

definition: A blight of bean plants.
Any of various sprouted beans: especially mung beans or lentils or edible soybeans.
example: Bean sprouts are a nutritious vegetarian ingredient for stir-fry.

definition: Any of numerous wild or cultivated irises with hairlike structures on the falls (the drooping sepals).
A worker who rouses wild game from under cover for a hunter.
etymology: From Middle English beter, betere, bettere, from Old English bēatere (“a beater; boxer, fighter; champion”), equivalent to beat + -er. Related to beetle (“a type of mallet”).

definition: A shop where hairdressers and beauticians work.
A quark with a charge of -1/3 and a mass about 10,000 times that of an electron.
Perennial herb of North America.
etymology: Because bees are attracted to its nectar-rich blossoms.

definition: European orchid whose flowers resemble bumble bees in shape and color.
A burrito with a beef filling.
Strips of dried beef.
etymology: From beef + jerky.

definition: Someone whose favorite drink is beer or ale.
A barrel that holds beer.
Biennial Eurasian plant usually having a swollen edible root; widely cultivated as a food crop.
etymology: From Middle English beten, from Old English bētan.

definition: Young leaves of the beetroot.
Sugar made from sugar beets.
Be beyond the resources of.
example: This beggars description!
etymology: From Middle English beggere, beggare, beggar (“beggar”), from Middle English beggen (“to beg”), equivalent to beg + -ar.

definition: Having had the head cut off.

definition: After the expected or usual time; delayed.

etymology: From belate (verb) + -ed (suffix forming adjectives, and past tense and past participle forms of regular verbs).

definition: (used in the plural) a mechanical device that blows a strong current of air; used to make a fire burn more fiercely or to sound a musical instrument.

definition: Small bottom-dwelling fish of warm seas having a compressed body and a long snout with a toothless mouth.

etymology: From Middle English benefactor, borrowed from Medieval Latin benefactor (“he who bestows a favor”), from Latin benefaciō (“benefit someone”), from bene (“good”) + faciō (“do, make”).

definition: A tumor that is not cancerous.
Avens of Virginia having pale or greenish yellow flowers.
etymology: From Middle English *benet (found in Middle English herbe-benet (“hemlock”, literally “blessed plant”)), from Old French benëit, benoit and Latin (herba) benedicta. Doublet of benedict.

definition: North American fern often bearing bulbils on the leaflets.
Wildly frenzied and out of control.

etymology: The noun is borrowed from Old Norse berserkr (“Norse warrior who fights in a frenzy”), probably from bjǫrn (“bear”) + serkr (“coat; shirt”), referring to the bearskins which the warriors wore.

definition: Annoy continually or chronically.
(of clothing) custom-made.

etymology: In sense “custom-made”, 1755, from earlier bespoken (c. 1600), form of bespeak, in sense “arrange beforehand” (1580s), a prefixed variant of speak; compare order, made-to-order.

definition: Any of various drugs used in treating hypertension or arrhythmia; decreases force and rate of heart contractions by blocking beta-adrenergic receptors of the autonomic nervous system.
etymology: From action of drug which blocks beta-adrenergic receptors.

definition: A house of worship (especially one for sailors).
etymology: From Hebrew בֵּית אֵל (beth el, literally “house of God”). See also Bethel on Wikipedia.Wikipedia

definition: A change for the better; progress in development.
etymology: From better + -ment.

definition: Perplexed by many conflicting situations or statements; filled with bewilderment.

definition: Blindly and obstinately attached to some creed or opinion and intolerant toward others.

definition: A digestive juice secreted by the liver and stored in the gallbladder; aids in the digestion of fats.

(plural) an optical instrument designed for simultaneous use by both eyes.

definition: Appraisal of the biological activity of a substance by testing its effect on an organism and comparing the result with some agreed standard.

definition: A chemical mechanism involved in vital processes occurring in living organisms.
Someone who writes an account of a person's life.

definition: With respect to biology.

etymology: From biological + -ly.

definition: Nuclear transplantation of a patient's own cells to make an oocyte from which immune-compatible cells (especially stem cells) can be derived for transplant.
The branch of molecular biology that studies the use of microorganisms to perform specific industrial processes.
example: Biotechnology produced genetically altered bacteria that solved the problem.
etymology: Clipping of biotechnology. Analyzable as bio- (“biological”) + tech (“technology”) or as a clipped compound, bio(logical) tech(nology).

definition: A zoologist who studies birds.
A right or privilege that you are entitled to at birth.

etymology: From birth + right. Compare West Frisian berterjocht (“birthright”), Dutch geboorterecht (“birthright”), German Geburtsrecht (“birthright”). Compare also Icelandic frumburðarréttur (“birthright”).

definition: A small informal restaurant; serves wine.
etymology: Attested from c. 1920, from the French bistro(t) with the original meaning "proprietor of a tavern" (1880s), of unknown origin, presumably regional French dialect. See the French etymology for more.

definition: Marked by or arising from malice.

definition: Of or relating to plants or botany.
example: Botanical garden.
etymology: From the Medieval Latin botanicus, perhaps via the French botanique, from the Ancient Greek βοτανικός (botanikós), from βοτάνη (botánē, “herb, pasture”).

definition: Spoiled through incompetence or clumsiness.
A plant where beverages are put into bottles with caps.
example: The franchisee who owns the local Pepsi bottling company has had a bottling plant in this city since 1948.

Fern of eastern North America with pale green fronds and an aroma like hay.
A person whose duty is to throw troublemakers out of a bar or public meeting.

definition: Elastic; rebounds readily.
example: Clean bouncy hair.
etymology: From bounce + -y.

definition: Seemingly boundless in amount, number, degree, or especially extent.

definition: The social class between the lower and upper classes.

definition: Of or relating to or belonging to the genus Bos (cattle).
etymology: PIE word *gʷṓws Borrowed from Late Latin bovīnus (“relating to cattle”), from Latin bōs (“ox”). Cognate to beef.

definition: The center of the Earth.
example: Down in the bowels of the Earth.

definition: A framework that supports climbing plants.
etymology: From Middle English bour, from Old English būr, from Proto-West Germanic *būr, from Proto-Germanic *būrą (“room, abode”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Búur (“storage room, utility room;

definition: Bending the head or body or knee as a sign of reverence or submission or shame or greeting.

etymology: Borrowed from French braille, named after French educator Louis Braille (1809–1852). The /eɪl/ seems to reflect a spelling pronunciation; French has /aj/ instead.

Resembling a fork; divided or separated into two branches.

Having branches.
A sling made with brandy.

etymology: From brazen + faced. Compare typologically French front d’airain, Russian ме́дный лоб (médnyj lob).

definition: Having separated or advocating separation from another entity or policy or attitude.
example: A breakaway faction.

example: The breakfast nook had a built in table and seats.

definition: Uttered without voice.
example: Could hardly hear her breathed plea, ‘Help me’.
etymology: From breathe + -ed.

definition: A short respite.
example: After a short breather she was ready to continue up the hill.
etymology: From breathe + -er (agent noun suffix) or + -er (relational noun suffix).

definition: Not breathing or able to breathe except with difficulty.
example: Breathless at thought of what I had done.
etymology: From breath + -less.

definition: A nuclear reactor that produces more fissile material than it burns.
Fresh and animated.

Chilean evergreen shrub having delicate spikes of small white flowers.

European food fish.
