definition: A nonparticipant spectator.
etymology: From by- + stander. Compare passerby.

definition: A sequence of 8 bits (enough to represent one character of alphanumeric data) processed as a single unit of information.
example: The word “hello” fits into five bytes of ASCII code.
etymology: An alteration of the word bite so it would not be accidentally misspelled as bit. Coined by Werner Buchholz in 1956, during the early design phase for the IBM 7030 Stretch computer.

definition: A spot that is open late at night and that provides entertainment (as singers or dancers) as well as dancing and food and drink.
example: Don't expect a good meal at a cabaret.

definition: (prosody) the accent in a metrical foot of verse.
example: The cadence in a galliard step refers to the final leap in a cinquepace sequence.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French cadence, from Old Italian cadenza (“conclusion of a phrase of music”), from Latin *cadentia (literally “a falling”), form of cadēns, the present participle of cadō (“to fall, to cease”).

definition: A small unit serving as part of or as the nucleus of a larger political movement.
etymology: Borrowed from French cadre, from Italian quadro (“framed painting, square”), from Latin quadrum, from quattuor (“four”).

definition: Poisoning resulting from excessive intake of caffeine containing products.
An event resulting in great loss and misfortune.
example: The whole city was affected by the irremediable calamity.
etymology: From Middle French calamité, from Latin calamitās (“loss, damage; disaster”).

definition: Any of a class of drugs that block the flow of the electrolyte calcium (either in nerve cell conduction or smooth muscle contraction of the heart); has been used in the treatment of angina or arrhythmia or hypertension or migraine.
A salt found in nature as chalk or calcite or aragonite or limestone.
A deliquescent salt that is soluble in water; sometimes used as a source of nitrogen in fertilizers.
A white salt (CaSO4).
Marked with or divided into degrees.
example: A calibrated thermometer.

definition: A degree or grade of excellence or worth.
example: An executive of low caliber.

definition: The territorial jurisdiction of a caliph.
etymology: From Medieval Latin calīphātus, equivalent to caliph + -ate.

definition: Lets you transfer your incoming calls to any telephone that you can dial direct.
Beautiful handwriting.
Emotionally hardened.
example: A callous indifference to suffering.
etymology: From Latin callōsus (“hard-skinned”), from callum (“hardened skin”) + -ōsus.

definition: A tripod used to support a camera.
Fabric dyed with splotches of green and brown and black and tan; intended to make the wearer of a garment made of this fabric hard to distinguish from the background.
etymology: From camouflage, by shortening.

definition: A politician who is running for public office.
etymology: From campaign (verb) + -er (agent noun suffix) or from campaign (noun) + -er (occupational suffix).

definition: A trailer equipped for occupancy (especially for holiday trips).
A small outdoor fire for warmth or cooking (as at a camp).
etymology: From camp + fire.

definition: A site where people on holiday can pitch a tent.
etymology: From camp + ground.

definition: A site where people on holiday can pitch a tent.
etymology: From camp + site.

definition: A buoy with a round bottom and conical top.
The light provided by a burning candle.
etymology: From Middle English candel lyght, candyllyght, candyll-lyȝht, candel liȝt, candle lyȝt, candeliȝt, candel-liht, from Old English candel lēoht (“candlelight”), equivalent to candle + light.

definition: A thermometer used to determine the temperature of candy syrups during cooking.
A disease affecting the canes of various bush fruits (e.g., raspberries or currants).
A person who eats human flesh.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish caníbal, from Taíno caniba, the Taíno form recorded by Christopher Columbus for the Caribs, who were greatly feared.

definition: The practice of eating the flesh of your own kind.
etymology: From cannibal + -ism.

definition: Small American birch with peeling white bark often worked into e.g. baskets or toy canoes.
etymology: The Native Americans used the bark of this tree for building canoes.

definition: A flask for carrying water; used by soldiers or travelers.
example: He ordered a salad at the canteen.
etymology: Borrowed from French cantine, itself borrowed from Italian cantina. Doublet of cantina.

definition: The musical director of a choir.
example: The cantor's place in church is on the right of the choir.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin cantor, agent noun from canere (“to sing”) + -tor (agent suffix). Doublet of chanter.

definition: A shroud attached near the masthead that stays the mast against athwartship loads.
An electrical device characterized by its capacity to store an electric charge.
etymology: From capacity + -or. Capacitor replaced the term condenser (coined by Alessandro Volta in 1782) to disambiguate it from steam condenser.

definition: Microphone consisting of a capacitor with one plate fixed and the other forming the diaphragm moved by sound waves.
Microphone consisting of a capacitor with one plate fixed and the other forming the diaphragm moved by sound waves.
Much-branched South African plant with reddish prickly succulent leaves.
Writing in capital letters.
etymology: From capitalize + -ation.

definition: A manual or automatic device that is used to cap bottles.
Strongly attracted.
Capturing interest as if by a spell.
example: Roosevelt was a captivating speaker.
etymology: From captivate + -ing.

definition: A long truck for carrying motor vehicles.
Rolled dough spread with sugar and nuts then sliced and baked in muffin tins with honey or sugar and butter in the bottom.
A diet of foods high in starch that increases carbohydrate reserves in muscles.
example: Carbo loading is used by endurance athletes just before competing.

definition: Turn into a carbonate.
etymology: From French carbonate, equivalent of carbon + -ate (“suffix used for salts of acids ending in -ic”).

definition: Any malignant tumor derived from epithelial tissue; one of the four major types of cancer.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin carcinōma (“tumour; ulcer; carcinoma”), from Ancient Greek κᾰρκῐ́νωμᾰ (kărkĭ́nōmă, “sore, ulcer;

definition: A professional card player who makes a living by cheating at card games.
Knitted jacket that is fastened up the front with buttons or a zipper.
The branch of medicine dealing with the heart and its diseases.
etymology: From cardio- + -logy.

definition: Free of trouble and worry and care.
example: The carefree joys of childhood.

definition: A person who helps in identifying or preventing or treating illness or disability.
etymology: From care + giver.

definition: A representation of a person that is exaggerated for comic effect.
etymology: Borrowed from French caricature, from Italian caricatùra, ultimately from Latin carrus, and so not related to character, which is instead ultimately from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, “type, nature, character”).

definition: Tropical Old World shrub having purple or red tubular flowers and leaf markings resembling the profile of a human face.
A conveyer belt that carries luggage to be claimed by air travelers.
example: After collecting his suitcase at the baggage carousel, he left the airport.
etymology: From French carrousel, from Italian carosello, from Sicilian caruseḍḍu and/or Neapolitan carusiello. Uncertain.

definition: The lean flesh of a fish that is often farmed; can be baked or braised.
etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English carpen, karpe (“to chat, converse, talk; to chatter, gossip; to ask; to cry out, wail; to find fault, carp; to relate, tell; to recite;

definition: Implement for beating dust out of carpets.
etymology: From carpet + beater.

definition: Low footwear that can be slipped on and off easily; usually worn indoors.
A knot used to connect the ends of two large ropes or hawsers.
A list of dishes available at a restaurant.
etymology: Borrowed from French carte, from Latin charta. Doublet of card and chart.

definition: Any bone that develops within cartilage rather than a fibrous tissue.
The quantity contained in a carton.
etymology: Borrowed from French carton, from Italian cartone. Doublet of cartoon.

definition: A person who draws cartoons.
A workman who makes and repairs carts and wagons.
etymology: From Middle English cartewright, kartwryght, equivalent to cart + wright.

definition: Shrub with white woolly branches and woolly leaves having fragrant flowers forming long sprays; flowers suitable for drying; sometimes placed in genus Helichrysum.
etymology: From cascade (from the region the plant grows in) + everlasting (species in genus "Ozothamnus").

definition: A number of transformers in series; provides a high-voltage source.
An unattended machine (outside some banks) that dispenses money when a personal coded card is used.
For which money has been paid.
example: A cashed check.

definition: A soft fabric made from the wool of the Cashmere goat.
example: A cashmere sweater.
etymology: Appellativization of Cashmere.

definition: Food cooked and served in a casserole.
example: A chicken casserole.
etymology: Borrowed from French casserole.

definition: A recorder for recording or playing cassettes.
A worker who casts molten metal into finished products.
example: A caster of spells.
etymology: From cast + -er; the wheel sense comes from obsolete cast (“to turn”).

definition: Very finely granulated sugar that was formerly sprinkled from a castor.
A shaker with a perforated top for sprinkling powdered sugar.
etymology: Named from Greek mythology; see Castor and Pollux. The name pollux was given to another mineral with which it was always found.

definition: The toxic seed of the castor-oil plant; source of castor oil.
A purgative extracted from the seed of the castor-oil plant; used in paint and varnish as well as medically.
etymology: From its medicinal use in succession to castor.

definition: Very finely granulated sugar that was formerly sprinkled from a castor.
Mediterranean germander having small hairy leaves and reddish purple flowers; attractive to cats.
Relating to or causing or involving catalysis.
example: Catalytic reactions.

definition: A converter that uses a platinum-iridium catalyst to oxidize pollutants and carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide and water; an antipollution device on an automotive exhaust system.
A chemical reactor for converting oils with high boiling points into fuels with lower boiling points in the presence of a catalyst.
A plaything consisting of a Y-shaped stick with elastic between the arms; used to propel small stones.
etymology: From Middle French catapulte, from Latin catapulta, from Ancient Greek καταπέλτης (katapéltēs), from κατά (katá, “downwards, into, against”) + πάλλω (pállō, “to poise or sway a missile before it is thrown”).

definition: A structure in which water is collected (especially a natural drainage area).
etymology: From catch + -ment.

definition: The entire geographical area drained by a river and its tributaries; an area characterized by all runoff being conveyed to the same outlet.
In an unqualified manner.
example: A welfare scheme for the categorically needy.
etymology: From categorical + -ly.

definition: Slanted across a polygon on a diagonal line.
An endless metal belt on which tracked vehicles move over the ground.
A thin flexible tube inserted into the body to permit introduction or withdrawal of fluids or to keep the passageway open.
A negatively charged electrode that is the source of electrons entering an electrical device.
etymology: From Ancient Greek κατα- (kata-, “down”) and ὁδός (hodós, “journey, way”), equivalent to Ancient Greek κάθοδος (káthodos, “way down, descent”).

definition: A beam of electrons emitted by the cathode of an electrical discharge tube.
A very large pot that is used for boiling.
example: A cauldron of discontent.
etymology: From Middle English caudroun, borrowed from Old Northern French caudron, ultimately from Late Latin caldāria (“cooking-pot”), from Latin caldus (“hot”). Spelling later Latinized by having an l inserted.

definition: A plant having a large edible head of crowded white flower buds.
etymology: From 16th century cole-florye, equivalent to cole (from Latin caulis) + flower, reformed to more closely match the Latin etymon. By surface analysis, caul(is) + -i- + flower.

definition: An auricle deformed by injury; common among boxers.
A soup made from cauliflower.
example: This rich and creamy cauliflower soup is just the thing on a chilly day - and it's inexpensive too.

definition: The act of causing something to happen.
etymology: From cause + -ation.

definition: Provide with a causeway.
example: A causewayed swamp.

definition: Given to haughty disregard of others.
etymology: First appears c. 1562 in a translation by Peter Whitehorne.

definition: A soft felt hat with a wide flexible brim.
A warning against certain acts.
example: A caveat against unfair practices.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin caveat (“may he/she/it beware”), third-person singular present active subjunctive of caveō (“to beware of”).

definition: Any large dark enclosed space.
example: His eyes were dark caverns.
etymology: From Middle English caverne, borrowing from Old French caverne, from Latin caverna (“hollow, cavity, cave”), from cavus (“hollow, excavated, concave”).

definition: Hollow out as if making a cavern.
Salted roe of sturgeon or other large fish; usually served as an hors d'oeuvre.
A semiaquatic reptile of Central and South America that resembles an alligator but has a more heavily armored belly.
Being one hundred more than two hundred.
Elm of southern United States and Mexico having spreading pendulous corky branches.
African tree having rather lightweight cedar-scented wood varying in color from pink to reddish brown.
Smelling like cedar.
Used for celebrating.
etymology: From celebrate + -ory.

definition: Plant with an elongated head of broad stalked leaves resembling celery; used as a vegetable in east Asia.
The great circle on the celestial sphere midway between the celestial poles.
A polysaccharide that is the chief constituent of all plant tissues and fibers.
Transparent or semitransparent adhesive tape (trade names Scotch tape and Sellotape) used for sealing or attaching or mending.
Someone who collects census data by visiting individual homes.
The person who plays center field.
example: The center fielder made a spectacular sliding catch.

definition: The central or most important feature.
example: Education was the centerpiece of the Democratic Party's political platform.
etymology: From center + piece.

definition: Supporting or pursuing a course of action that is neither liberal nor conservative.
etymology: From French centriste, equivalent to centre + -ist.

definition: (ancient Rome) the leader of 100 soldiers.
etymology: From Middle English centurioun, from Latin centuriō, centuriōnis (“a commander of a hundred, centurion”), from Latin centum (“a hundred”).

definition: A loss or deficiency of motor control with involuntary spasms caused by permanent brain damage present at birth.
An absolute certainty.
example: It's a dead cert.

definition: Provide evidence for; stand as proof of; show by one's behavior, attitude, or external attributes.
etymology: From Old French certefier (“confirm, assure, make certain”). Compare French certifier.

definition: An artery that supplies the muscles of the neck.
Mucus-secreting glands in the mucosa of the uterine cervix.
A sample of secretions and superficial cells of the uterine cervix and uterus; examined with a microscope to detect any abnormal cells.
The part of an organism (human or animal) that connects the head to the rest of the body.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin cervīx (“neck”), see below.

definition: Portable power saw; teeth linked to form an endless chain.
example: He used a chainsaw to cut through the fallen tree on the roadway.
etymology: Compound of chain + saw in reference to the chain-cutting mechanism.

definition: The officer who presides at the meetings of an organization.
example: Address your remarks to the chairperson.
etymology: From chair + person, after chairman and chairwoman.

definition: A Swiss house with a sloping roof and wide eaves or a house built in this style.
etymology: Borrowed from French chalet, from Franco-Provençal çhalè (“herdsman's hut in the mountains”).

definition: A bowl-shaped drinking vessel; especially the Eucharistic cup.
etymology: From Middle English chalis, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French chalice, collateral form of calice, borrowed from Latin calix, calicem (“cup”), of uncertain etymology.

definition: Extensive tract of level open land.
etymology: From Old French champaigne, from Late Latin campānia.

definition: Branched lighting fixture; often ornate; hangs from the ceiling.
etymology: Borrowed from French chandelier, from Latin candelabrum, from candela (“a candle”). Doublet of candelabrum. See also candle.

definition: Musical notation for Gregorian chant, traditionally written using neumes.
example: This is a description of the traditional Gregorian Chant notation, so that anyone will be able to read the notation and sing it.

definition: A quark with an electric charge of +2/3 and a mass 2900 times that of an electron and a charm of +1.
A person who is pursuing and trying to overtake or capture.
example: Straight, no chaser.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English chaser, chacer, chasour, borrowed from Old French chaceür, chaceor, from chacier (“to chase, hunt”); later senses from or influenced by chase (“pursue”) + -er. Doublet of chasseur.

definition: A person paid to drive a privately owned car.
Someone who leads you to believe something that is not true.
etymology: From cheat + -er. The sense referring to welding hood lenses was inspired by cheaters (plural) as a pair of reading glasses.

definition: The part of a check that is retained as a record.
An attendant who checks coats or baggage.
example: There was a long line at the grocery store because the checker was so slow.
etymology: From check + -er.

definition: A board having 64 squares of two alternating colors.
A checkerboard game for two players who each have 12 pieces; the object is to jump over and so capture the opponent's pieces.
Bright and pleasant; promoting a feeling of cheer.
example: A cheery hello.
etymology: From Middle English cheri, equivalent to cheer + -y.

definition: A hamburger with melted cheese on it.
etymology: Blend of cheese + hamburger (1928). By surface analysis, cheese + -burger.

definition: Made with sweetened cream cheese and eggs and cream baked in a crumb crust.
With chemicals.
example: Chemically fertilized.
etymology: From chemical + -ly.

definition: An overstuffed davenport with upright armrests.
etymology: From Chesterfield. Named after Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield (1694–1773), who commissioned the first such couch.

definition: A disease of American chestnut trees.
Chicken cooked and served in a casserole.
Chicken excreta used as fertilizer.
Without offspring.
example: In some societies a childless woman is rejected by her tribesmen.
etymology: From Middle English childles; equivalent to child + -less.

definition: Plant bearing very hot and finely tapering long peppers; usually red.
A percussion instrument consisting of a set of tuned bells that are struck with a hammer; used as an orchestral instrument.
example: Hugo had a recording of someone playing the chimes against a background of surf noise that she found calming.
etymology: From Middle English chymbe, chyme, probably from Old Northern French chimbe (“cymbal”), a back-formation from chimble, cimble, from Latin cymbalum;

definition: Break into a conversation.
example: Her husband always chimes in, even when he is not involved in the conversation.

definition: A coarse twilled cotton fabric frequently used for uniforms.
etymology: A term used by American veterans of the Spanish-American war. It is theorized that the cloth or the trousers were made in China.

definition: A ripe jalapeno that has been dried for use in cooking.
etymology: From Spanish chipotle, from Classical Nahuatl chīlpōctli, compound of chīlli (“pepper”) + pōctli (“smoke”).

definition: The act of chipping something.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: A dismissive term for a girl who is immature or who lacks respect.
example: She was incensed that this chit of a girl should dare to make a fool of her in front of the class.
etymology: From Middle English chitte (“a young animal, cub, whelp”), from Old English *ċytten, *ċietten, *ċitten, from Proto-West Germanic *kittīn, from Proto-Germanic *kittīną (“young animal, fawn, kid”).

definition: Light informal conversation for social occasions.
Light informal conversation for social occasions.
etymology: Reduplication of chat. Compare tittle-tattle, flim-flam, pitter-patter, etc.

definition: Courtesy towards women.
Creamy chocolate candy.
etymology: From chocolate + truffle, so called because it resembles a black truffle, but is composed of chocolate.

definition: Related to or written for or performed by a chorus or choir.
example: Choral composition.
etymology: From Late Latin choralis, from Latin chorus.

definition: A specific piece of work required to be done as a duty or for a specific fee.
example: The farmer's morning chores.
etymology: Possibly derived from Romani ćor (“thief”), see also Geordie word chor.

definition: Someone who creates new dances.
etymology: From choreograph + -er.

definition: Breed of medium-sized dogs with a thick coat and fluffy curled tails and distinctive blue-black tongues; believed to have originated in northern China.
A violet-colored salt used in hide tanning and as a mordant in dyeing.
A hard brittle multivalent metallic element; resistant to corrosion and tarnishing.
etymology: From New Latin, from French chrome (from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”)) + -ium. So called because of the striking colors of its compounds.

definition: Steel containing chromium that makes it resistant to corrosion.
Plate with chromium.
example: Chrome bathroom fixtures.

definition: Eczema characterized by thickening of the skin with accentuated skin lines.
In a habitual and longstanding manner.
example: Smoking chronically.
etymology: From chronic + -ally.

definition: An arrangement of events in time.
example: The film's chronology is not entirely obvious, but can be worked out by the clothes the characters are wearing in the scenes.
etymology: From chrono- (“relating to time”) + -logy (“study of, account of”), after New Latin chronologia from Ancient Greek χρόνος (khrónos, “time”) + λόγος (lógos, “reason, explanation”). Literally "time reason" in Modern Greek.

definition: A type of wide heel that is usually square; comes in various heights.
Stir (cream) vigorously in order to make butter.
example: Now the cream is churned to make butter.
etymology: Noun from Middle English chyrne, cherne, kyrne ( > Scots kirn), from Old English ċyrn, ċyrin, ċirin (“churn”), from Proto-Germanic *kirnijǭ (“churn”);

definition: Perform in a mechanical way.
example: Barbara Cartland was renowned for her ability to churn out romantic novels.

definition: Cause aversion in; offend the moral sense of.
example: Just the footfall will churn up the wet turf.

definition: Moving with or producing or produced by vigorous agitation.
example: Winds whipped the piled leaves into churning masses.

definition: Rescue equipment consisting of a device that fills with air and retards your fall.
etymology: From French chute.

definition: A linear unit of the size of type slightly larger than an em.
etymology: From its use in Pannartz and Sweynheim's Roman edition (1467) of Cicero's Epistulae ad Familiares ("Letters to My Friends").

definition: A smoker of cigars.
The act of making a film.
etymology: From cinematograph + -y. Compare French cinématographie. Possibly analysable as cinemato- + -graphy.

definition: New World fern having woolly cinnamon-colored spore-bearing fronds in early spring later surrounded by green fronds; the early uncurling fronds are edible.
Smelling of cinnamon.
A message written in a secret code.
example: A painter's cipher.
etymology: 14th century. From Middle English cifre, from Old French cyfre, cyffre (French chiffre), ultimately from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “zero, empty”), from صَفَرَ (ṣafara, “to be empty”). Doublet of chiffre and zero.

definition: Electronic equipment consisting of a system of circuits.
etymology: From circuit + -ry.

definition: Become widely known and passed on.
example: To circulate money or gossip.

definition: A decimal with a sequence of digits that repeats itself indefinitely.
The act of circumcising performed on males eight days after birth as a Jewish and Muslim religious rite.
example: The ancient Egyptians practiced circumcision by creating a dorsal incision in the foreskin.
etymology: From Middle English circumcisioun, from Old French circumcisiun (modern French circoncision) and its etymon Latin circumcīsiō, from circumcīdō (“cut around”), from circum (“about, around; through”) + caedō (“cut, hew”).

definition: The size of something as given by the distance around it.
etymology: From Latin circumferentia, from circum (“around”) + ferō (“to carry”). Displaced native Old English ymbgang.

definition: Fully detailed and specific about particulars.
example: A circumstantial report about the debate.
etymology: From Latin circumstantia + English -al, equivalent to circumstance + -ial.

definition: Surround so as to force to give up.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin circumveniō.

definition: A financier who works in one of the banks in the City of London.
Having a high state of culture and development both social and technological.
example: Terrorist acts that shocked the civilized world.

definition: Formal or perfunctory politeness.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin civilitas: compare French civilité. English equivalent civil + -ity.

definition: Someone who claims a benefit or right or title.
example: Claimants of unemployment compensation.
etymology: From Old French and Anglo-Norman clamant, present participle of the verb clamer and its variants, from Latin clāmō (“to cry out”), equivalent to claim + -ant. Compare clamant.

definition: A dip made of clams and soft cream cheese.
Refuse to talk or stop talking; fall silent.
etymology: By analogy with a clam closing itself. Compare clamshell (“mouth”), clam (“mouth”).

definition: Informal terms for money.
Conducted with or marked by hidden aims or methods.
example: Clandestine intelligence operations.
etymology: From Latin clandestīnus (“secret, concealed”); compare French clandestin.

definition: Worn from age or heavy use and no longer able to operate (of cars or machines or people).
That makes clear.
example: A clarifying example.

definition: A single-reed instrument with a straight tube.
The section of a band or orchestra that plays clarinets.
Hold firmly and tightly.
example: They clasped hands and parted as friends.
etymology: Noun dated ca. 1300 and verb dated ca. 1400;

definition: A large knife with one or more folding blades.
Smoothly and without difficulty; precisely and deftly.
example: She played the piano accompaniment cleanly.
etymology: From Middle English clenly, clenliche, clanly, from Old English clǣnlīċ (“cleanly, pure, excellent”), equivalent to clean + -ly.

definition: A preparation used in cleaning something.
etymology: From Middle English clansere, clenser, clensere; equivalent to cleanse + -er.

definition: The fluid-filled cavity inside a blastula.
A butcher's knife having a large square blade.
etymology: From Middle English clevere, equivalent to cleave + -er.

definition: Large swift fly the female of which sucks blood of various animals.
A male member of the clergy and a spiritual leader of the Christian Church.
etymology: From clergy + -man.

definition: In a clever manner.
example: They were cleverly arranged.
etymology: From clever + -ly.

definition: A trite or obvious remark.
Customers collectively.
example: They have an upper class clientele.
etymology: Borrowed from French clientèle, ultimately from Latin cliēns (English client).

definition: Of or relating to a climate.
example: Climatic changes.
etymology: From climate + -ic.

definition: Any of the geographical zones loosely divided according to prevailing climate and latitude.
Twining shrub of North America having yellow capsules enclosing scarlet seeds.
Any of several ferns of the genus Lygodium that climb by twining.
A small perch of India whose gills are modified to allow it to breathe air; has spiny pectoral fins that enable it to travel on land.
Closed or squeezed together tightly.
example: His clenched (or clinched) teeth.

definition: (neurology) the branch of medicine that deals with the nervous system and its disorders.
A mercury thermometer designed to measure the temperature of the human body; graduated to cover a range a few degrees on either side of the normal body temperature.
(electronics) a nonlinear electronic circuit whose output is limited in amplitude; used to limit the instantaneous amplitude of a waveform (to clip off the peaks of a waveform).
etymology: From Middle English clipper, equivalent to clip (“cut, shorten”) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns). The type of sailing ship is probably also from clip, in the sense of “move or run rapidly”.

definition: A fast sailing ship used in former times.
An excerpt cut from a newspaper or magazine.
example: He searched through piles of letters and clippings.
etymology: By surface analysis, clip + -ing.

definition: An exclusive circle of people with a common purpose.
example: This school used to be really friendly, but now everyone keeps to their own cliques.
etymology: The noun is borrowed from French clique (“exclusive group of individuals; (archaic or obsolete) group of people hired to applaud or boo, claque”), from cliquer (“to clap;

definition: A physical pendulum used to regulate a clockwork mechanism.
A worker preoccupied with the arrival of quitting time.
In the same direction as the rotating hands of a clock.
example: In the southern hemisphere the flow of air around a low-pressure system is clockwise.
etymology: From clock + -wise.

definition: Rotation to the right.
Any mechanism of geared wheels that is driven by a coiled spring; resembles the works of a mechanical clock.
etymology: From clock + -work.

definition: The view that the universe resembles a clock built by God and ticking along according to Newtonian mechanics.
A general term for the research activity that creates a copy of some biological entity (a gene or organism or cell).
A feeling of being intimate and belonging together.
example: Their closeness grew as the night wore on.
etymology: From close + -ness.

definition: Change from a liquid to a thickened or solid state.
etymology: From Middle English clot, clotte, from Old English clott, from Proto-West Germanic *klott (“lump”). Cognate with German Klotz (“block”). Doublet of clod and klutz.

definition: A kind of pharmaceutical that can break up clots blocking the flow of blood to the heart muscle.
A dryer that dries clothes wet from washing.
A hanger that is shaped like a person's shoulders and used to hang garments on.
Made troubled or apprehensive or distressed in appearance.
example: His face was clouded with unhappiness.
etymology: From cloud + -ed.

definition: A target used in archery.
etymology: From Middle English clout (“piece of cloth”), from Old English clūt (“piece of cloth, patch;

definition: A short nail with a flat head; used to attach sheet metal to wood.
Any of several water ferns of the genus Marsilea having four leaflets.
Growing close together but not in dense mats.
A grouping of a number of similar things.
example: A cluster of admirers.

definition: The act of grasping.
example: Once the organization was in his clutches, her future there was bleak.

definition: A confused multitude of things.
etymology: From Middle English cloteren (“to form clots; coagulate; heap on”), from clot (“clot”), equivalent to clot + -er (frequentative suffix). Compare Welsh cludair (“heap, pile”), cludeirio (“to heap”).

definition: Fill a space in a disorderly way.
example: Why do you clutter up your mind with such useless knowledge?

definition: The codefendant charged with adultery with the estranged spouse in a divorce proceeding.
A chute for coal.
Having coarse hair or fur.
Lofty evergreen of United States coastal foothills from Oregon to Big Sur; it flourishes in wet, rainy, foggy habitats.
A hanger that is shaped like a person's shoulders and used to hang garments on.
Nut of any of several trees of the genus Corylus.
example: Here is also the pica marina or seapye many sorts of Lari, seamewes & cobs.
etymology: Of uncertain origin. The word has many disparate senses, which are likely of diverse origin. The specifics of these origins have long been debated, as has the question of which senses arise from which origins.

definition: Any of numerous chiefly nocturnal insects; some are domestic pests.
A shaker for mixing cocktails.
Small tropical American tree bearing edible plumlike fruit.
Retreat as if into a cocoon, as from an unfriendly environment.
example: Families cocoon around the T.V. set most evenings.
etymology: From French cocon, a diminutive of coque (“shell”).

definition: An official list of chemicals or medicines etc.
example: The French codex.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōdex, variant form of caudex (“tree trunk, book, notebook”); compare caudex (in botany). Doublet of code.

definition: Coexist peacefully, as of nations.
example: Peacefully coexist.
etymology: From co- + exist. Compare Latin coexsistō.

definition: A blight affecting the coffee plant.
An urn in which coffee is made and kept hot.
A subordinate who performs an important but routine function.
example: He was a small cog in a large machine.
etymology: See also dialectal English cag (“stump”), keg; Old Norse kaggi (“keg”) + -gi (diminutive suffix), from the Germanic base *kagô (“bush, branch, stalk, stump”); also found in Bavarian Kag (“the stalk or stem of a cabbage”);

definition: Coins collectively.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English coynage, from Old French coignage, from coignier. By surface analysis, coin + -age.

definition: Happening at the same time.
etymology: From coincidental + -ly.

definition: A cathode that is a source of electrons without being heated.
An oval large stadium with tiers of seats; an arena in which contests and spectacles are held.
example: The London Coliseum.
etymology: From Medieval Latin coliseum, from Latin Colosseum, from neuter of colosseus (“gigantic”), from Ancient Greek κολοσσιαῖος (kolossiaîos), from κολοσσός (kolossós, “giant statue”). See also: w:Colosseum § Name on Wikipedia.

definition: Someone who assists in a plot.
A disease affecting the trunks of pear and apple trees.
Subject to or requiring payment especially as specified.
example: A collectible bill.
etymology: From collect + -ible.

definition: The timbre of a musical sound.
example: The recording fails to capture the true color of the original music.
etymology: From French coloration, from Latin colōrātiō.

definition: Lacking in variety and interest.
example: A colorless and unimaginative person.
etymology: From color + -less.

definition: Someone that is abnormally large and powerful.
etymology: From Latin colossus, from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós, “large statue, especially the colossus of Rhodes”), from an unknown Pre-Greek etymon (and erroneously associated with κολοφών).

definition: A digestible substance used to give color to food.
Any material used for its color.
The act of drawing a comb through hair.
example: My hair needs frequent combings; otherwise, it gets matted.

definition: Made comfortable or more comfortable in a time of distress.
example: The news make her feel comforted.

definition: Arousing or provoking laughter.
example: A comic hat.
etymology: From Middle English comicalle, from Latin cōmicus + Middle English -alle (modern -al). By surface analysis, comic + -al.

definition: Anglewing butterfly with a comma-shaped mark on the underside of each hind wing.
An officer in command of a military unit.
etymology: From French commandant.

definition: Something that is commanded.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English comaundement, from Old French comandement, from comander. See command.

definition: Intended as a commemoration.
example: A commemorative plaque.

definition: Intended as a commemoration.
example: A commemorative plaque.
etymology: First attested in 1612; borrowed from New Latin commemorātīvus, from commemorō. By surface analysis, commemorate + -ive, cognate with French commémoratif.

definition: Worthy of high praise.
example: A commendable sense of purpose.

definition: An official award (as for bravery or service) usually given as formal public statement.
example: Letter of commendation.
etymology: From Middle English commendacioun, from Old French commendacion (“approval, praise”), from Latin commendatio (“recommendation, commendation”), from commendare.

definition: Biennial Eurasian plant usually having a swollen edible root; widely cultivated as a food crop.
An integer that is a common multiple of the denominators of two or more fractions.
example: Least common denominator.

definition: Eels that live in fresh water as adults but return to sea to spawn; found in Europe and America; marketed both fresh and smoked.
Densely branching shrub or small tree having pungent blue berries used to flavor gin; widespread in Northern Hemisphere; only conifer on coasts of Iceland and Greenland.
Large European lilac naturalized in North America having heart-shaped ovate leaves and large panicles of highly fragrant lilac or white flowers.
Of northern Eurasia.
Important food fish of the northern Atlantic and Mediterranean; its body is greenish-blue with dark bars and small if any scales.
Small semiaquatic salamander.
Gregarious bird having plumage with dark metallic gloss; builds nests around dwellings and other structures; naturalized worldwide.
etymology: Calque of translingual Sturnus vulgaris, via common + starling.

definition: Common aromatic garden perennial native to the western Mediterranean; used in seasonings and formerly as medicine.
A disorderly outburst or tumult.
etymology: From Middle French commocion, from Latin commōtiōnem, accusative singular of commōtiō, from commoveō + -tiō.

definition: A publication containing a variety of works.
etymology: From the Latin compendium (“that which is weighed together; a sparing, a saving, an abbreviation”), from com- (“with”) + pendō (“to weigh”).

definition: In competition.
example: The companies should bid competitively.
etymology: From competitive + -ly.

definition: The feeling you have when you are satisfied with yourself.
example: His complacency was absolutely disgusting.
etymology: Late Middle English complacence, from Late Latin complacentia. Compare French complaisance.

definition: Contented to a fault with oneself or one's actions.
example: He had become complacent after years of success.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin complacēns (“very pleasing”), present participle of complacēre (“to please at the same time, be very pleasing”), from com- (“together”) + placēre (“to please”); see please and compare complaisant.

definition: A person who brings an action in a court of law.
example: 1708-1714 Jeremy Collier, Ecclesiastical History of Great Britain Eager complainants […] in the dispute.
etymology: From Old French complaignant, present participle of complaindre.

Involved with others in an activity that is unlawful or morally wrong.
Guilt as an accomplice in a crime or offense.

etymology: From French complicité, from Middle French, from Old French complice (“accomplice”), from Late Latin complic-, stem of complex (“partner, confederate”), from Latin complicō (“fold together”).

definition: A mixture of decaying vegetation and manure; used as a fertilizer.
example: Dig plenty of compost into clay or sandy soil to improve its structure.
etymology: From Middle English compost, from Old Northern French compost (“a mixture of leaves, manure, etc., for fertilizing land, also a condiment”), from Latin compositus (“composed”), from componere.

definition: A heap of manure and vegetation and other organic residues that are decaying to become compost.
A heap of manure and vegetation and other organic residues that are decaying to become compost.
Steadiness of mind under stress.
example: He accepted their problems with composure and she with equanimity.
etymology: From compose + -ure.

definition: Pendulum consisting of an actual object allowed to rotate freely around a horizontal axis.
The act of combining things to form a new whole.

definition: Make more compact by or as if by pressing.

definition: Bandage that stops the flow of blood from an artery by applying pressure.
Someone who maintains and audits business accounts.

definition: An urge to do or say something that might be better left undone or unsaid.

definition: Curving inward.

definition: Excuse, overlook, or make allowances for; be lenient with.

definition: Set up for a particular purpose.

definition: A bounded scope.

Summon into action or bring into existence, often as if by magic.
example: He conjured wild birds in the air.

Keep company with; hang out with.

definition: Irregular and infrequent or difficult evacuation of the bowels; can be a symptom of intestinal obstruction or diverticulitis.

definition: According to the constitution.

definition: A long and thoughtful observation.

definition: Relating to or determined by or in context.

Very close or connected in space or time.

etymology: From Spanish contrabanda (modern spelling contrabando), from Italian contrabando (modern spelling contrabbando), from contra (“against”) + bando (“ban”), and reinforced by French contrebande.

definition: Capable of preventing conception or impregnation.

Birth control by the use of devices (diaphragm or intrauterine device or condom) or drugs or surgery.
A contraceptive in the form of a pill containing estrogen and progestin to inhibit ovulation and so prevent conception.
Showing effects of planning or manipulation.
example: A novel with a contrived ending.

definition: A difficult problem.
etymology: A word of unknown origin with several variants, gaining popularity for its burlesque imitation of scholastic Latin, as hocus-pocus or panjandrum.

definition: In a conventional manner.
example: He usually behaves rather conventionally.

definition: Be adjacent or come together.

etymology: From Latin convergere, from con- (“together”) + vergere (“to bend”).

Characteristic of informal spoken language or conversation.

Lens such that a beam of light passing through it is brought to a point or focus.

In a convincing manner.

Large in number or quantity (especially of discourse).

definition: Variety of European beech with shining purple or copper-colored leaves.
A copper salt made by the action of sulfuric acid on copper oxide.

definition: Diffusing warmth and friendliness.

A series of sentinels or of military posts enclosing or guarding some place or thing.

Crisp flake made from corn.
A defensive football player stationed outside the linebackers.

definition: Forced to turn and face attackers.
example: She had me cornered between the porch and her car.

definition: Dull and tiresome but with pretensions of significance or originality.

definition: (botany) the whorl of petals of a flower that collectively form an inner floral envelope or layer of the perianth.

A short sinus receiving most of the veins of the heart; empties into the right atrium.
A viral disease caused by SARS-CoV-2 that caused a global pandemic in 2020.
Acute disease caused by a virus of the family Orthocoronavirinae.

definition: Any of several long-stemmed tulips that flower in May; have egg-shaped variously colored flowers.

A sharp steel wedge that precedes the plow and cuts vertically through the soil.
