Cow excreta used as fertilizer.
Coarse erect biennial Old World herb introduced as a weed in eastern North America.
The trait of lacking courage.
etymology: From Middle English cowardise, borrowed from Anglo-Norman cuardise (modern French couardise).

definition: Affectedly modest or shy especially in a playful or provocative way.
etymology: From Middle English coy, from Old French coi, earlier quei (“quiet, still”), from Latin qu(i)ētus (“resting, at rest”). Doublet of quit, quiet, quite, and quietus.

definition: South American jointed cactus with usually red flowers; often cultivated as a houseplant; sometimes classified as genus Schlumbergera.
Crumbs of crackers used especially for coating or thickening.
A male creator of great skill in the manual arts.
etymology: From craft + -s- + -man.

definition: Skill in an occupation or trade.
example: The craftsmanship on the antique chair was exquisite.
etymology: From craftsman + -ship.

definition: Marked by skill in deception.
example: I took a crafty look at his hand of cards while he was out of the room.
etymology: From Middle English crafty, crefty, craftiȝ, from Old English cræftiġ (“ingenious; skilful; crafty; cunning; virtuous;

definition: Crowd or pack to capacity.
example: To cram fruit into a basket; to cram a room with people.
etymology: From Middle English crammen, from Old English crammian (“to cram;

definition: Packed full to capacity.
A strip of metal with ends bent at right angles; used to hold masonry together.
Any of numerous shrubs of genus Vaccinium bearing cranberries.
etymology: Adapted in the 1640s from Dutch Low Saxon or German Low German Kraanbeere, from Kraan m (which means and is cognate with crane) + Beere f (which means and is cognate with berry). Equivalent to cran- + berry.

definition: Deciduous North American shrub or small tree having three-lobed leaves and red berries.
The cultivation of cranberries.
Small prostrate or ascending shrub having scarlet flowers and succulent fruit resembling cranberries; sometimes placed in genus Styphelia.
The juice of cranberries (always diluted and sweetened).
Sauce made of cranberries and sugar.
Deciduous thicket-forming Old World shrub with clusters of white flowers and small bright red berries.
(used of boats) inclined to heel over easily under sail.
example: He got home from a long day at work tired and cranky.
etymology: From crank + -y. Compare Middle Low German krankich (“sickly, unwell”).

definition: Lacking even the rudiments of courage; abjectly fearful.
example: The craven fellow turned and ran.
etymology: From Middle English cravant, either borrowed from Old French cravanté (“defeated”), past participle of cravanter (ultimately from Latin crepare), or a modification of creaunt (“defeated”) after craven (“to crave”).

definition: Writing implement consisting of a colored stick of composition wax used for writing and drawing.
etymology: Borrowed from French crayon (“pencil”), from craie (“chalk”) + -on (diminutive suffix), from Latin crēta (“chalk, clay”), perhaps from crētus.

definition: Driven insane.
example: The crazed look in his eyes made everyone back away.

definition: Informal terms for insanity.
example: The craziness of a ship, or of the limbs.
etymology: From crazy + -ness.

definition: A patchwork quilt without a design.
A skin cleanser that comes in a thick liquid form, similar in texture to a lotion.
example: Cream cleanser is recommended for dry skin.

definition: Of fabric that does not wrinkle easily.
In a creative manner.
example: She solved the problem creatively.
etymology: From creative + -ly.

definition: The mental attitude that something is believable and should be accepted as true.
example: He gave credence to the gossip.
etymology: From Middle English credence, from Old French credence, from Medieval Latin crēdentia (“belief, faith”), from Latin crēdēns, present active participle of crēdō (“loan, confide in, trust, believe”).

definition: A person to whom money is owed by a debtor; someone to whom an obligation exists.
example: The creditor demanded immediate payment.
etymology: From Middle English creditour, from Anglo-Norman creditour, from Latin crēditor, from crēditum (“loan”), from crēditus, perfect passive participle of crēdō (“lend”).

definition: Delicate fern of the eastern United States having a twining stem and palmately-lobed sterile fronds and forked fertile fronds.
Low to prostrate shrub of Canada and northern United States; bronzed purple in winter.
European thistle naturalized in United States and Canada where it is a pernicious weed.
A mother tongue that originates from contact between two languages.
etymology: See Creole. Attested in English to refer to language from the 18th century.

definition: Deep-sea fish of tropical Atlantic.
An adjustable wrench designed to fit hexagonal nuts with the adjusting screw built into the head of the wrench.
Abounding in chalk.
etymology: From Latin cretaceus (“chalky”), from Latin creta.

definition: In a shameful manner.
example: The garden was criminally neglected.
etymology: From criminal + -ly.

definition: The scientific study of crime and criminal behavior and law enforcement.
example: Criminology will help you understand the motivations of lawbreakers.
etymology: From criminal + -logy.

definition: Southern European annual with spiky heads of crimson flower; extensively cultivated in United States for forage.
Find fault with; express criticism of; point out real or perceived flaws.
example: The paper criticized the new movie.
etymology: From critic + -ise, see criticize.

definition: A needle with a hook on the end; used in crocheting.
A needle with a hook on the end; used in crocheting.
Any one of a number of stitches made by pulling a loop of yarn through another loop with a crochet needle.
Suffer a nervous breakdown.
A small farm worked by a crofter.
etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English croft, crofft, croffte, croofte, crofte (“croft”), from Old English croft (“enclosed field”); further etymology uncertain, but possibly from Proto-Germanic *kruftaz (“a hill;

definition: The dispersion of fungicides or insecticides or fertilizer on growing crops (often from a low-flying aircraft).
A crosspiece spreading the gunnels of a boat; used as a seat in a rowboat.
(of snakes) having crossing bands on the back.
etymology: From cross- + banded.

definition: Fertilization by the union of male and female gametes from different individual of the same species.
etymology: From cross- + fertilization.

definition: A side bond that links two adjacent chains of atoms in a complex molecule.
Relating to different sense modalities.
Of or relating to an older kind of automobile tire that had a flexible tread and relatively stiff sidewalls.
A bow fixed transversely on a wooden stock grooved to direct the arrow (quarrel).
A lively or heated interchange of ideas and opinions.
example: The two factions were either side of the road. A civilian lorry was caught in the crossfire and became collateral damage.
etymology: From cross- + fire.

definition: A puzzle in which words corresponding to numbered clues are to be found and written in to squares in the puzzle.
A puzzle in which words corresponding to numbered clues are to be found and written in to squares in the puzzle.
A situation in which people or things are crowded together.
example: He didn't like the crowding on the beach.

definition: Representing a level of the highest possible achievement or attainment.
example: The crowning accomplishment of his career.
etymology: From Middle English crowninge, crounende, equivalent to crown + -ing.

definition: A vessel made of material that does not melt easily; used for high temperature chemical reactions.
etymology: From Latin crucibulum (“night-lamp, metallurgic melting-pot”), apparently a derivative of crux (“cross”), perhaps by analogy to thūribulum (“censer”) and suffix -bulum, or from crucio (“to torment”).

definition: A furnace for heating the metal charge contained in refractory crucibles.
Steel made by the mixture of molten wrought iron, charcoal, and other substances in a crucible.
Representation of the cross on which Jesus died.
example: Plain crosses are preferred by Protestants, but crucifixes by Catholics.
etymology: From Middle English crucifix, from Old French crocefis (French crucifix), from Latin crucifixus.

definition: Sea catfish of the Caribbean area.
A device that crushes something.
etymology: From crush + -er (agent noun suffix), or, for one who elicits a crush, + -er (patient suffix).

definition: Having a hardened crust as a covering.
example: The door opened with a crusty squeak that echoed in the silent room.
etymology: From Middle English crusty, equivalent to crust + -y.

definition: The most important point.
example: The crux of her argument was that the roadways needed repair before anything else could be accomplished.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin crux (“cross, wooden frame for execution”), possibly from the Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, to bend”). Doublet of cross and crouch (“cross”).

definition: A cellar or vault or underground burial chamber (especially beneath a church).
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin crypta (“vault”), from Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós, “hidden”). Doublet of grotto.

definition: Of an obscure nature.
example: The new insurance policy is written without cryptic or mysterious terms.
etymology: From Late Latin crypticus, from Ancient Greek κρυπτικός (kruptikós), from κρυπτός (kruptós, “hidden”), from κρύπτω (krúptō, “to hide”). Doublet of kryptic.

definition: Staring into a crystal ball to arouse visions of future or distant events.
Consisting of or containing or of the nature of crystals.
example: Granite is crystalline.

definition: Biconvex transparent body situated behind the iris in the eye; its role (along with the cornea) is to focus light on the retina.
A metric measure of volume or capacity equal to a cube 1 millimeter on each edge.
Small room in which a monk or nun lives.
A man who is a stupid incompetent fool.
etymology: From Middle English cokkou, kokkow, cukkuk, gokkouȝ, probably from Old French cocu, coquu, cucu (whence French coucou);

definition: Eurasian plant with heart-shaped trifoliate leaves and white purple-veined flowers.
Clock that announces the hours with a sound like the call of the cuckoo.
A bitter cress of Europe and America.
A melon vine of the genus Cucumis; cultivated from earliest times for its cylindrical green fruit.
Inviting cuddling or hugging.
example: A cuddlesome baby.
etymology: From cuddle + -y.

definition: Widely cultivated herb with aromatic leaf stalks that are eaten raw or cooked.
Difficult to handle or use especially because of size or weight.
example: A cumbersome piece of machinery.
etymology: From Middle English cumbyrsum, cummyrsum; equivalent to cumber (“hindrance”) + -some. Compare encumber and incumbent.

definition: A person authorized to conduct religious worship.
etymology: Back-formation from curator on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: In a manner differing from the usual or expected.
example: Had a curiously husky voice.
etymology: From Middle English curiusly, curyously, curiosly, curiouseliche, curyouslyche, equivalent to curious + -ly.

definition: Of or relating to an academic course of study.
etymology: From curriculum + -ar.

definition: Marked by rude or peremptory shortness.
example: A curt reply.
etymology: From the Latin curtus (“shortened”). Cognate with Dutch kort, German kurz, Galician curto, French court, Italian corto, Portuguese curto, and Spanish corto. Doublet of short.

definition: (medicine) a curving or bending; often abnormal.
example: Curvature of the spine.
etymology: From Latin curvare, from Latin curvatura. See also curve. Displaced native Old English ġebīeġednes.

definition: Having or marked by a curve or smoothly rounded bend.
example: A curving path.

definition: Having curves.
example: A settee with only one curvy end.
etymology: From curve + -y.

definition: Point formed by two intersecting arcs (as from the intrados of a Gothic arch).
etymology: From Latin cuspis (“a point, spear, pointed end”); first used in astrology. Doublet of cuspid and cuspis.

definition: Sweetened mixture of milk and eggs baked or boiled or frozen.
etymology: Alteration of croustade.

definition: Any of several tropical American trees bearing fruit with soft edible pulp.
etymology: From the fancied resemblance of the fruit's flesh to custard.

definition: A prop consisting of an open pie filled with real or artificial custard; thrown in slapstick comedies.
Resembling custard in consistency.
Providing protective supervision; watching over or safeguarding.
example: Daycare that is educational and not just custodial.
etymology: From custody + -al; compare French custodial.

definition: A brokerage firm account that parents have created for a minor.
One having charge of buildings or grounds or animals.
example: After their parents' death, their aunt became the children's custodian.
etymology: From a shortening of Latin custōdiānātus, from Latin custōdia (“a keeping, watch, guard, prison”), from custōs (“a keeper, watchman, guard”). By surface analysis, custody + -ian.

definition: A cutting implement; a tool for cutting.
example: Proper maintenance of your cutlery will keep the blades from dulling.
etymology: From Middle English cotellerie, cutleri (“the cutler’s art or craft”), from Old French coutelerie (modern French coutellerie).

definition: A designated limit beyond which something cannot function or must be terminated.
etymology: Deverbal from cut off.

definition: Handsaw that cuts at right angles to the grain (or major axis).
A rule that when literal compliance is impossible the intention of a donor or testator should be carried out as nearly as possible.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman cy pres (“as close”) (i.e. as close as possible), equivalent to Modern French si près or aussi près.

definition: Any of a class of organic compounds containing the cyano radical -CN.
etymology: From cyan- + -ide.

definition: The monovalent group -CN in a chemical compound.
Poisoning due to ingesting or inhaling cyanide; common in smoke from fires and in industrial chemicals.
An industrial process for extracting gold and silver by treating ore with a sodium cyanide solution.
The monovalent group -CN in a chemical compound.
A human being whose body has been taken over in whole or in part by electromechanical devices.
example: A cyborg is a cybernetic organism.
etymology: Blend of cybernetic + organism. Coined by Austrian-born scientist and musician Manfred Clynes in 1960.

definition: Conforming to the Carnot cycle.
example: The weather had a cyclic pattern of rain and sun.
etymology: From French cyclique or its etymon Classical Latin cyclicus, from Ancient Greek κυκλικός (kuklikós). By surface analysis, cycle + -ic. Piecewise doublet of chakric.

definition: A mild bipolar disorder that persists over a long time.
Recurring in cycles.
example: A cyclical embryo.
etymology: From cyclic + -al.

definition: A deficit that is related to the business or economic cycle.

Minute free-swimming freshwater copepod having a large median eye and pear-shaped body and long antennae used in swimming; important in some food chains and as intermediate hosts of parasitic worms that affect man e.g. Guinea worms.
A cylindrical metal lining used to reduce friction.
A cynical feeling of distrust.
etymology: From Cynicism, cynic + -ism; compare cynism.

definition: Wood of any of several evergreen trees or shrubs of Australia and northern New Caledonia.
Any of numerous evergreen conifers of the genus Cupressus of north temperate regions having dark scalelike leaves and rounded cones.
Tropical American annual climber having red (sometimes white) flowers and finely dissected leaves; naturalized in United States and elsewhere.
A closed sac that develops abnormally in some body structure.
etymology: From Late Latin cystis, from Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis, “anatomical sac”).

definition: A male monarch or emperor (especially of Russia prior to 1917).
etymology: See tsar. The spelling czar, the older spelling in English, comes from the book Notes on Muscovite Affairs (1549) by Sigismund von Herberstein. It was supplanted by the alternative tsar in the 19th century.

definition: An informal term for a father; probably derived from baby talk.
etymology: Imitative of a child's first syllables; see dad.

definition: North American evergreen fern having pinnate leaves and dense clusters of lance-shaped fronds.
The longer of the two telegraphic signals used in Morse code.
etymology: From Burmese ဓား (dha:). Possibly a doublet of dao.

definition: Tropical woody herb with showy yellow flowers and flat pods; much cultivated in the tropics.
Delicately beautiful.
example: A dainty teacup.
etymology: From Middle English deynte (as noun), from Old French deintié, from Latin dignitātem. Doublet of dignity.

definition: East Indian tree bearing a profusion of intense vermilion velvet-textured blooms and yielding a yellow dye.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindustani डाक / ڈاک (ḍāk).

definition: Threatening with damnation.
example: Damning evidence was clear for all to see.
etymology: From Middle English dampnynge; equivalent to damn + -ing.

definition: An infectious disease of the tropics transmitted by mosquitoes and characterized by rash and aching head and joints.
etymology: Often said to be named after the gait of dengue patients.

definition: (of fabrics and paper) grown dark in color over time.
example: The darkened margins of the paper.

definition: An act (or failure to act) that disappoints someone.
Common black-and-grey Eurasian bird noted for thievery.
etymology: From Middle English dawe, from Old English *dāwe, from Proto-West Germanic *dāhwā. Cognate with German Dahle, Dohle, dialectal Tach.

definition: Large fast-growing Chinese monoecious tree having flat bright-green deciduous leaves and small globular cones; commonly cultivated in United States as an ornamental; known as a fossil before being discovered in China.
The first light of day.
etymology: From day + break.

definition: In a state of mental numbness especially as resulting from shock.
example: He had a dazed expression on his face.

definition: To cause someone to lose clear vision, especially from intense light.
example: She was dazzled by the bright headlights.
etymology: From daze + -le, a frequentative form.

definition: From the beginning.
example: Having found the lower court's analysis wrong, the appellate court undertook a review de novo.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dē novō (adverb, literally “from the new”), from dē (“from”) + novō, ablative singular of novus (“new”).

definition: Reduce the emphasis.
A person who is almost identical to another.
example: He is a dead ringer for his grandfather at that age.
etymology: See ringer (“substitute”) and ring the changes

definition: A young woman making her debut into society.
etymology: Clipping of debutante or debut.

definition: A sudden and violent collapse.
etymology: From French débâcle, from débâcler (“to unbar;

definition: Open to doubt or debate.
example: Those data are debatable: no one has been able to replicate them.
etymology: From Old French debatable (French débattable), equivalent to debate + -able.

definition: Impairing the strength and vitality.
A person who owes a creditor; someone who has the obligation of paying a debt.
example: The debtor agreed to repay the loan within six months.
etymology: From Middle English dettour, from Old French detour, from Latin debitor, equivalent to debt + -or. Doublet of debitor. Displaced native Old English *sċola.

definition: Luxuriously self-indulgent.
example: I spent a decadent day at a spa.
etymology: From French décadent, a back-formation from décadence (see -ent), from Medieval Latin dēcadentia, from Late Latin dēcadēns, present participle of dēcadō, dēcidō (“sink, fall; perish”), from Latin dē- + cadō (“fall”).

definition: Either a design that is fixed to some surface or a paper bearing the design which is to be transferred to the surface.
etymology: Clipping of decalcomania.

definition: The quality of being fraudulent.
example: The whole conversation was merely a deceit.
etymology: From Middle English deceyte, from Old French deceite, deçoite, from decevoir (“to deceive”), from Latin dēcipere (“to cheat, mislead”).

definition: (of plants and shrubs) shedding foliage at the end of the growing season.
example: A deciduous tree.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dēciduus (“falling down or off”), from dēcidō (“to fall down or off”) + -uus.

definition: A forest comprising mainly of broad-leaved trees that shed all their leaves during one season.
A plant having foliage that is shed annually at the end of the growing season.
A digit from 0 to 9 in decimal notation.
A proper fraction whose denominator is a power of 10.
Any notation that uses 10 different characters (usually the digits 0 to 9).
Convert code into ordinary language.
etymology: As decypher, but not retaining the y from the Old French etyma of cipher (cyfre, cyffre);

definition: With firmness of purpose.
example: ‘I will come along,’ she said decisively.
etymology: From decisive + -ly.

definition: Convert code into ordinary language.
example: The cryptographer decoded the secret message and sent the result to the officer.
etymology: From de- + code.

definition: The activity of making clear or converting from code into plain text.
A beguiler who leads someone into danger (usually as part of a plot).
etymology: From Dutch de + kooi, literally "the cage". Possibly related to verb coy (which itself may have been influenced by decoy).

definition: Fixed or established especially by order or command.
Make a subtraction.
example: I will deduct the cost of the can of peas from the money I owe you.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin deductus, perfect passive participle of verb deducere (“lead from”).

definition: Make more intense, stronger, or more marked.
example: This event only deepened my convictions.
etymology: From deep + -en.

definition: Accumulating and becoming more intense.
example: The deepening gloom.

definition: Fern with erect fronds of Europe and western North America; often cultivated for deer browse.
Lacking protection or support.
example: A defenseless child.
etymology: From defense + -less.

definition: Hold back to a later time.
example: We're going to defer the decision until we have all the facts.
etymology: Originally a variant of (and hence a doublet of) differ; from Middle English differren (“to postpone”), from Old French differer, from Latin differō. Doublet of differ and dilate.

definition: Boldly resisting authority or an opposing force.
example: Brought up to be aggressive and defiant.
etymology: Borrowed from French défiant, from the verb défier. Doublet of diffident. By surface analysis, def(i) + -ant.

definition: In a rebellious manner.
etymology: From defiant + -ly.

definition: Prevent the occurrence of; prevent from happening; to protect from or to keep away anything undesirable; to ward off.
example: The defender deflected the cross into his own net.
etymology: From Latin deflecto, from de- (“away”) + flecto (“to bend”).

definition: A twist or aberration; especially a perverse or abnormal way of judging or acting.
example: Russell's goalbound shot took a deflection off a defender and went out for a corner.
etymology: From Latin dēflexiō, from dēflectere (“to deflect”; participle stem dēflex-) + -iō (suffix forming abstract nouns).

definition: A change for the worse.
example: Plastic deformation versus elastic deformation.
etymology: From Old French deformation, see deform. Morphologically deform + -ation.

definition: So badly formed or out of shape as to be ugly.
example: Deformed thalidomide babies.

definition: The process of declining from a higher to a lower level of effective power or vitality or essential quality.
example: Fatty degeneration of the liver.
etymology: From French dégénération, from Latin dēgenerātiō.

definition: (of illness) marked by gradual deterioration of organs and cells along with loss of function.
example: Degenerative diseases of old age.
etymology: From degenerate + -ive.

definition: Food preserved by dehydration.
Any process whereby sounds or words are left out of spoken words or phrases.
example: The file contained errors that required deletion.
etymology: From Latin dēlētiōnem (“destruction, effacement”), from the past-participle stem of dēlēre (“to blot out, destroy, efface”). Equivalent to delete + -ion.

definition: (usually plural) discussion of all sides of a question.
example: The deliberations of the jury.
etymology: From Middle English deliberacioun, from Old French deliberation, from Latin deliberātiō. Morphologically deliberate + -ion.

definition: The quality of being beautiful and delicate in appearance.
example: A Chinese delicacy.
etymology: From Middle English delicacie, from Middle English delicat, from Latin delicatus. Equivalent to delic(ate) + -acy.

definition: In a delicate manner.
example: The gingerbread was delicately, if imprecisely, captured by the brushstrokes.
etymology: From delicate + -ly.

definition: Recovery or preservation from loss or danger.
example: Work is the deliverance of mankind.
etymology: From Old French deliverance (French délivrance), equivalent to deliver + -ance.

definition: An overwhelming number or amount.
example: The deluge continued for hours, drenching the land and slowing traffic to a halt.
etymology: From Middle English deluge, from Old French deluge, alteration of earlier deluvie, from Latin dīluvium, from dīluō (“wash away”). Doublet of diluvium.

definition: Turn up, loosen, or remove earth.
etymology: From Middle English delven, from Old English delfan (“to dig, dig out, burrow, bury”), from Proto-Germanic *delbaną (“to dig”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰelbʰ- (“to dig”).

definition: (behavioral attributes) the way a person behaves toward other people.
example: The man's demeanor made others suspicious of his intentions.

definition: In military architecture, a bastion constructed of one face, and one flank.
Sauce Espagnole with extra beef stock simmered down and seasoned with dry wine or sherry.
In a democratic manner; based on democratic principles.
example: It was decided democratically.
etymology: Partly from democratical + -ly (suffix forming adverbs), and from democratic + -ally (variant of -ly), modelled after Middle French democratiquement (modern French démocratiquement).

definition: Destroy completely.
example: The wrecking ball demolished the building.
etymology: Attested since the 16th century; from Middle French demoliss-, the stem of some conjugated forms of the verb demolir (“to destroy”, “to tear down”), from Latin dēmōlior (“to tear down”).

definition: The divisor of a fraction.
example: Common denominator.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēnōminātor (“that which names”).

definition: Speak out against.
example: He denounced the Nazis.
etymology: From Old French denuncier, from Latin dēnūntiō (“to announce, to denounce, to threaten”), from de + nūntiō (“to announce, to report, to denounce”), from nūntius (“messenger, message”). Doublet of denunciate.

definition: A consonant articulated with the tip of the tongue near the gum ridge.
A soft thread for cleaning the spaces between the teeth.
A toiletry applied to the skin in order to mask unpleasant odors.
etymology: From Latin de- + odorans, present participle of odorare (“to smell”), from odor (“a smell”); see odor. By surface analysis, de- + odor + -ant.

definition: The act of decreasing something markedly.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin depletio, depletionem, from depleō.

definition: Hand over to the authorities of another country.
etymology: Borrowed from French déporter. With the meaning of "behave", from Old French deporter (“behave”), from Latin deportō, from de- + portō.

definition: Deviating from what is considered moral or right or proper or good.
example: Depraved criminals.

definition: Take away possessions from someone.
etymology: From Middle English depryven, from Old French depriver, from Medieval Latin dēprīvō, from Latin dē- + prīvō.

definition: A gauge for measuring the depth of grooves or holes or other concavities.
Cause to run off the tracks.
example: They had planned to derail the trains that carried atomic waste.
etymology: From French dérailler (“to go off the rails”). Analyzable as de- + rail.

definition: Driven insane.
etymology: Borrowed from French dérangé.

definition: The act of freeing from regulation (especially from governmental regulations).
example: Some say the airline industry has been profitable since the government began deregulation of it.
etymology: From de- + regulation.

definition: The source or origin from which something derives (i.e. comes or issues).
example: He prefers shoes of Italian derivation.
etymology: From Middle English derivacioun, borrowed from Middle French dérivation, from Latin dērīvātiō, dērīvātiōnem. Morphologically derive + -ation.

definition: A doctor who specializes in the physiology and pathology of the skin.
etymology: From dermatology + -ist or dermato- + -logist.

definition: Expressive of low opinion.
example: Derogatory comments.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin dērogātōrius, from Latin dērogō; corresponding to derogate + -ory.

definition: An adjective that ascribes to its noun the value of an attribute of that noun (e.g., ‘a nervous person’ or ‘a musical speaking voice’).
Of deserts of northern Africa and southern Asia.
Perennial of southwestern United States having leathery blue-green pinnatifid leaves and thick plumelike spikes of yellow flowers; sometimes placed in genus Cleome.
Burrowing tortoise of the arid western United States and northern Mexico; may be reclassified as a member of genus Xerobates.
Choose not to consume.
example: Please desist from telephoning me at this number.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French desister, from Latin dēsistō, from dē- + sistō (whence de-).

definition: Leave someone who needs or counts on you; leave in the lurch.
etymology: From Middle English desolat(e). See Etymology 2 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

definition: Poor enough to need help from others.
etymology: From Middle English destitute, destitut, from Latin dēstitūtus.

definition: Deprive of freedom; take into confinement.
etymology: From Old French detenir. Doublet of détente. Cognate with Italian detenere, Portuguese deter, Romanian deține, and Spanish detener.

definition: Capable of being detected.
A surface-active chemical widely used in industry and laundering.
example: Laundry detergent.
etymology: From French détergent, from Latin dētergēns, the present participle of dētergeō, from dē (“off”) + tergeō (“wipe, polish”).

definition: A substance added to soaps or detergents to increase their cleansing action.
Become worse or disintegrate.
example: His mind deteriorated.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēteriorātus, perfect passive participle of Late Latin dēteriorō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), further from Latin dēterior (“worse”). Cognate with French détériorer.

definition: A violent release of energy caused by a chemical or nuclear reaction.
example: The detonation of gun cotton.
etymology: From French détonation; equivalent to detonate + -ion.

definition: Take away a part from; diminish.
example: His bad manners detract from his good character.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French détracter, from Latin detractum, past participle of detraho.

definition: Markedly different from an accepted norm.
example: Deviant ideas.
etymology: From Middle English devyaunt (“deviating, different”), from Late Latin dēviāns, present participle of dēviō (“to stray, deviate or detour”).

definition: Turn aside; turn away from.
example: His exhibition of nude paintings deviated from the norm.
etymology: From Late Latin dēviātus, perfect passive participle of dēviō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more. Compare French dévier.

definition: Indirect in departing from the accepted or proper way; misleading.
example: Used devious means to achieve success.
etymology: 1590s, "out of the common or direct way," from Latin devius (“out of the way, remote, off the main road”), from de via, from de (“off”) (see de-) + via (“way, road”). Compare deviate.

definition: Come up with (an idea, plan, explanation, theory, or principle) after a mental effort.
example: To devise an argument; to devise a machine, or a new system of writing.
etymology: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle English devisen, devysen, from Old French deviser, from Vulgar Latin devisō, from Latin dīvisō, frequentative of dīvidō.

definition: Relating to worship.
example: A devotional exercise.
etymology: From devotion + -al.

definition: To consume.
example: Fire had devoured our home.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English devouren, from Old French devorer (Modern French dévorer), from Latin dēvorō, from vorō.

definition: Adroitness in using the hands.
example: Playing computer games can improve your manual dexterity.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French dextérité, from Latin dexteritas, from dexter (“on the right”), this is in reference to most people having greater fine motor skills in their right hand.

definition: Identifying the nature or cause of some phenomenon.
An assay conducted for diagnostic purposes.
The branch of medical science dealing with the classification of disease.
example: Diagnostics is the area in which this molecule is most useful, whereas it is not a treatment target in itself.
etymology: From diagnostic + -ics.

definition: A mechanical device in a camera that controls size of aperture of the lens.
example: The new cameras adjust the diaphragm automatically.
etymology: From Middle English diafragma, Ancient Greek διάφραγμα (diáphragma, “partition”), from διά (diá, “across”) and φράγμα (phrágma, “barrier”), from the verb φράσσω (phrássō). First attested in the late 14th century.

definition: Frequent and watery bowel movements; can be a symptom of infection or food poisoning or colitis or a gastrointestinal tumor.
Being twofold; a classification into two opposed parts or subclasses.
example: The dichotomy between eastern and western culture.
etymology: From Ancient Greek διχοτομία (dikhotomía, “dichotomy”).

definition: A person who diets.
The act of restricting your food intake (or your intake of particular foods).
example: They found out that dieting can harm you if you do it wrong. She advised them to talk with a doctor before doing anything too extreme.

definition: When light passes sharp edges or goes through narrow slits the rays are deflected and produce fringes of light and dark bands.
etymology: From New Latin diffrāctiō (in which coined by Francesco Maria Grimaldi), from Latin diffrāctus, past participle of Latin diffringo (“to shatter, to break into pieces”).

definition: Any gland having ducts that pour secretions into the digestive tract.
In deplorable condition.
Quietly and steadily persevering especially in detail or exactness.
example: A diligent (or patient) worker.

definition: With diligence; in a diligent manner.
example: We may diligently observe the Lord's supper on the first day of the week, diligently preach the gospel, or minister to the saint.
etymology: From diligent + -ly.

definition: Aromatic Old World herb having aromatic threadlike foliage and seeds used as seasoning.
etymology: From Middle English dile, from Old English dile (“dill, anise”); from Proto-Germanic *deliz, of uncertain, probably non-Indo-European origin, possibly a west European substrate.

definition: Seed of the dill plant used as seasoning.
A beverage of a dill infusion.
Aromatic threadlike foliage of the dill plant used as seasoning.
Lessen the strength or flavor of a solution or mixture.
example: It dilutes easily.
etymology: From Latin dīlūtus, from dīluere (“to wash away, dissolve, cause to melt, dilute”), from dī-, dis- (“away, apart”) + luere (“to wash”). See lave, and compare deluge.

definition: A diluted solution.
etymology: From dilute + -ion.

definition: Very small.
example: Diminutive in stature.

definition: A large napkin used when dinner is served.
A thermionic tube having two electrodes; used as a rectifier.
etymology: From di- (“two”) + -ode.

definition: Solder by immersion in a bath of molten solder.
An antenna that transmits or receives signals only in a narrow angle.
A microphone that is designed to receive sound from a particular direction.
That cripples or disables or incapacitates.
Consider bad or wrong.
example: She disapproves of rap music because of its sometimes aggressive lyrics.
etymology: From dis- + approve.

definition: Act of reducing or depriving of arms.
example: The disarmament of the aggressor nations must be complete.
etymology: From disarm + -ment, modeled after armament. By surface analysis, dis + armament.

definition: A harrow with a series of disks set on edge at an angle.
A plow that consists of a gang of concave steel cutting disks, used for work in hard dry soils.
A plow that consists of a gang of concave steel cutting disks, used for work in hard dry soils.
Detect with the senses.
example: He was too young to discern right from wrong.
etymology: From Middle English discernen, from Old French discerner, from Latin discernere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, discern”), from dis- (“apart”) + cernere (“to distinguish”); see certain.

definition: Having or revealing keen insight and good judgment.
example: A discerning critic.

definition: A descriptive catalog of musical recordings.
etymology: From disco- + -graphy. First attested in 1933.

definition: Put an end to a state or an activity.
example: They plan to discontinue that design.
etymology: From Old French descontinuer, equivalent to dis- + continue.

definition: Depriving of confidence or hope or enthusiasm and hence often deterring action.
example: Where never is heard a discouraging word.

definition: Being unjustly brought into disrepute.
example: A discredited politician.

definition: With discretion; prudently and with wise self-restraint.
example: I sent for the sergeant of the platoon both men were in and asked him to try to find out discreetly what lay behind this.
etymology: From discreet + -ly.

definition: Showing or indicating careful judgment and discernment especially in matters of taste.
example: The discriminating eye of the connoisseur.

definition: Caused by or altered by or manifesting disease or pathology.
example: Diseased tonsils.
etymology: * disease + -ed

definition: A person suffering from an illness.
Suffering shame.
example: A disgraced politician.

definition: In a state of sulky dissatisfaction.
example: Disgruntled employees preparing to strike over the lack of progress in talks with their employer on pay and conditions.
etymology: From disgruntle + -ed (suffix forming past tense and past participle forms of verbs).

definition: The quality of being dishonest.
etymology: From Middle English dishoneste (“disgrace, filth”), from Old French deshoneste, equivalent to dis- + honesty or dishonest + -y.

definition: Freed from illusion.
etymology: From disillusion + -ed.

definition: In a decomposed state.
example: The sample exhibited an activity of three disintegrations per second.
etymology: From disintegrate + -ion or dis- + integration.

definition: A harrow with a series of disks set on edge at an angle.
Separated at the joint.
example: A dislocated knee.

definition: Tear down so as to make flat with the ground.
etymology: From Middle French desmanteler, itself from des- (“dis-”), mantel (“coat”) + -er (verbal suffix). By surface analysis, dis- + mantle. Compare typologically uncloak, reveal, unmask.

definition: The act of taking something apart (as a piece of machinery).
example: Russia and the United States discussed the dismantling of their nuclear weapons.

definition: Showing indifference or disregard.
example: A dismissive shrug.
etymology: From dismiss + -ive.

definition: Undisciplined and unruly.
example: Disorderly youths.
etymology: From disorder + -ly (adjectival suffix) or from dis- + orderly.

definition: Any act of molesting, interrupting, hindering, agitating, or arousing from a state of repose or otherwise depriving inhabitants of the peace and quiet to which they are entitled.
Any act of molesting, interrupting, hindering, agitating, or arousing from a state of repose or otherwise depriving inhabitants of the peace and quiet to which they are entitled.
Lacking order or methodical arrangement or function.
example: A disorganized enterprise.

definition: The official who signals the beginning of a race or competition.
etymology: From dispatch + -er.

definition: Force to go away; used both with concrete and metaphoric meanings.
example: Dispel doubts.
etymology: From Middle English dispelen, from Latin dispellere (“to disperse; to dispel”).

definition: Clinic where medicine and medical supplies are dispensed.
Administer or bestow, as in small portions.
example: The machine dispenses soft drinks.

definition: Give up what is not strictly needed.
example: I wish he would dispense with the pleasantries and get to the point.

definition: A container so designed that the contents can be used in prescribed amounts.
example: A toilet-paper dispenser.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman dispensour, from Old French despenseor, from Latin dispensator. By surface analysis, dispense + -er.

definition: The act of dispersing or diffusing something.
example: The dispersion of the troops.
etymology: From disperse + -al.

definition: Spreading widely or driving off.
etymology: From disperse + -ion, from Middle English dispersioun, from Old French dispersion, from Latin dispersiō.

definition: (of colloids) a substance in which another is colloidally dispersed.
The feeling of being displeased or annoyed or dissatisfied with someone or something.
etymology: From Old French desplaisir, equivalent to dis- + pleasure. See displease.

definition: Unfitness that bars you from participation.
example: The disqualification of certain people for holding certain positions.
etymology: From dis- + qualification.

definition: Not noticed inadvertently.
A high explosive that is used to damage the target that is under attack.
Treat, mention, or speak to rudely.
example: The student who had betrayed his classmate was dissed by everyone.
etymology: Originated in Jamaican English or African American Vernacular English, probably originally a clipping of disrespect or disparage, both from the prefix dis-, ultimately from Latin dis-.

definition: Cutting so as to separate into pieces.
example: Neck dissection.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dissectiōnem, perhaps via Middle French dissection. By surface analysis, dissect + -ion.

definition: Cause to become widely known.
example: The values of the human rights movement have disseminated throughout the world.

definition: Disagreeing, especially with a majority.
An opinion that disagrees with the court's disposition of the case.
Characterized by departure from accepted beliefs or standards.
etymology: From Latin dissidēns, present participle of dissideō (“to sit apart; to disagree”), from dis- (“asunder, apart, in two”) + sedeō (“to sit”).

definition: Not similar.
example: A group of very dissimilar people.
etymology: From dis- + similar.

definition: Unrestrained by convention or morality.
example: Deplorably dissipated and degraded.

definition: The process of going into solution.
example: The dissolving of salt in water.

definition: A liquid substance capable of dissolving other substances.
A conflict of people's opinions or actions or characters.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French dissonance, from Latin dissonantia; by surface analysis, dis- + son- + -ance.

definition: Turn away from by persuasion.
example: Negative campaigning will only dissuade people.
etymology: From Middle French dissuader, from Latin dissuādeō (“to urge differently”, “to advise against”, “to dissuade”), from dis- (“away from”, “asunder”) + suādeō (“to recommend”, “to advise”, “to urge”).

definition: The process of purifying a liquid by boiling it and condensing its vapors.
etymology: From Middle English distillacioun, from Anglo-Norman distillacioun, from Latin distīllātiōnem, accusative of distīllātiō.

definition: A plant and works where alcoholic drinks are made by distillation.
etymology: From distill + -ery (“place of”).

definition: Make false by mutilation or addition; as of a message or story.
example: In their articles, journalists sometimes distort the truth.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin distortum, past participle of distorqueō (“to twist, torture, distort”).

definition: Deeply agitated especially from emotion.
example: Distraught with grief.
etymology: From Middle English distraught, blend of distract (“distracted”) and straught (“stretched, distraught”), past participle of strecchen (“to stretch”). Compare also bestraught, extraught, forstraught, etc.

definition: Causing distress or worry or anxiety.
example: Distressing (or disturbing) news.

definition: A laborer who digs ditches.
Large deeply rooted fern of worldwide distribution with upright bipinnate compound tufted fronds.
A spade with a long handle for digging narrow ditches.
The act of moving away in different direction from a common point.
example: An angle is formed by the divergence of two straight lines.
etymology: By surface analysis, diverge + -ence.

definition: A thinker who moves away from the problem as stated and often has novel ideas and solutions.
The act of introducing variety (especially in investments or in the variety of goods and services offered).
example: My broker recommended a greater diversification of my investments.
etymology: From Medieval Latin diversificatiō, from diversificātus, past participle of diversificō (“diversify”), from Latin diversus (“turned in different ways”) + faciō (“make, do”). By surface analysis, diverse + -ification.

definition: Make (more) diverse.
example: Diversify a course of study.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French diversifier, equivalent to diverse + -ify.

definition: Providing enjoyment; pleasantly entertaining.
example: A diverting story.

definition: White creamy fudge made with egg whites.
A reeling sensation; a feeling that you are about to fall.
etymology: From Middle English disynes, duysenes, from Old English dysiġnes (“dizziness, folly, foolishness, blasphemy”), equivalent to dizzy + -ness.

definition: Capable of existing or taking place or proving true; possible to do.
example: Look at that chick — she's so doable!
etymology: From Middle English doable, equivalent to do + -able.

definition: Large brown aquatic larva of the dobsonfly; used as fishing bait.
etymology: Back-formation from dobsonfly.

definition: Large soft-bodied insect having long slender mandibles in the male; aquatic larvae often used as bait.
A sled pulled by dogs.
Informal terms for dogs.
etymology: From dog + -ie.

definition: Gently and sweetly.
etymology: From Italian dolce. Doublet of douce, doux, and dulce.

definition: Large Old World freshwater bottom-feeding fish introduced into Europe from Asia; inhabits ponds and sluggish streams and often raised for food; introduced into United States where it has become a pest.
Any of various animals that have been tamed and made fit for a human environment.
A loose hooded cloak worn with a half mask as part of a masquerade costume.
example: Look here, you chaps, don't you chew it too quick, or you'll break your dominoes on the nails!
etymology: 1801, borrowed from French domino (1771), originally the term for a hooded garment, itself from Medieval Latin domino, oblique case of dominus (“lord, master”); compare Medieval Latin dominicale (“a kind of veil”).

definition: The consequence of one event setting off a chain of similar events (like a falling domino causing a whole row of upended dominos to fall).
etymology: An allusion to a row of dominoes in which the fall of one leads to a cascade of falling pieces.

definition: The political theory that if one nation comes under communist control then neighboring nations will also come under communist control.
etymology: An allusion to a row of dominoes in which the fall of one leads to a cascade of falling pieces.

definition: (New Testament) day at the end of time following Armageddon when God will decree the fates of all individual humans according to the good and evil of their earthly lives.
etymology: From Middle English domes + dai, from Old English dom (“judgment”) + dæg (“day”). Equivalent to doom + -s- + day. Compare Old Norse dómsdagr (“judgement day, doomsday”).

definition: A push button at an outer door that gives a ringing or buzzing signal when pushed.
etymology: From door + bell.

definition: A college or university building containing living quarters for students.
etymology: From Middle English dormitory, dormytory, dormytorye, borrowed from Latin dormītōrium (“a sleeping-room”), from dormiō (“to sleep”). Doublet of dormitorium and dorter.

definition: A large sleeping room containing several beds.
A small boat of shallow draft with cross thwarts for seats and rowlocks for oars with which it is propelled.
etymology: Attested in American English from 1709 C.E.; possibly derived from an indigenous language of the West Indies or Central America, perhaps Miskito.

definition: Cream with a fat content of 48% or more.
A kind of crochet stitch.
An illegal dribble in basketball (the player uses both hands to dribble or the player starts to dribble a second time after coming to a stop).
A window with two panes of glass and a space between them; reduces heat and noise transmission through the window.
Two saucepans, one fitting inside the other.
(of clothing) fastened by lapping one edge of the front well over the other usually with a double row of buttons.
example: Double-breasted jacket.

definition: To double the degree.
example: She was doubly rewarded.
etymology: From Middle English dowbly, doubli, dubli, doubeliche, equivalent to double + -ly.

definition: Without doubt; certainly.
example: It's undoubtedly very beautiful.
etymology: From Middle English douteles, dowteles, equivalent to doubt + -less.

definition: A machine used to fry large quantities of doughnuts at once.
Shaped like a ring.
A stable quark with an electric charge of -1/3 and a mass 607 times that of an electron.
A drug that reduces excitability and calms a person.
example: Normally those pills give me a boost, but last night they gave me a downer.
etymology: From down + -er.

definition: The property possessed by a slope or surface that descends.
etymology: From down- + grade.

definition: A period of time when something (as a machine or factory) is not operating (especially as a result of malfunctions).
example: I’ve been working all weekend. I need some downtime.
etymology: From down (“out of order; out of service; inoperable”) + time.

definition: A worsening of business or economic activity.
example: The market took a downturn.
etymology: From down- + turn.

definition: Spatially or metaphorically from a higher to a lower level or position.
example: Prices plunged downward.
etymology: From down + -wards.

definition: Money or property brought by a woman to her husband at marriage.
etymology: From Middle English dowarye, dowerie, from Anglo-Norman dowarie, douarie, from Old French douaire, from Medieval Latin dōtārium, from Latin dōs. Doublet of dower.

definition: Lacking in liveliness or charm or surprise.
example: Her drab personality.
etymology: Probably from Middle French and Old French drap (“cloth”), either: * from Late Latin drappus (“drabcloth, kerchief; piece of cloth”), most likely from Gaulish *drappo, from Proto-Indo-European *drep- (“to scratch, tear”);

definition: Someone who is drafted and illegally refuses to serve.
example: During the Vietnam War, thousands of draft dodgers fled to Canada to avoid serving.

definition: Covered with or as if with clothes or a wrap or cloak.
example: A beam draped with cobwebs.

definition: A serving of drink (usually alcoholic) drawn from a keg.
example: She could feel a draught where she was sitting.
etymology: From Middle English draught, draght, draȝt, from Old English *dreaht, *dræht (related to dragan (“to draw, drag”)), from Proto-Germanic *drahtuz, noun form of *draganą; equivalent to draw + -t.

definition: Beer drawn from a keg.
Horse adapted for drawing heavy loads.
The quality of being a hindrance.
example: He pointed out all the drawbacks to my plan.
etymology: From draw + back. Compare setback.

definition: Dreamy in mood or nature.
example: I love the doctor in that American TV show: he is so dreamy!
etymology: From dream + -y.

definition: Lacking in liveliness or charm or surprise.
example: A series of dreary dinner parties.

definition: Cover before cooking.
example: Dredge the chicken in flour before frying it.
etymology: From Scots dreg-boat, dreg-bot (from Old English *dreċġ); or alternatively from Middle Dutch dregghe (“drag-net”), probably ultimately from the same root as drag.

definition: Mention something unpleasant from the past.
example: Where did you dredge up the idea that they didn't know what hospital he was born in?

definition: A bucket for lifting material from a channel or riverbed.
Abundantly covered or supplied with; often used in combination.
example: Drenched in moonlight.

definition: Abundantly covered or supplied with; often used in combination.
example: Drenched in moonlight.

definition: A hanger that is shaped like a person's shoulders and used to hang garments on.
A substance that promotes drying (e.g., calcium oxide absorbs water and is used to remove moisture).
etymology: From Middle English driere, dreyere (“one who dries”), equivalent to dry + -er (agent noun suffix).

definition: A person who drinks liquids.
example: A heavy drinker.
etymology: From Middle English drinkere, drynkere, from Old English drincere (“drinker”), from Proto-Germanic *drinkārijaz (“drinker”), equivalent to drink + -er.

definition: (architecture) a projection from a cornice or sill designed to protect the area below from rainwater (as over a window or doorway).
Pretentious or silly talk or writing.
etymology: From earlier drule, apparently a corruption of drivel (compare snool from snivel). Compare also Middle English drullen (“to stagger, drool”), Dutch druilen (“to be listless, snooze”).

definition: Envy without restraint.
An earring with a pendant ornament.
A retractable fin keel used on sailboats to prevent drifting to leeward.
Someone who quits school before graduation.
example: The politicians of the world are mere political university dropouts.
etymology: Deverbal from drop out.

definition: A retail shop where medicine and other articles are sold.
etymology: From drug + store.

definition: The act of playing drums.
example: He practiced his drumming several hours every day.

definition: A kiln for drying and seasoning lumber.
A United States dry unit equal to 2 pints or 67.2 cubic inches.
Being twofold; a classification into two opposed parts or subclasses.
example: The moral duality of certain characters.
etymology: From Latin duālitās. Equivalent to dual + -ity.

definition: A genre of electronic music descended from 2-step garage, characterised by its dark mood, sparse, half-step and two-step rhythms, an average bpm of 140 and an emphasis on sub-bass.
etymology: From dub + 2-step garage; originally dub step, from 2001.

definition: The domain controlled by a duke or duchess.
etymology: From Middle English duche, from Anglo-Norman duché, from Old French duc, or from Medieval Latin ducātus, from Latin dux. Doublet of ducat and dogate.

definition: Hunting ducks.
example: They gave him a ducking in the river as a punishment.
etymology: By surface analysis, duck + -ing.

definition: A gland that secretes externally through a duct.
Either of two low shelters on either side of a baseball diamond where the players and coaches sit during the game.
etymology: From the verb phrase dug out.

definition: Small balls or strips of boiled or steamed dough.
Having a dun color.
A recreational vehicle with large tires used on beaches or sand dunes.
Bicycling or motorcycling on sand dunes.
Fertilize or dress with dung.
example: You must dung the land.
etymology: From Middle English dung, dunge, donge, from Old English dung (“dung; excrement; manure”), from Proto-West Germanic *dungu, from Proto-Germanic *dungō (“dung”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʰ- (“to cover”).

definition: Any of numerous beetles that roll balls of dung on which they feed and in which they lay eggs.
(used technically of a device or process) having two parts.
example: A duplex transaction.
etymology: PIE word *dwóh₁ Borrowed from Latin duplex (“double, two-fold”), from duo (“two”) + plico (“fold together”); compare the roots of διπλόος (diplóos, “double”); compare also πλέκω (plékō, “twist, braid”).

definition: An apartment having rooms on two floors that are connected by a staircase.
A house with two units sharing a common wall.
A copy that corresponds to an original exactly.
example: He made a duplicate for the files.
etymology: From Middle English duplicacioun, from Middle French duplication, from Late Latin duplicātiō, duplicātiōnem, from Latin duplicō. Morphologically duplicate + -ion.

definition: Compulsory force or threat.
example: Confessed under duress.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English duresse, from Old French duresse, from Latin dūritia (“hardness”), from dūrus (“hard”).

definition: A paper jacket for a book; a jacket on which promotional information is usually printed.
A fine powder for spreading on the body (as after bathing).
Low-growing tufted deciduous shrub of northern and alpine North America having pink to coral-red flowers followed by sweet blue berries.
Fast-growing shrubby Asian tree naturalized in United States for shelter or ornament.
A procumbent variety of the common juniper.
Creeping raspberry of north temperate regions with yellow or orange berries.
Small early blooming tulip.
Gradually decreasing until little remains.
example: There is dwindling support for New Labour.

definition: A becoming gradually less.
example: There is no greater sadness that the dwindling away of a family.

definition: A measure of the resistance to flow of a fluid under an applied force.
In a forceful dynamic manner.
example: This pianist plays dynamically.
etymology: From dynamic + -ally.

definition: Generator consisting of a coil (the armature) that rotates between the poles of an electromagnet (the field magnet) causing a current to flow in the armature.
example: That new Vice President of Marketing is a real dynamo; sales have already gone up this quarter.
etymology: A shortening of dynamo-electric machine. The element dynamo- is ultimately from Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”).

definition: Impaired ability to learn to read.
Of or pertaining to or resembling a dystopia.
etymology: From dystopia + -an.

definition: Jewelry to ornament the ear; usually clipped to the earlobe or fastened through a hole in the lobe.
etymology: From Middle English erering, from Old English ēarhring (“ear-ring”), from Proto-West Germanic *auʀahring, equivalent to ear + ring.

definition: A small earthquake.
Conspicuously and tastelessly indecent.
example: An earthy sense of humor.
etymology: From Middle English erthy, equivalent to earth + -y. Compare German erdig (“earthy”), Swedish jordig (“earthy”).

definition: Moving toward the east.
example: Eastbound trains.
etymology: From east + -bound.

definition: Moving toward the east.
etymology: From Middle English estward, from Old English ēastweard, ēasteweard; equivalent to east + -ward.

definition: Flow back or recede.
example: The tides ebbed at noon.
etymology: From Middle English ebbe, from Old English ebba (“ebb, tide”), from Proto-West Germanic *abbjā, from Proto-Germanic *abjô, *abjǭ, from Proto-Germanic *ab (“off, away”), from Proto-Indo-European *apó.

definition: Flow back or recede.
example: The tides ebbed at noon.

definition: Flow back or recede.
example: The tides ebbed at noon.

definition: Flow back or recede.
example: The tides ebbed at noon.

definition: Flow back or recede.
example: The tides ebbed at noon.

definition: Attire that is appropriate to wear in a church.
Attire that is appropriate to wear in a church.
Concerned with promoting unity among churches or religions.
example: Ecumenical thinking.
etymology: From ecumenic + -al. By surface analysis, ecumene + -ical.

definition: (early Christian church) one of seven gatherings of bishops from around the known world under the presidency of the Pope to regulate matters of faith and morals and discipline.

definition: Border consisting of anything placed on the edge to finish something (such as a fringe on clothing or on a rug).
Plant whose succulent young shoots are cooked and eaten as a vegetable.

definition: Eel-shaped freshwater fish of South America having electric organs in its body.

definition: The activity of thrilling or markedly exciting some person or group.

definition: A sweet flavored liquid (usually containing a small amount of alcohol) used in compounding medicines to be taken by mouth in order to mask an unpleasant taste.

definition: Exceedingly; extremely.
example: He painted fantastically with everything as if in a dream.
etymology: From fantastic + -ally.

definition: To the greatest distance in space or time (‘farthest’ is used more often than ‘furthest’ in this physical sense).
example: See who could jump the farthest.

definition: (baseball) a pitch thrown with maximum velocity.
example: He swung late on the fastball.

definition: Firmly closed or secured.

definition: Having momentous consequences; of decisive importance.

definition: A regulator for controlling the flow of a liquid from a reservoir.

definition: Showing approval.

definition: Causing fear or dread or terror.

definition: A long thin fluffy scarf of feathers or fur.

definition: Adorned with feathers or plumes.
example: A feathered hat.

definition: Solid excretory product evacuated from the bowels.
Solid excretory product evacuated from the bowels.
etymology: From Latin faecēs, nominative plural of faex (“residue, dregs”), further origin unknown; possibly borrowed from a substrate language.

definition: An advocate of federalism.
etymology: From federal + -ist.

definition: A hat made of felt with a creased crown.
etymology: From a 19th-century play by Victorien Sardou titled Fédora. The heroine, Fédora Romazov, wore a center-creased, soft brimmed hat.

definition: Pathetically lacking in force or effectiveness.
example: A feeble excuse.

definition: Showing courage.
example: The champion is faced with a feisty challenger.
etymology: First use appears c. 1875 in the US. From feist (“a small, aggressive dog”) + -y;

definition: Of or relating to cats.
example: Feline fur.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin fēlīnus, from fēlēs (“wildcat, marten”).

definition: Someone who has committed a crime or has been legally convicted of a crime.
etymology: The adjective is derived from Middle English feloun, felun (“base, wicked; hostile; of an animal: dangerous; of words: angry, harsh, slanderous; of things: dangerous, deadly; false, fraudulent;

example: Phimosis of the prepuce of the clitoris: indication for female circumcision by D G McLintock in J R Soc Med. 1985 March; 78(3): 257–258.
etymology: From female + circumcision.

definition: The trait of behaving in ways considered typical for women.
etymology: From Middle English femynynytee, femyninytee, variants of femynyte (archaic modern English feminity), equivalent to feminine + -ity.

definition: The longest and thickest bone of the human skeleton; extends from the pelvis to the knee.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin femur (“thigh”).

definition: A person who won't take sides in a controversy.
Try to manage without help.
example: The youngsters had to fend for themselves after their parents died.
etymology: From Middle English fēnd, feond, from Old English fēond (“adversary, foe, enemy, fiend, devil, Satan”), from Proto-Germanic *fijandz, present participle of *fijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hate”).

definition: Argue or speak in defense of.
Prevent the occurrence of; prevent from happening; to protect from or to keep away anything undesirable; to ward off.
example: They tried citronella to fend off the mosquitos, to no avail.

definition: A collision between motor vehicles that produces minor damage.
example: My insurance went up even though all my accidents were just fender-benders.

definition: Pteridophytes of other classes than Filicopsida.
Genera of ferns and fern allies.
Southeastern Indian cycad with palmlike foliage.
The asexual spore of ferns that resembles dust; once thought to be seeds and to make the possessor invisible.
example: Superstition held that fern seed renders one invisible.

definition: Marked by extreme and violent energy.
example: A ferocious beating.
etymology: Taken from Latin ferōx (“wild, bold, savage, fierce”) + -ous.

definition: Search and discover through persistent investigation.
example: She ferreted out the truth.

definition: Creation by the physical union of male and female gametes; of sperm and ova in an animal or pollen and ovule in a plant.
etymology: From French fertilisation; equivalent to fertilize + -ation.

definition: The age of an embryo counting from the time of fertilization.
Characterized by intense emotion.
example: A fervent desire to change society.

definition: Feelings of great warmth and intensity.
example: The coach trains his water polo team with fervor.
etymology: From Middle English fervour, from Old French, from Latin fervor (“a boiling or raging heat, heat, vehemence, passion”), from fervere (“to boil, be hot”); see fervent.

definition: The position and authority of a feudal lord.
(superlative of ‘few’ used with count nouns and usually preceded by ‘the’) quantifier meaning the smallest in number.
example: The fewest birds in recent memory.

definition: A covering material made of glass fibers in resins.
Development of excess fibrous connective tissue in an organ.

definition: Marked by erratic changeableness in affections or attachments.
example: Fickle friends.
etymology: From Middle English fikil, fikel, from Old English ficol (“fickle, cunning, tricky, deceitful”), equivalent to fike + -le. More at fike.

definition: An imaginary person represented in a work of fiction (play or film or story).
Relating to or of the nature of a legal trust (i.e. the holding of something in trust for another).
example: A fiduciary contract.
etymology: From Latin fīdūciārius (“held in trust”), from fīdūcia (“trust”).

definition: The legal duty of a fiduciary to act in the best interests of the beneficiary.
The legal relation that exists when one person justifiably places reliance on another whose aid or protection is sought in some matter.
Rations issued for United States troops in the field.

definition: Seeds used as livestock feed.
Stout North American thistle with purplish-pink flower heads.
A member of the baseball team that is in the field instead of at bat.

etymology: From Middle English feldere (“one who works in the field; rustic”), from Old English feldeware (“field-dweller”), equivalent to field + -er. The baseball sense is from 1832.

definition: A cruel wicked and inhuman person.

definition: The decade from 1950 to 1959.

definition: (used of the meanings of words or text) not literal; using figures of speech.

definition: A very slender natural or synthetic fiber.

definition: A young female horse under the age of four.

etymology: From Old Norse fylja (whence Danish føl), related to foal. Cognate with Dutch veulen, German Fohlen.

definition: A metal plate projecting from the keel of a shallow vessel to give it greater lateral stability.

definition: Having a smooth, fine-grained structure.
Having fine teeth set close together.

definition: Play in which children pretend to put out a fire.
example: The fireman's job was about to get very interesting; they had just run out of coal!

definition: Wood used for fuel.

definition: (computer science) coded instructions that are stored permanently in read-only memory.

Australasian fern with clusters of sporangia on stems of fertile fronds.

Shrubby raspberry of eastern North America having showy rose to purplish flowers and red or orange thimble-shaped fruit.

definition: Powerful and effective language.

A rapid active commotion.

definition: Move along rapidly and lightly; skim or dart.

Being in focus or brought into focus.
The system of numbering pages.

definition: (used only in combinations) the height or length of something in feet.

definition: Covered with forest.
example: Efforts to protect forested lands of the northwest.
etymology: From forest + -ed.

definition: A short introductory essay preceding the text of a book.
etymology: Morphologically fore- + word. Calque of German Vorwort, itself a calque of Latin praefatio (“preface”).

definition: Surrendered as a penalty.
Something that is lost or surrendered as a penalty.

etymology: From Middle English forfeture, from Old French forfaiture.

definition: A copy that is represented as the original.

definition: A requirement of etiquette or custom.
example: A mere formality.

definition: (computer science) the usable capacity of a disk drive; the amount of space that is left after the sector headings and boundary definitions and timing information have been added by formatting the disk.

definition: An asset of special worth or utility.

The time of life between 40 and 50.

Separating something into fine particles.

Pleasant-smelling.

Cause to lose courage; to be daunted; to be scared away.
