etymology: Borrowed from Italian gusto, from Latin gustus (“taste”). Doublet of cost (see Etymology 3 there).

definition: Athletic facility equipped for sports or physical training.
etymology: From Latin gymnasium, from Ancient Greek γυμνάσιον (gumnásion, “exercise, school”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”), because Greek athletes trained naked.

definition: An athlete who is skilled in gymnastics.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek γυμναστής (gumnastḗs, “trainer of athletes”), from γυμνάζω (gumnázō, “I train naked, exercise”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”).

definition: European moth introduced into North America; a serious pest of shade trees.
Commonly used or practiced; usual.
example: His habitual comment.
etymology: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English habitual (“of one's inherent disposition”), from Medieval Latin habituālis (“customary; habitual”), from Latin habitus (“character; disposition; habit;

definition: Someone who is repeatedly arrested for criminal behavior (especially for the same criminal behavior).
A carriage for hire.
A carriage for hire.
An epigrammatic Japanese verse form of three short lines.
example: Haiku, a poem.
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 俳(はい)句(く) (haiku), from Middle Chinese 俳 (beaj, “paralleled [writing]”) + 句 (kɨoᴴ, “line”).

definition: A hand-held electric blower that can blow warm air onto the hair; used for styling hair.
Someone who cuts or beautifies hair.
etymology: From hair + dress + -er.

definition: A very thin line.
example: It's just a receding hairline — it's not like you're going bald.
etymology: From hair + line.

definition: The fifth pillar of Islam is a pilgrimage to Mecca during the month of Dhu al-Hijja; at least once in a lifetime a Muslim is expected to make a religious journey to Mecca and the Kaaba.
example: For a Muslim the hajj is the ultimate act of worship.
etymology: From Arabic حَجّ (ḥajj, “pilgrimage”), from حَجَّ (ḥajja, “to go, to repair”).

definition: A hatchet with a half axe head.
A small short-billed Old World snipe.
A tennis return made by hitting the ball immediately after it bounces.
Driven insane.
A primitive shelter, often temporary, having a significant portion of its structure dug below ground level; commonly has sod walls and a sod roof.
Worthy of religious veneration.
example: Jerusalem's hallowed soil.
etymology: From Middle English halwed (“hallowed, sacred, sanctified”), from Old English ġehālgod (“hallowed, sacred, sanctified”), past participle of hālgian (“to hallow, make holy”). Equivalent to hallow + -ed. More at hallow.

definition: A blight affecting the leaves of oats and other grasses.
Disabled in the feet or legs.
example: His halting speech.

definition: A round bun shaped to hold a hamburger patty.
The act of pounding (delivering repeated heavy blows).
example: The sudden hammer of fists caught him off guard.

definition: A small natural hill.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish hamaca, from Taíno *hamaka (compare Lokono hamaka, Wayuu jama'a), from Proto-Arawak *maka.

definition: Make ineffective or powerless.
example: The teachers were hamstrung by the overly rigid schedules.
etymology: From ham (“region back of the knee joint”) + string.

definition: A lawn mower that is operated by hand.
A small rubber ball used in playing the game of handball.
etymology: From hand + ball.

definition: The court on which handball is played.
A square piece of cloth used for wiping the eyes or nose or as a costume accessory.
Telephone set with the mouthpiece and earpiece mounted on a single handle.
etymology: From hand + set.

definition: A rider of a hang glider.
etymology: Calque of German Hängegleiter, from hängen (“hang”) + gleiten (“glide”).

definition: Gliding in a hang glider.
A worker who hangs something.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English hanger, haunger, hangere, equivalent to hang + -er.

definition: Someone who persistently (and annoyingly) follows along.
etymology: Agent noun of hang on.

definition: A frequently visited place.
example: Every Friday, Geoff and his group of friends all met at their favorite hangout to talk and have a good time.
etymology: From hang + out, as a deverbal from hang out.

definition: An accidental happening.
example: He recorded all the little haps and mishaps of his life.
etymology: The verb is from Middle English happen, perhaps from Old English hæppan (“to move accidentally, slip”) and/or from Old Norse *happa, *heppa, from Proto-Germanic *hampijaną (“to fit in, be fitting”), from the noun.

definition: An edible American clam; the heavy shells were used as money by some American Indians.
Solder that contains copper; melts at a relatively high temperature; used for brazing.
(often plural) a subtitle whose text is irreversibly merged in original video frames.
example: Also, since you're not really encoding the video itself, the quality of the subbed version is a lot better for softsubs than hardsubs.

definition: Guided by practical experience and observation rather than theory.
example: A hard-nosed labor leader.
etymology: hard + nosed; originally referred to hard-tipped bullets.

definition: Of animals or plants that have a hard shell.
The property of being rigid and resistant to pressure; not easily scratched; measured on Mohs scale.
example: The hardness of the material was high.
etymology: From Middle English hardness, hardnesse, from Old English heardnes, from heard + -nes, equivalent to hard + -ness.

definition: Living quarters reserved for wives and concubines and female relatives in a Muslim household.
etymology: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish حرم (harem) (whence Turkish harem), from Arabic حَرَم (ḥaram, “something prohibited; sanctuary, women”);

definition: (mathematics) a progression of terms whose reciprocals form an arithmetic progression.
Musically pleasing.
example: The team worked in a harmonious atmosphere, achieving great results.
etymology: From Middle French harmonieux; by surface analysis, harmony + -ous.

definition: A cultivator that pulverizes or smooths the soil.
etymology: From Middle English harwe, harow, from Old English *hearwa (perhaps ultimately cognate with harvest), or from Old Norse harfr/herfi; compare Danish harve (“harrow”), Dutch hark (“rake”). Akin to Latin carpere.

definition: Extremely painful.
etymology: By surface analysis, harrow + -ing.

definition: Larval mite that sucks the blood of vertebrates including human beings causing intense irritation.
Erect perennial Old World herb of dry grassy habitats.
Sweetened porridge made of tapioca or flour or oatmeal cooked quickly in milk or water.
A false accusation of an offense or a malicious misrepresentation of someone's words or actions.
example: That article about the mayor is nothing more than a hatchet job.

definition: The production of young from an egg.
example: We got a good hatching from the swallowtail eggs.

definition: A spring-flowering shrub or small tree of the genus Crataegus.
etymology: From Middle English ha (interjection). Compare Old Norse há (interjection), Middle Low German ha, hā (interjection), Old High German aha, hei (interjection).

definition: The act of selling goods for a living.
A spring-flowering shrub or small tree of the genus Crataegus.
etymology: From Middle English hawthorn, from Old English hagaþorn, hæguþorn, from Proto-West Germanic *haguþorn; equivalent to haw (“hedge, enclosure”) + thorn.

definition: Fern of eastern North America with pale green fronds and an aroma like hay.
Filled or abounding with fog or mist.
example: A hazy view of the polluted city street.
etymology: From earlier hawsey (1625), a nautical term of uncertain origin. Possibly from Middle English *hasi, *haswy, from Old English haswiġ (“grey; ashen; dusky”), from Old English hasu (“dusky; grey;

definition: A blight of the heads of cereals.
Infestation of the scalp with lice.
A band worn around or over the head.
example: The earphones were held in place by a headband.
etymology: From Middle English *hedband, from Old English hēafodbænd, hēafodbend (“headband”), equivalent to head + band. Cognate with Old High German houbitbant (“headband”), Dutch hoofdband (“headband”).

definition: Not having a head or formed without a head.
example: The headless horseman.
etymology: From Middle English heedles, hevedles, from Old English hēafodlēas (“headless”), equivalent to head + -less.

definition: Vertical space available to allow easy passage under something.
etymology: Partly from Middle English hauedwei, from Old English hēafodweġ (“head-road, main-road”); partly as a shortening of ahead-way, the source of the nautical sense. By surface analysis, head + way.

definition: Heard through another rather than directly.
example: Hearsay information.
etymology: From Middle English hyere-zigginge (1340), here sey (ca. 1438), from the phrase heren seien (“to hear [people] say”). Compare equally old Middle High German hœrsagen (14th c.), whence modern Hörensagen.

definition: Evidence based on what someone has told the witness and not of direct knowledge.
A rule that declares not admissible as evidence any statement other than that by a witness.
An open recess in a wall at the base of a chimney where a fire can be built.
example: He laid a fire in the hearth and lit it.
etymology: From Middle English herth, herthe, from Old English heorþ, from Proto-West Germanic *herþ, from Proto-Germanic *herþaz, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kerh₃- (“heat; fire”).

definition: An annual contribution made by Roman Catholics to support the papal see.
Causing gladness and pleasure.
example: Is there a sight more heartwarming than a family reunion?

definition: Not acknowledging the God of Christianity and Judaism and Islam.
etymology: From Middle English hethen, from Old English hǣþen, from Proto-West Germanic *haiþin, from Proto-Germanic *haiþīnaz (“heathen, pagan”, adjective), equivalent to heath (“heathland”) + -en.

definition: A white or colorless mineral (BaSO4); the main source of barium.
(abbreviated ‘ha’) a unit of surface area equal to 100 ares (or 10,000 square meters).
etymology: Borrowed from French hectare, formed from Ancient Greek ἑκατόν (hekatón, “hundred”) + are, equivalent to hect- + are.

definition: Cactus of the genus Echinocactus having stout sharp spines.
The dominance or leadership of one social group or nation over others.
example: The hegemony of a single member state is not incompatible with a genuine confederation.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἡγεμονία (hēgemonía, “supremacy or leadership, chief command”), from ἡγεμών (hēgemṓn, “a leader, guide, commander, chief”), from ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “to lead”).

definition: A female heir.
etymology: From heir + -ess.

definition: The constant angle at which a helix cuts the elements of a cylinder or cone.
Any of numerous orchids of the genus Pterostylis having leaves in a basal rosette and green flowers often striped purple or brown or red with the dorsal sepal incurved to form a hood.
etymology: Calque of translingual Corybas, though an incorrect calque, as the taxonomic name is from Ancient Greek Κορῠ́βᾱς (Korŭ́bās), not κόρῠς (kórŭs, “helmet”).

definition: The edge of a piece of cloth; especially the finished edge that has been doubled under and stitched down.
example: The hem of her dress was stained.
etymology: A sound uttered in imitation of clearing the throat (onomatopoeia)

definition: Surround in a restrictive manner.
example: The building was hemmed in by flowers.

definition: The flow of blood from a ruptured blood vessel.
example: We got news that he died of a hemorrhage.

definition: Willow with long flexible twigs used in basketry.
Bother persistently with trivial complaints.
From this time forth; from now on.
example: Henceforth she will be known as Mrs. Smith.
etymology: From Middle English hennes forth, hens-forþ, hennes-forþ, from modification of Old English heonan forþ with an adverbial genitive suffix. By surface analysis, hence (“from here”) + forth (“forward”).

definition: Pertaining to or affecting the liver.
example: Hepatic ducts.
etymology: From Middle English epatik, from Late Latin hepaticus, from Ancient Greek ἡπατικός (hēpatikós, “of the liver”), from ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”).

definition: Proclaimed.
example: The royal couple's much heralded world tour.

definition: Hairy Eurasian plant with small yellow flowers and an astringent root formerly used medicinally.
etymology: From Middle English herbe-benet, from Old French herbe beneite (“blessed herb”) (because of its medicinal properties).

definition: In a subsequent part of this document or statement or matter etc.
etymology: From Old English hēræfter (“in the aftertime; later on”). By surface analysis, here + after.

definition: A person who holds religious beliefs in conflict with the dogma of the Roman Catholic Church.
One retired from society for religious reasons.
Small soft-bodied marine crustaceans living in cast-off shells of gastropods.
Rupture in smooth muscle tissue through which a bodily structure protrudes.
example: Give someone a hernia.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin hernia (“protruded viscus”). See also yarn and cord.

definition: The common porpoise of the northern Atlantic and Pacific.
Made warm or hot (‘het’ is a dialectal variant of ‘heated’).
example: He was all het up and sweaty.
etymology: From Middle English hette (simple past), het (past participle), from Old English hǣtte (simple past), (ġe)hǣted (past participle), conjugations of hǣtan (“to heat”); see heat (“to make hot”).

definition: Made warm or hot (‘het’ is a dialectal variant of ‘heated’).
example: He was all het up and sweaty.
etymology: Irregular form of heat up.

definition: Consisting of elements that are not of the same kind or nature.
example: The population of the United States is vast and heterogeneous.
etymology: From Medieval Latin heterogeneus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερογενής (heterogenḗs, “of different kinds”), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + γένος (génos, “kind”). Compare hetero- and -ous.

definition: A nut with a hexagonal shape.
The period of greatest prosperity or productivity.
example: The early twentieth century was the heyday of the steam locomotive.
etymology: Late 16th century, from earlier heyda (1520s), as exclamation; compare hey, hei and Swedish hej då.

definition: A small inflamed elevation of the skin; a pustule or papule; common symptom in acne.
example: Take a hickey.

definition: Valuable tough heavy hardwood from various hickory trees.
Small hard-shelled nut of North American hickory trees especially the shagbark hickories.
A small two-needled upland pine of the eastern United States (Appalachians) having dark brown flaking bark and thorn-tipped cone scales.
American hardwood tree bearing edible nuts.
A hiding place; usually a remote place used by outlaws.
example: They'll never find us in this makeshift hideout we've got in the woods.
etymology: From hide + out.

definition: A secondary menu that appears while you are holding the cursor over an item on the primary menu.
Noisy and mischievous merrymaking.
In a domineering high-handed manner.
example: He behaved high-handedly toward his employees.
etymology: From high-handed + -ly.

definition: Used of gasoline; having a high octane number.
etymology: From high + octane. First use appears c. 1931 in the Oakland Tribune.

definition: Having high principles.
A vigorous Scottish reel.
A headscarf worn by Muslim women; conceals the hair and neck and usually has a face veil that covers the face.
Take arbitrarily or by force.
example: Hijack the radio show.
etymology: Possibly from a blend of highway + jacker (“one who holds up”) (1915).

definition: Robbery of a traveller or vehicle in transit or seizing control of a vehicle by the use of force.
etymology: From hijack + -ing.

definition: In a hilarious manner.
example: Hilariously funny.
etymology: From hilarious + -ly.

definition: The peak of a hill.
Having hills and crags.
example: Hilly terrain.
etymology: From Middle English hilly, hylly, hully, equivalent to hill + -y.

definition: Something immaterial that interferes with or delays action or progress.
example: High-heeled shoes may be fashionable, but they can also be a hindrance to walking.
etymology: From Middle English hinderance, hinderaunce, hindraunce, hynderaunce, hynderawnce, hynderawns, hyndrance; equivalent to hinder + -ance.

definition: A youth subculture (mostly from the middle class) originating in San Francisco in the 1960s; advocated universal love and peace and communes and long hair and soft drugs; favored acid rock and progressive rock music.
Someone who rejects the established culture; advocates extreme liberalism in politics and lifestyle.
Make a sharp hissing sound, as if to show disapproval.
example: As I started to poke it, the snake hissed at me.
etymology: From Middle English hissen, probably of onomatopoeic origin (compare Arabic هَسْهَسَ (hashasa)). Compare Middle Dutch hissen, hisschen (“to chase away, shoo”), Middle Low German hissen (“to chase, hound, incite”).

definition: Used in negative statement to describe a situation that has existed up to this point or up to the present time.
etymology: The adverb is derived from Middle English hiderto (“to the present time, until now; up to this point”), from hider (“in this direction, to or toward this place;

definition: An itchy skin eruption characterized by weals with pale interiors and well-defined red margins; usually the result of an allergic response to insect bites or food or drugs.
etymology: Uncertain, but frequently connected with heave, even if such a derivation is phonologically difficult.

definition: Save up as for future use.
etymology: From Middle English hord, from Old English hord (“an accumulation of valuable objects cached for preservation or future use; treasure; hoard”), from Proto-West Germanic *hoʀd, from Proto-Germanic *huzdą (“treasure;

definition: Large outdoor signboard.
etymology: From hoard (“structure”) + -ing.

definition: A vagrant.
etymology: Unknown. Possibly a contraction of ho, boy or the dialectal English term hawbuck (“lout, clumsy fellow, country bumpkin”).

definition: A place where hoboes camp.
The handle of a hoe.
Southeast Asian badger with a snout like a pig.
Highly infectious virus disease of swine.
Evergreen mat-forming shrub of North America and northern Eurasia having small white flowers and red berries; leaves turn red in autumn.
A sheep up to the age of one year; one yet to be sheared.
example: They sent a lorryload of hoggs to the auction mart, and they will keep the rest for their own flock.
etymology: See hogget (“young sheep”)

definition: Raise or haul up with or as if with mechanical help.
example: Hoist the bicycle onto the roof of the car.
etymology: Alteration of earlier hoise (“to hoist”), apparently based on the past tense forms, from Middle Dutch hisen (“to hoist”). Compare modern Dutch hijsen (“to hoist”), German hissen (“to hoist”), Danish hejse (“to hoist”).

definition: A pen where livestock is temporarily confined.
Any of various ferns of the genus Polystichum having fronds with texture and gloss like holly.
The intermediate photograph (or photographic record) that contains information for reproducing a three-dimensional image by holography.
Of or relating to holography or holograms.
example: A holographic will or testament.
etymology: By surface analysis, holo- + -graph + -ic.

definition: A sheath (usually leather) for carrying a handgun.
etymology: From Dutch holster (“pistol-case, holster”), from Middle Low German holster, from Old Saxon *holster, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hulastrą, *hulistrą (“hull, case, covering”).

definition: Tall Old World biennial thistle with large clasping white-blotched leaves and purple flower heads; naturalized in California and South America.
Brewed at home.
example: Home-brewed beer.

definition: Someone who owns a home.
etymology: From home + owner.

definition: All of the same or similar kind or nature.
example: A close-knit homogeneous group.
etymology: From Medieval Latin homogeneus, from Ancient Greek ὁμογενής (homogenḗs, “of the same race, family or kind”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) + γένος (génos, “kind”). Compare homo- (“same”) and -ous (adjectival suffix).

definition: A whetstone made of fine gritstone; used for sharpening razors.
etymology: Cognate with Icelandic hnúður. Distantly related to knot.

definition: A disorderly outburst or tumult.
A long cloak with a hood that can be pulled over the head.
Medium-sized blackish-grey seal with large inflatable sac on the head; of Arctic and northern Atlantic waters.
Walk.
example: Let's hoof it to the disco.

definition: A visible impression on a surface made by the hoof of an animal.
A hooked tool, usually of metal, used to clean the hooves of a horse; some designs include a small, very stiff brush for removing additional mud or dirt.
A visible impression on a surface made by the hoof of an animal.
Having an aquiline nose.
A device providing a connection between a power source and a user.
example: Some campsites have electrical hookups for trailers.
etymology: A deverbal from hook up.

definition: In a hopeless manner.
example: The papers were hopelessly jumbled.
etymology: From hopeless + -ly.

definition: A vast multitude.
example: We were beset by a horde of street vendors who thought we were tourists and would buy their cheap souvenirs.
etymology: Recorded in English since 1555.

definition: Having a horn or horns or hornlike parts or horns of a particular kind.
example: Horned viper.
etymology: From Middle English horned, hornyd, from Old English hyrned, ġehyrned (“having horns; horned”), from Proto-Germanic *hurnidaz (“horned”), past participle of Proto-Germanic *hurnijaną (“to horn;

definition: Large stinging paper wasp.
A prediction of someone's future based on the relative positions of the planets.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French horoscope, from Medieval Latin horoscopus, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκόπος (hōroskópos), from ὥρα (hṓra, “any limited time”) + σκοπός (skopós, “watcher”). By surface analysis, horo- + -scope.

definition: Erect perennial strong-scented with serrate pointed leaves and a loose panicle of yellowish flowers; the eastern United States.
Largest tuna; to 1500 pounds; of mostly temperate seas: feed in polar regions but breed in tropics.
European annual wild lettuce having prickly stems; a troublesome weed in parts of United States.
A man skilled in equitation.
etymology: From Middle English horsman, equivalent to horse + man.

definition: Game equipment consisting of an open ring of iron used in playing horseshoes.
example: The horseshoe of the Carpathians.
etymology: Calks (identified by the letter "C" on the shown horseshoe) consist of spur-point and a shank to form an antislipping device.

definition: A round arch that widens before rounding off.
Any of numerous bats of the family Hipposideridae of northwest Africa or Philippines or Australia having a horseshoe-shaped leaf on the nose.
etymology: The name refers to a horseshoe-shaped protuberance which these bats have on their noses.

definition: Large marine arthropod of the Atlantic coast of North America having a domed carapace that is shaped like a horseshoe and a stiff pointed tail; a living fossil related to the wood louse.
etymology: From horseshoe + crab, referencing this animal's horseshoe-like shape.

definition: Of or relating to the cultivation of plants.
etymology: From horticulture + -al.. By surface analysis, horti- + cult + -ure + -al.

definition: The cultivation of plants.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin *horticultūra. Attested since 1678.

definition: A period of time when you are confined to a hospital.
example: Now they try to shorten the patient's hospitalization.
etymology: From hospitalize + -ation. Piecewise doublet of hotelization.

definition: A place of political unrest and potential violence.
A rash or impetuous person.
A custodian who lives in and cares for a house while the regular occupant is away (usually without an exchange of money).
Common American wren that nests around houses.
The work of cleaning and running a house.
example: The computer program does some general housekeeping involving initializing variables and opening files before beginning the main processing.
etymology: From house + keeping.

definition: The work of cleaning and running a house.
etymology: From house + work. Cognate with Dutch huiswerk (“homework”).

definition: An expression of greeting.
etymology: Clipping of howdy-do, from how-d'ye-do (“how do you do”).

definition: Emit long loud cries.
example: Howl with sorrow.
etymology: From Middle English howlen, houlen, from Old English *hūlian, from Proto-West Germanic *hūilōn, from Proto-Germanic *hūwilōną, *hiuwilōną (“to howl”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *kū-, *kew- (“to howl, scream”).

definition: A flatbottom boat for carrying heavy loads (especially on canals).
example: Per packet per Hoy.
etymology: Borrowed from German Heu or Dutch gooi.

definition: Any of several winter squash plants producing large greyish-green football-shaped fruit with a rough warty rind.
An oriental tobacco pipe with a long flexible tube connected to a container where the smoke is cooled by passing through water.
Crowd or draw together.
example: Let's huddle together — it's cold!

definition: Crowded or massed together.
example: Give me … your huddled masses.
etymology: From huddle + -ed.

definition: Inhale recreational drugs.
example: The kids were huffing glue.
etymology: Probably an altered spelling of earlier *hough, represented by Scots hech (“to breathe hard, pant”). Compare also German hauchen (“to breathe”).

definition: A Polynesian rain dance performed by a woman.
etymology: Borrowed from Hawaiian hula.

definition: A highly energetic and indefatigable person.
Of or pertaining to Renaissance humanism.
example: The humanistic revival of learning.
etymology: From Middle French humaniste.

definition: All of the living human inhabitants of the earth.
example: She always used ‘humankind’ because ‘mankind’ seemed to slight the women.
etymology: From human + -kind.

definition: An automaton that resembles a human being.
etymology: From human (from Latin hūmānus m (“of or belonging to a man, human, humane”, adjective)) + -oid.

definition: Causing awareness of your shortcomings.
example: Golf is a humbling game.

definition: In a humble manner.
example: He humbly lowered his head.
etymology: From Middle English humbely, humbliche. By surface analysis, humble + -ly. Displaced Old English ēaþmōdlīċe.

definition: Cause to feel shame; hurt the pride of.
example: He humiliated his colleague by criticising him in front of the boss.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin humiliātus, perfect passive participle of humiliō (“to abase, humble”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin humilis (“lowly, humble”), from humus (“ground; earth, soil”); see humble.

definition: A humming noise.
etymology: From hum + -ing.

definition: A top that makes a humming noise as it spins.
An impression that something might be the case.
example: The old man walked with a hunch.
etymology: Assibilated variant of hunk, of uncertain origin. Alternatively, a derivative of hump, via an earlier Middle English *hunche, *humpchin, from *hump + -chin, -chen (diminutive suffix), equivalent to hump + -kin.

definition: Round one's back by bending forward and drawing the shoulders forward.
Round one's back by bending forward and drawing the shoulders forward.
A traditional Irish game resembling hockey; played by two teams of 15 players each.
Moving rapidly or performed quickly or in great haste.
example: A hurried trip to the store.

definition: Conducted with or marked by hidden aims or methods.
example: The spy program was very hush-hush: no-one ever spoke of it.

definition: A cage (usually made of wood and wire mesh) for small animals.
etymology: From Middle English hucche (“storage chest”), variation of whucce, from Old English hwiċe, hwiċċe (“box, chest”).

definition: (genetics) the tendency of a crossbred organism to have qualities superior to those of either parent.
Supply water or liquid to in order to maintain a healthy balance.
example: The bicyclists must be hydrated frequently.
etymology: From French hydrate, from Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + -ate.

definition: A caustic substance produced by heating limestone.
A compound of an oxide with water.
An organic compound containing only carbon and hydrogen.
etymology: From hydro- + carbon.

definition: Of or relating to or used in the production of electricity by waterpower.
example: Hydroelectric power.
etymology: From hydro- + electric.

definition: Turbine consisting of a large and efficient version of a water wheel used to drive an electric generator.
A salt of carbonic acid (containing the anion HCO3) in which one hydrogen atom has been replaced; an acid carbonate.

A highly poisonous gas or volatile liquid that smells like bitter almonds; becomes a gas at around 90 degree Fahrenheit and is most dangerous when inhaled; the anhydride of hydrocyanic acid; used in manufacturing.
A colorless poisonous corrosive liquid made by the action of sulphuric acid on calcium fluoride; solutions in water are hydrofluoric acid.
A viscous liquid with strong oxidizing properties; a powerful bleaching agent; also used (in aqueous solutions) as a mild disinfectant and (in strong concentrations) as an oxidant in rocket fuels.
A salt or an ester of sulphuric acid with the chemical formula HSO4-.
Enlarged beyond truth or reasonableness.
example: A hyperbolic style.
etymology: From Latin hyperbolic(us), from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολικός (huperbolikós). First attested in the 15th century. By surface analysis, hyperbol(e) + -ic.

definition: (mathematics) a non-Euclidean geometry in which the parallel axiom is replaced by the assumption that through any point in a plane there are two or more lines that do not intersect a given line in the plane.
example: Karl Gauss pioneered hyperbolic geometry.
etymology: The terminology was introduced in 1871 by Felix Klein, who classified some non-Euclidean geometries as hyperbolisch (“hyperbolic”), elliptisch (“elliptical”), and parabolisch (“parabolic”).

definition: Of or relating to hypnosis.
example: Hypnotic seeds.

definition: Lettuce with crisp tightly packed light-green leaves in a firm head.
example: Iceberg is still the most popular lettuce.

definition: A plastic or metal utensil used for cake and pastry decoration, similar in principle to a pastry bag.
(philosophy) the philosophical theory that ideas are the only reality.
etymology: First attested 1796, from ideal + -ism.

definition: Of or relating to the philosophical doctrine of the reality of ideas.
etymology: From idealist + -ic or ideal + -istic.

definition: A symbol that establishes the identity of the one bearing it.
With respect to ideology.
example: Ideologically, we do not see eye to eye.
etymology: From ideological + -ly.

definition: Excellent and delightful in all respects.
example: An idyllic spot for a picnic.
etymology: From idyll + -ic.

definition: Set afire.
example: The ignited paper.

definition: Marked by or promising bad fortune.
example: An ill-fated business venture.
etymology: From ill + fated.

definition: Socially incorrect in behavior.
example: He was extremely ill-mannered and caused offence wherever he went.
etymology: Compare Middle English ille-ymanerite.

definition: Having an irritable and unpleasant disposition.
Lacking in correct logical relation.
example: I received an illogical reply and that left me standing there feeling confused.
etymology: From il- + logical.

definition: Tending to increase knowledge or dissipate ignorance.
example: An illuminating lecture.
etymology: From illuminate + -ing.

definition: Clarifying by use of examples.
example: This latest incident is illustrative of his continued bad behavior.
etymology: From illustrate + -ive.

definition: Immediate intuitive awareness.
A heating element that is immersed in the liquid that is to be heated (as in a hot-water tank).
The act of making immune (especially by inoculation).
example: Immunization against influenza is important for all child-care workers.
etymology: From French immunisation. Coined by Albert Calmette. Equivalent to immunize + -ation or immune + -ization.

definition: The branch of medical science that studies the body's immune system.
etymology: From immune + -ology.

definition: (folklore) fairies that are somewhat mischievous.
etymology: From Middle English impen, ympen (“to plant; (figuratively) to bury; to graft; to add to, insert, put into, set in;

definition: African antelope with ridged curved horns; moves with enormous leaps.
etymology: Borrowed from Zulu ímpala, from Proto-Bantu *mpàdá.

definition: South African shrub having a swollen succulent stem and bearing showy pink and white flowers after the leaves fall; popular as an ornamental in tropics.
Transmit (knowledge or skills).
example: Impart a new skill to the students.
etymology: From Middle English imparten, borrowed from Middle French impartir, empartir, from Late Latin impartiō, impertiō, from im- (“in”) + Latin partiō (“divide”).

definition: Challenge the honesty or veracity of.
example: The lawyers tried to impeach the credibility of the witnesses.
etymology: From Middle English empechen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman empecher, from Old French empeechier (“to hinder”), from Latin impedicāre (“to fetter”). Cognate with French empêcher (“to prevent”).

definition: A material's opposition to the flow of electric current; measured in ohms.
etymology: From impede + -ance. In sense 2 and sense 3 it was coined by English mathematician and physicist Oliver Heaviside in 1886.

definition: Be a hindrance or obstacle to.
example: She is impeding the progress of our project.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin impediō (“to shackle”), from pēs (“foot”) (compare pedestrian). First attested use as a verb was in William Shakespeare's Macbeth, see quotations.

definition: Something immaterial that interferes with or delays action or progress.
example: Working in a noisy factory left me with a slight hearing impediment.
etymology: From Middle English impediment, borrowed from Latin impedimentum.

definition: Not admitting of penetration or passage into or through.
example: An impenetrable fortress.
etymology: From Middle English inpenetrabel, inpenetrabyle, from Middle French impenetrable or directly from its etymon, Latin impenetrābilis. By surface analysis, im- + penetrable.

definition: Of or relating to imperialism.
example: Imperialistic wars.
etymology: From imperial + -ist, after French impérialiste.

definition: (embryology) the organic process whereby a fertilized egg becomes implanted in the lining of the uterus of placental mammals.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French implantation.

definition: Without doubting or questioning.
example: I implicitly trust him.
etymology: From implicit + -ly.

definition: The commercial activity of buying and bringing in goods from a foreign country.
etymology: From import + -ation.

definition: Someone whose business involves importing goods from outside (especially from a foreign country).
example: India is the world's biggest importer of gold.
etymology: From import + -er.

definition: The act of imposing something (as a tax or an embargo).
etymology: From Middle English imposicioun, from Old French imposicion, from Latin impositio.

definition: Incapability of existing or occurring.
example: Meeting the deadline is an impossibility; there is no way we can be ready in time.
etymology: From Middle French impossibilité, from Latin impossibilitās. By surface analysis, im- + possibility and impossible + -ity.

definition: Lacking power or ability.
example: Technology without morality is barbarous; morality without technology is impotent.
etymology: From Old French impotent, from Latin impotēns, from in- (expresses negation) + potēns (“powerful”).

definition: An extemporaneous speech or remark.
example: A witty impromptu must not sound premeditated.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French impromptu.

definition: A creation spoken or written or composed extemporaneously (without prior preparation).
example: He played a quick improvisation on the keyboard.
etymology: From French improvisation. Morphologically improvise + -ation.

definition: Exemption from punishment or loss.
etymology: From Middle French impunité, from Latin impunitas, from impunis (“without punishment”).

definition: In debt.
example: He fell behind with his mortgage payments.

definition: Without question and beyond doubt.
example: She told him off in spades.
etymology: From the card game of bridge, in which spades is the highest suit. Perhaps influenced by phrases with similar meaning, in spadefuls or in spate.

definition: In entirety.
example: They bought the business in toto.
etymology: From Latin in tōtō (“in all”).

definition: Belonging to the class of nouns denoting nonliving things.
example: The word ‘car’ is inanimate.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English inanimat(e), from Late Latin inanimātus, from Latin in- + animātus (“animated”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, in- + animate.

definition: In an inappropriate manner.
example: He was inappropriately dressed.
etymology: From inappropriate + -ly.

definition: Emitting light as a result of being heated.
example: An incandescent bulb.
etymology: Borrowed from French incandescent, from Latin incandescens, from incandesco (“be heated, glow”), from in- (intensifying prefix) + candesco (“become white”), from candidus (“white”).

definition: Lacking in or deprived of strength or power.
Involving deliberate burning of property.
example: An incendiary fire.

definition: A bomb that is designed to start fires; is most effective against flammable targets (such as fuel).
Any of several attractive trees of southwestern South America and New Zealand and New Caledonia having glossy evergreen leaves and scented wood.
Uninterrupted in time and indefinitely long continuing.
example: Night and day we live with the incessant noise of the city.
etymology: From Late Middle English incessaunte, from Late Latin incessāns, incessantem, from Latin in- + cessāns.

definition: A depression scratched or carved into a surface.
etymology: From Middle English inscicioun, from Middle French incision, from Late Latin incisiō from the verb incidō (“to cut into”) + action noun suffix -iō.

definition: Give an incentive for action.
example: The judge was told by the accused that his friends had incited him to commit the crime.
etymology: From Middle French inciter, from Latin incitō (“to set in motion, hasten, urge, incite”), from in (“in, on”) + citō (“to set in motion, urge”), frequentative of cieō (“to rouse, excite, call”).

definition: Have a tendency or disposition to do or be something; be inclined.
example: He inclined to corpulence.
etymology: From Middle English enclinen, from Old French encliner (modern incliner), from Latin inclīnō (“incline, tilt”), from in- + clīnō (compare -cline), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (English lean).

definition: With your identity concealed.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian incognito, from Latin incognitus (“unknown”), from in- (“not”) + cognitus (“known”), perfect passive participle of cognoscere.

definition: Without logical or meaningful connection.
example: A turgid incoherent presentation.
etymology: From in- + coherent.

definition: Incapable of being explained or accounted for.
etymology: From Middle French incomprehensible, from Latin incomprehēnsibilis. Equivalent to in- + comprehensible.

definition: Totally unlikely.
etymology: From in- + conceivable.

definition: Not conclusive; not putting an end to doubt or question.
example: An inconclusive reply.
etymology: From in- + conclusive.

definition: Lacking regard for the rights or feelings of others.
example: Shockingly inconsiderate behavior.
etymology: From in- + considerate.

definition: The relation between propositions that cannot both be true at the same time.
Charging or suggestive of guilt or blame.
example: Incriminatory testimony.
etymology: From incriminate + -ing.

definition: Maintaining something at the most favorable temperature for its development.
etymology: From Latin incubātiō, from incubō (“to lie on”).

definition: The period between infection and the appearance of symptoms of the disease.
Apparatus consisting of a box designed to maintain a constant temperature by the use of a thermostat; used for chicks or premature infants.
etymology: From incubate + -or.

definition: Incapable of being cured.
example: An incurable disease.
etymology: From Old French incurable, from Late Latin incurabilis.

definition: Owing gratitude or recognition to another for help or favors etc.
Not in keeping with accepted standards of what is right or proper in polite society.
example: Was buried with indecent haste.
etymology: From in- + decent.

definition: Not easily destroyed.
etymology: From in- + destructible.

definition: The act of classifying and providing an index in order to make items easier to retrieve.
example: Minimizing the number of indexings will make the algorithm more efficient.

definition: A feeling of righteous anger.
example: He protested in indignation.

definition: Much-branched erect herb with bright yellow flowers; distributed from Massachusetts to Florida.
Small deep blue North American bunting.
Failing to make or recognize distinctions.
example: How can anyone be so indiscriminate in making friends as he is?
etymology: First attested in 1598; from in- + discriminate.

definition: Not clearly defined or easy to perceive or understand.
example: Indistinct shapes in the gloom.
etymology: From Middle French indistinct, from Latin indistinctus. English equivalent in- + distinct.

definition: Exactly alike; incapable of being perceived as different.
example: They wore indistinguishable hats.
etymology: From in- + distinguishable.

definition: The quality of being individual.
example: So absorbed by the movement that she lost all sense of individuality.
etymology: Borrowed from French individualisme, equivalent to individual + -ism.

definition: The quality of being individual.
example: So absorbed by the movement that she lost all sense of individuality.
etymology: From individual + -ity. Displaced native Old English hād.

definition: Made for or directed or adjusted to a particular individual.
Accelerates a continuous beam of electrons to high speeds by means of the electric field produced by changing magnetic flux.
An inability to resist the gratification of whims and desires.
etymology: From Middle English indulgence, indulgens, from Middle French indulgence and its source, Latin indulgentia.

definition: Characterized by or given to yielding to the wishes of someone.
example: Indulgent grandparents.
etymology: From Latin indulgēns, indulgentem, present participle of indulgēre.

definition: The act of indulging or gratifying a desire.
The development of industry on an extensive scale.
etymology: From French industrialisation. Analyzable as industrial + -ization or industrialize + -ation.

definition: Made industrial; converted to industrialism.
example: Industrialized areas.
etymology: From industrialize + -ed.

definition: Not elegant or graceful in expression.
example: If the rumor is true, can anything be more inept than to repeat it now?
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French inepte, from Latin ineptus, from in- + aptus (whence English apt).

definition: Unable to move or resist motion.
etymology: From French inerte, from Latin iners (“inactive, inert”).

definition: Any of the chemically inert gaseous elements of the helium group in the periodic table.
Incapable of being explained or accounted for.
example: Inexplicable errors.
etymology: From Middle English inexplicable, from Middle French inexplicable, from Latin inexplicābilis, from in- (“not”) + explicābilis (“explicable”). By surface analysis, in- + explicable.

definition: In a manner differing from the usual or expected.
etymology: From inexplicable + -ly.

definition: Incapable of failure or error.
example: An infallible antidote.
etymology: From Medieval Latin īnfallibilis, from Latin in- + fallibilis. Compare French infaillible. By surface analysis, in- + fallible.

definition: Reason by deduction; establish by deduction.
etymology: From Latin inferō, from Latin in- (“in, at, on; into”) + Latin ferō (“bear, carry;

definition: Characteristic of or resembling Hell.
example: Infernal noise.
etymology: From Middle French infernal, from Medieval Latin infernalis, from Latin īnfernus, from īnferum (“netherworld, underworld, hell”), equivalent to inferno + -al.

definition: (Christianity) the abode of Satan and the forces of evil; where sinners suffer eternal punishment.
The area of a baseball field that is enclosed by 3 bases and home plate.
example: Let’s keep this problem in the infield.
etymology: From in- + field.

definition: A process in which individuals (or small groups) penetrate an area (especially the military penetration of enemy positions without detection).
etymology: From Middle English infiltracioun, from Medieval Latin infiltrātiōnem, infiltrātiō. By surface analysis, infiltrat(e) + -ion.

definition: Resulting from inflammation; hot and swollen and reddened.
example: Eyes inflamed with crying.

definition: A cushion usually made of rubber or plastic that can be inflated.
Exaggerate or make bigger.
example: The charges were inflated.
etymology: From Latin īnflātus, perfect passive participle of īnflō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of inblow.

definition: Without formality.
example: He visited us informally.
etymology: From informal + -ly.

definition: The sciences concerned with gathering, manipulating, storing, retrieving, and classifying recorded information.
etymology: German Informatik dates from 1957, French informatique from 1962.

definition: Relating to or having the nature of information.
example: The subway map was quite informational, allowing us to determine the most efficient route to our destination.
etymology: From information + -al.

definition: Not many times.
etymology: From infrequent + -ly or in- + frequently.

definition: Extremely annoying or displeasing.
example: Her infuriating indifference.
etymology: From infuriate + -ing.

definition: The power of creative imagination.
example: The pyramids demonstrate the ingenuity of the ancient Egyptians.
etymology: From Latin ingenuitās. Compare genius.

definition: (used especially of ideas or principles) deeply rooted; firmly fixed or held.
example: Ingrained habits of a lifetime.
etymology: From ingrain + -ed.

definition: The act of inhaling; the drawing in of air (or other gases) as in breathing.
etymology: From inhale + -ation.

definition: Inborn pattern of behavior often responsive to specific stimuli.
Held back or restrained or prevented.
example: In certain conditions previously inhibited conditioned reactions can reappear.

definition: Lacking and reflecting lack of pity or compassion.
example: Humans are innately inhumane; this explains much of the misery and suffering in the world.
etymology: Originally a variant spelling and pronunciation of inhuman, ultimately from Latin inhūmānus; it appears to have died out 17c. but returned c. 1822, probably a reformation as a negative of humane from in- + humane.

definition: Manifold that carries vaporized fuel from the carburetor to the inlet valves of the cylinders.
An automatic instinctive unlearned reaction to a stimulus.
Not injurious to physical or mental health.
etymology: From Latin innocuus (“harmless”) (therefore, no gemination in + nocuous).

definition: Bring something new to an environment.
example: To innovate a word or an act.
etymology: First attested in 1548; borrowed from Latin innovātus, perfect passive participle of innovō (“to renew”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: Someone who helps to open up a new line of research or technology or art.
etymology: From Late Latin innovātor, from innovō; equivalent to innovate + -or.

definition: Too numerous to be counted.
example: Innumerable difficulties.
etymology: From in- + numerable; from Middle English innumerable, from Latin innumerābilis, from in- + numerābilis.

definition: Relating or belonging to the class of compounds not having a carbon basis.
example: Hydrochloric and sulfuric acids are called inorganic substances.
etymology: From in- + organic.

definition: The chemistry of compounds that do not contain hydrocarbon radicals.
Any compound that does not contain carbon.
A salt of phosphoric acid.
A patient who is residing in the hospital where they are being treated.
etymology: From in- (“internal”) + patient.

definition: Impossible to satisfy.
example: An insatiate appetite.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English insaciable, from Middle French insatiable, from Old French insaciable, from Late Latin insatiabilis. By surface analysis, in- + satiable.

definition: Not capable of being separated.
example: Inseparable pieces of rock.
etymology: From Middle English, from Middle French inséparable, from Latin īnsēparābilis. Constructed as in- + separable.

definition: Internal organs collectively (especially those in the abdominal cavity).
Beguiling but harmful.
example: Insidious pleasures.

definition: A badge worn to show official position.
etymology: From Latin īnsīgnia, nominative plural of īnsīgne (“emblem, token, symbol”). Doublet of ensign.

definition: Repetitive and persistent.
example: The bluejay's insistent cry.
etymology: From Latin insistens, participle of insisto.

definition: To the degree or extent that.
example: Insofar as it can be ascertained, the horse lung is comparable to that of man.
etymology: Univerbation of in + so + far.

definition: The lack of financial resources.
example: The company faces insolvency.
etymology: From insolvent + -cy.

definition: A part of a broadcast serial.
Occurring with no delay.
example: Relief was instantaneous.
etymology: From New Latin īnstāntāneus, from Latin īnstantem.

definition: Impart gradually.
example: Her presence instilled faith into the children.

definition: Unthinking; prompted by (or as if by) instinct.
example: Offering to help was as instinctive as breathing.
etymology: From instinct + -ive.

definition: Officially placed in or committed to a specialized institution.
example: Had hopes of rehabilitating the institutionalized juvenile delinquents.

definition: Relating to or characteristic of or situated on an island.
example: Insular territories.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin īnsulāris (“of or belonging to an island”), from īnsula (“an island”), of uncertain origin.

definition: A water-resistant adhesive tape used to insulate exposed electrical conductors.
A person who takes part in an armed rebellion against the constituted authority (especially in the hope of improving conditions).
Not capable of being surmounted or overcome.
example: Insurmountable disadvantages.
etymology: From in- + surmountable.

definition: Organized opposition to authority; a conflict in which one faction tries to wrest control from another.
etymology: From Late Middle English insurreccion (“uprising against a government, rebellion, revolt; civil disorder, riot;

definition: A manifold consisting of a pipe to carry fuel to each cylinder in an internal-combustion engine.
(of especially business assets) not having physical substance or intrinsic productive value.
example: Intangible assets such as good will.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French intangible, from Medieval Latin intangibilis, from Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tango.

definition: Assets that are saleable though not material or physical.
In an intelligent manner.
example: She acted intelligently in this difficult situation.
etymology: From intelligent + -ly.

definition: Increase in extent or intensity.
example: To intensify the heat or cold.
etymology: From intense + -ify. Compare French intensifier.

definition: Among other things.
example: The committee recommended, inter alia, that he be promoted.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin inter alia.

definition: Extending or taking place between or among continents.
example: Intercontinental exploration.
etymology: From inter- + continental.

definition: An intervening period or episode.
etymology: From Latin inter- (“between”) + lūdō (“to play”).

definition: A negotiator who acts as a link between parties.
example: The intermediary between the manufacturer and retailer is the wholesaler.
etymology: From French intermédiaire, adjusted to simulate a borrowing from Medieval Latin *intermediārius.

definition: A shroud fitted on rigs with multiple spreaders.
The act of suspending activity temporarily.
example: We ordered some drinks for the intermission.
etymology: Derived from Latin intermissiō, from intermittō (“interrupt, omit”) + -tiō.

definition: In an intermittent manner.
example: Intermittently we questioned the barometer.
etymology: From intermittent + -ly.

definition: The secretion of an endocrine gland that is transmitted by the blood to the tissue on which it has a specific effect.
Reciprocal action and reaction.
etymology: From inter- + play.

definition: That provides interpretation.
A form of modern dance in which the dancer's movements depict an emotion or tell a story.
A form of modern dance in which the dancer's movements depict an emotion or tell a story.
North American fern having tall erect pinnate fronds and a few sporogenous pinnae at or near the center of the fertile fronds.
Meet at a point.
example: Parallel lines don't intersect.
etymology: From Latin intersecare (“to cut between, cut off”), from inter (“between”) + secare (“to cut”).

definition: An artery that is a branch of the superior mesenteric artery that supplies the jejunum.
Surgical operation that shortens the small intestine; used in treating obesity.
Harmless microorganisms (as Escherichia coli) that inhabit the intestinal tract and are essential for its normal functioning.
Inflammation of the stomach and intestines; can be caused by Salmonella enteritidis.
Blockage of the intestine (especially the ileum) that prevents the contents of the intestine from passing to the lower bowel.
In a close manner.
example: The two phenomena are intimately connected.
etymology: From intimate + -ly.

definition: Incapable of being tolerated or endured.
example: An intolerable degree of sentimentality.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English intolerable, borrowed from Middle French intolerable, from Latin intolerābilis. By surface analysis, in- + tolerable.

definition: The physiological state produced by a poison or other toxic substance.
example: He suffered acute intoxication from the combined effects of several drugs.

definition: Located or occurring within a cell or cells.
example: Intracellular fluid.
etymology: From intra- + cellular.

definition: Within or by means of a vein.
example: An intravenous inflammation.
etymology: From intra- + venous.

definition: Slow continuous drip introducing solutions intravenously (a drop at a time).
Administration of nutrients through a vein.
An injection into a vein.
Invulnerable to fear or intimidation.
example: Intrepid pioneers.
etymology: From French intrépide, from Latin intrepidus, from in- (“not”) + trepidus (“anxious, nervous”).

definition: With respect to its inherent nature.
etymology: From intrinsic + -ally.

definition: In an intuitive manner.
example: Inventors seem to have chosen intuitively a combination of explosive and aggressive sounds as warning signals to be used on automobiles.
etymology: From intuitive + -ly.

definition: Covered with water.
example: Inundated farmlands.

definition: Declare invalid.
example: The circuit court judge's ruling was invalidated by a superior judge.
etymology: First attested in 1649; borrowed from Middle French invalider, from invalide + -er. By surface analysis, in- + validate or invalid + -ate.

definition: Unaffected by a designated operation or transformation.
etymology: From in- + variant.

definition: A punctuation mark used to attribute the enclosed text to someone else.
etymology: From the appearance of an inverted comma. In lead type, an opening quote is not a separate casting. It is the result of rotating a comma 180°, inverting the comma. It is used singly or as double quotes.

definition: Pertaining to or characteristic of an invitation.
etymology: From invitation + -al.

definition: Large yellow American moth having a large eyelike spot on each hind wing; the larvae have stinging spines.
A nonmetallic element belonging to the halogens; used especially in medicine and photography and in dyes; occurs naturally only in combination in small quantities (as in sea water or rocks).
etymology: From French iode + -ine, from Ancient Greek ἰοειδής (ioeidḗs, “violet”). Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1814.

definition: Containing or involving or occurring in the form of ions.
example: Ionic charge.
etymology: From ion + -ic.

definition: A beam of ions moving in the same direction at the same speed.
A chemical bond in which one atom loses an electron to form a positive ion and the other atom gains an electron to form a negative ion.
The charge on an ion is equal to a constant charge e multiplied by an integer from 1 to 15.
Therapy that uses a local electric current to introduce the ions of a medicine into the tissues.
The condition of being dissociated into ions (as by heat or radiation or chemical reaction or electrical discharge).
example: The ionization of a gas.
etymology: From ionize + -ation.

definition: A measuring instrument that measures the amount of ionizing radiation.
The equilibrium constant for the ionization of an electrolyte (a weak one).
A measuring instrument that measures the amount of ionizing radiation.
A strong emotion; a feeling that is oriented toward some real or supposed grievance.
example: To raise the ire of someone.
etymology: From Middle English ire, yre, from Old English īre, ȳre, īr, ȳr, shortened form of īren (“iron”). More at iron.

definition: Diaphragm consisting of thin overlapping plates that can be adjusted to change the diameter of a central opening.
etymology: Derives from its action which is reminiscent of the iris of the eye.

definition: Garments (clothes or linens) that are to be (or have been) ironed.
example: There was a basketful of ironing to do.

definition: Narrow padded board on collapsible supports; used for ironing clothes.
A home appliance used for dry or steam pressing of clothes.
A strong man of exceptional physical endurance.
etymology: From iron + man. First applied to Joe McGinnity, a baseball player who pitched 48 complete games in one season and worked in an iron foundry during the offseason.

definition: The condition of being exposed to radiation.
etymology: From Middle French irradiacion, from Latin irradiatio. Morphologically irradiate + -ion.

definition: Impossible to replace.
example: Irreplaceable antiques.
etymology: From ir- + replaceable.

definition: Easily irritated or annoyed.
example: An irritable old man.
etymology: Borrowed from French irritable, from Latin irritabilis.

definition: Cause annoyance in; disturb, especially by minor irritations.
example: It irritates me that she never closes the door after she leaves.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin irrītātus, perfect passive participle of irrītō (“excite, irritate, incite, stimulate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: A pump in a service station that draws gasoline from underground storage tanks.
An inhabitant of an island.
A belief (or system of beliefs) accepted as authoritative by some group or school.
etymology: From the suffix -ism (“belief”), particularly (in the 19th century) in the sense of "social movement". Compare phobia, from -phobia, sophy, from -sophy, itis, from -itis, and ana, from -ana.

definition: Relating to or being a language in which each word typically expresses a distinct idea and part of speech and syntactical relations are determined almost exclusively by word order and particles.
An institution that issues something (securities or publications or currency etc.).
etymology: From issue + -er.

definition: An established line of travel or access.
etymology: From Middle English itinerarie, from Latin itinerārium (“an account of a journey, a road-book”), from iter (“a way, journey”). By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ary.

definition: A California food fish.
Small penguin of South America and southern Africa with a braying call.

The time of life between 40 and 50.
The time of life between 90 and 100.
The time of life between 30 and 40.
An amateur boxer who weighs no more than 165 pounds.
etymology: From middle + weight.

definition: June 21, when the sun is at its northernmost point.
etymology: From Middle English midsomer, midsumer, from Old English midsumer, midsumor (“midsummer”), from Proto-West Germanic *midisumar, from Proto-Germanic *midjasumaraz (“midsummer”), equivalent to mid- + summer.

definition: Eurasian mountain plant with fleshy pink-tipped leaves and a cluster of yellow flowers.
Of a region of the United States generally including Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Iowa, Missouri, Kansas, Nebraska, and sometimes Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota.
example: A midwestern city.
etymology: From mid- + western.

definition: Similar in habit to Alytes obstetricians.
etymology: Referring to the behavior in which males carry fertilized eggs on their backs.

definition: Behaving in or having a mild or gentle manner.
With respect to the military.
example: On a militarily significant scale.
etymology: From military + -ly.

definition: A face cleanser that is similar in texture to condensed milk.
A mild form of smallpox caused by a less virulent form of the virus.
Any of several Old World coarse prickly-leaved shrubs and subshrubs having milky juice and yellow flowers; widely naturalized; often noxious weeds in cultivated soil.
The serum or watery part of milk that is separated from the curd in making cheese.
The ability to produce milk.
example: They are also extremely functional females which excel in fertility and milking ability.

definition: Machine consisting of a suction apparatus for milking cows mechanically.
Low three-legged stool with a half round seat; used to sit on while milking a cow.
Frothy drink of milk and flavoring and sometimes fruit or ice cream.
example: This milkshake under the oil cap, or on the dipstick, indicates a blown head gasket.
etymology: From milk + shake.

definition: A metric unit of length equal to one thousandth of a meter.
etymology: From French millimètre, as if milli- + meter.

definition: Small drought-resistant sorghums having large yellow or whitish grains.
An actor who communicates entirely by gesture and facial expression.
Make less severe or harsh.
example: Butchers often use machines to mince meat.
etymology: From Middle English mincen, minsen; partly from Old English minsian, ġeminsian (“to make less, make smaller, diminish”), from Proto-West Germanic *minnisōn, from Proto-Germanic *minnisōną (“to make less”);

definition: Intellectually or emotionally overwhelming.
example: A mind-boggling display.
etymology: From mind + boggling.

definition: Lacking the thinking capacity characteristic of a conscious being.
example: The shrieking of the mindless wind.
etymology: From Middle English myndles, myndelees, myndeles, mendlees, from Old English myndlēas, ġemyndlēas (“foolish, senseless”), equivalent to mind + -less.

definition: To bring or combine together or with something else.
example: Resourcefully he mingled music and dance.
etymology: From earlier mingil, mengle, from Middle English menglen, equivalent to ming + -le. Cognate with Dutch mengelen (“to mingle, mix”), German mengen (“to mingle, mix”). More at ming.

definition: To a minimal degree.
example: The cells minimally responsive to lines in this orientation will not fire.
etymology: From minimal + -ly.

definition: Represent as less significant or important.
Reduced to the smallest possible size or amount or degree.
A servile or fawning dependant.
example: The archvillain deployed his minions to simultaneously rob every bank in the city.
etymology: First use appears c.

definition: A small box-shaped passenger van; usually has removable seats; used as a family car.
etymology: From mini- + van. First widely used in the 1980s, when this class of vehicles became widely popular as an alternative to station wagons (estate cars). Attested earlier in technical usage, usually as mini-van.

definition: Smelling of mint.
In a miraculous manner.
example: My hand grasped the gun that was, miraculously, lying on the ground beside my finger tips.
etymology: From miraculous + -ly.

definition: Domestic carp with some large shining scales.
etymology: From the resemblance of their large scales to mirrors.

definition: Naughtily or annoyingly playful.
example: Matthew had a twin brother called Edward, who was always mischievous and badly behaved.
etymology: From Middle English myschevous, mischevous, from Anglo-Norman meschevous, from Old French meschever, from mes- (“mis-”) + chever (“come to an end”) (from chef (“head”)). By surface analysis, mischief + -ous.

definition: An incorrect conception.
example: There are several common misconceptions about the theory of relativity.
etymology: From mis- + conception.

definition: In a miserable manner.
example: I bit my lip miserably and nodded.
etymology: From Middle English myserablie; equivalent to miserable + -ly.

definition: An unpredictable outcome that is unfortunate.
example: Since the mishap with the banana peel, he watches his step.
etymology: From Middle English mishap, myshappe, myssehappe, equivalent to mis- + hap.

definition: Lead someone in the wrong direction or give someone wrong directions.
example: The preacher elaborated Satan's ways to mislead us into sin.
etymology: From Middle English mysleden, from Old English mislǣdan (“to mislead”), from Proto-Germanic *missalaidijaną (“to mislead”). By surface analysis, mis- + lead.

definition: Management that is careless or inefficient.
example: He accomplished little due to the mismanagement of his energies.
etymology: From mis- + management.

definition: A bad or unsuitable match.
etymology: From mis- + match (verb sense).

definition: Hatred of women.
etymology: From Ancient Greek μισογυνία (misogunía) and μισογύνης (misogúnēs, “woman hater”), from μισέω (miséō, “I hate”) + γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”). By surface analysis, miso- + -gyny.

definition: Putting the wrong interpretation on.
example: There was no mistaking her meaning.

definition: Subjected to cruel treatment.
Doubt about someone's honesty.
etymology: From Middle English mistrust; equivalent to mis- + trust.

definition: Interpret in the wrong way.
etymology: From Middle English mys-understanden, equivalent to mis- + understand.

definition: Used incorrectly or carelessly or for an improper purpose.
example: Misused words are often laughable but one weeps for misused talents.

definition: A slight but appreciable amount.
Box for collecting alms, especially one in a church.
etymology: From (widow's) mite (“small donation”) + box.

definition: Single faucet for separate hot and cold water pipes.
Ditch dug as a fortification and usually filled with water.
etymology: From Middle English mote, from Old French mote (“mound, embankment”);

definition: A restaurant outside; often for soldiers or policemen.
Make ready for action or use.
etymology: From French mobiliser.

definition: Relating to or constituting the most frequent value in a distribution.
example: The modal age at which American novelists reach their peak is 30.
etymology: From Middle French modal, from Medieval Latin modālis (“pertaining to a mode”), from Latin modus (“mode”). Compare to French, Spanish, and Portuguese modal and Italian modale. By surface analysis, mod(e) + -al.

definition: An auxiliary verb (such as ‘can’ or ‘will’) that is used to express modality.
The logical study of necessity and possibility.
The most frequent value of a random variable.
An auxiliary verb (such as ‘can’ or ‘will’) that is used to express modality.
Genre of art and literature that makes a self-conscious break with previous genres.
etymology: From modern + -ism.

definition: An artist who makes a deliberate break with previous styles.
etymology: From modern + -ist.

definition: Make repairs, renovations, revisions or adjustments to.
etymology: From modern + -ize or French moderniser.

definition: With modesty; in a modest manner.
example: The dissertation was entitled, modestly, ‘Remarks about a play by Shakespeare’.
etymology: From modest + -ly.

definition: Freedom from vanity or conceit.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French modestie, from Latin modestia; equivalent to modest + -y.

definition: A bump on a ski slope.
example: A Silicon Valley tech mogul.
etymology: Figurative use of Moghul, which originally meant Mongol, or person of Mongolian descent.

definition: A sauce similar to Worcestershire sauce, manufactured by John Burgess & Son and Crosse & Blackwell; used for meat.
Haircut in which the head is shaved except for a band of hair down the middle of the scalp.
Haircut in which the head is shaved except for a band of hair down the middle of the scalp.
The molecular weight of a substance expressed in grams; the basic unit of amount of substance adopted under the Systeme International d'Unites.
etymology: Borrowed from German Mol (1897).

definition: Thick dark syrup produced by boiling down juice from sugar cane; especially during sugar refining.
example: Boiled some cornstalk juice into molasses.
etymology: From Portuguese melaços or Spanish melazos, from Late Latin mellacium (“must, honey-sweet thing”), from mel (“honey”) + -āceus (“-aceous”) + -ium, q.v.

definition: Shaped to fit by or as if by altering the contours of a pliable mass (as by work or effort).
example: The molded steel plates.

definition: Salad of meats or vegetables in gelatin.
The act of creating something by casting it in a mold.
etymology: From Middle English moldynge; equivalent to mold + -ing.

definition: For an instant or moment.
example: We paused momentarily before proceeding.
etymology: From momentary + -ly.

definition: Lasting for a markedly brief time.
example: Rapid momentaneous association of things that meet and pass.
etymology: From Middle English momentare, from Late Latin mōmentārius (“of brief duration”), from mōmentum (“a short time, an instant”). By surface analysis, moment + -ary.

definition: Of very great significance.
example: A momentous event.
etymology: From moment (“weight, importance”) + -ous.

definition: Of communal life sequestered from the world under religious vows.
example: New monastic people.
etymology: From Middle French monastique, from Late Latin monasticus.

definition: A long loose habit worn by monks in a monastery.
A group of person living under a religious rule.
A familiar name for a person (often a shortened version of a person's given name).
example: The rookie was upset at being called Lemon Drop until she realized that everyone on the team had a silly moniker.
etymology: Unknown; first attested in 1849. Suggested derivations are: * Backslang for ekename (compare nickname); * From Shelta munik, munika; * From monk;

definition: Painting done in a range of tones of a single color.
etymology: From Ancient Greek μονόχρωμος (monókhrōmos), from μόνος (mónos, “one”) + χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”); mono- + -chrome.

definition: A graphic symbol consisting of 2 or more letters combined (usually your initials); printed on stationery or embroidered on clothing.
etymology: From French monogramme, from the Classical Latin adjective monogrammus, from the conjectured Ancient Greek * μονόγραμμος (monógrammos, “outlined”, “drawn with single lines”).

definition: A detailed and documented treatise on a particular subject.
etymology: From mono- (“one”) + -graph (“write”).

definition: Imposing in size or bulk or solidity.
example: The monolithic proportions of Stalinist architecture.
etymology: From French monolithique. By surface analysis, monolith + -ic.

definition: A mound of fatty tissue covering the pubic area in women.
example: Olympus Mons.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin mōns (“mountain”). Doublet of mount.

definition: Female of domestic cattle:.
etymology: Compare German Muhkuh and Italian mucca.

definition: Splashed or covered patchily with moonlight.
example: The moon-splashed world.

definition: Of no legal significance (as having been previously decided).
example: That point may make for a good discussion, but it is moot.
etymology: From Middle English mōt, ȝemōt, from Old English *mōt, ġemōt (“meeting”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtą, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“to encounter, come”).

definition: A mock court where law students argue hypothetical cases.
A legally authorized postponement before some obligation must be discharged.
example: Canada may put a moratorium on cloning for research.
etymology: New Latin from Late Latin morātōrium, noun use of the neuter of morātōrius (“moratory, delaying”), from Latin moror (“to delay”), from mora (“delay”), from Proto-Indo-European *mere (“to delay, hinder”).

definition: A direct mate with the stipulation ‘White to move and checkmate Black in no more than n moves against any defence’ where n is greater than 3.
example: This week's problem is a more-mover by a composer better known for his endgame study and theory work.

definition: The time period between dawn and noon.
example: I spent the morning running errands.

definition: Cause to change shape in a computer animation.
example: The computer programmer morphed the image.
etymology: Back-formation from morpheme, from Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “form, shape”). Compare German Morph, from Morphem. Attested since the 1940s.

definition: Relating to or concerned with the formation of admissible words in a language.
etymology: From morphology + -ical.

definition: A linguistic rule for the formation of words.
Small free-floating aquatic fern from the eastern United States to tropical America; naturalized in western and southern Europe.
etymology: From the belief that no mosquito can penetrate the coating to lay its eggs in the water.

definition: A clever remark.
example: 1597–1598, Joseph Hall, Virgidemiarum With his big title, an Italian mot.
etymology: From French mot. Doublet of motto.

definition: Any of various orchids of the genus Phalaenopsis having often drooping glossy broad obovate or oval leaves usually dark green flushed purple or mottled grey and silver.
The country where you were born.
example: After many years abroad, he returned to his motherland.
etymology: From mother + land. First attested in 1711.

definition: A collection containing a variety of sorts of things.
etymology: From Middle English motle, from Anglo-Norman motteley (“parti-colored”), from Old English mot (“speck”). Doublet of mote. The English word can be analysed as mottle + -y.

definition: A professional clown employed to entertain a king or nobleman in the Middle Ages.
etymology: From motley (“multi-colored cloth; a jester's clothes”) + fool (“a jester”).

definition: A lawn mower powered by a gasoline motor.
A neuron conducting impulses outwards from the brain or spinal cord.
Small motorcycle with a low frame and small wheels and elevated handlebars.
etymology: From motor + bike.

definition: The act of driving an automobile.
Someone who drives (or travels in) an automobile.
etymology: From motor + -ist.

definition: Equipped with a motor or motors.
example: A motorized wheelchair.

definition: A wheelchair propelled by a motor.
Ornamental evergreen shrub of southeastern United States having small white bell-shaped flowers.
Creeping mat-forming evergreen shrub of high mountain regions of Northern Hemisphere grown for its rose-pink flowers.
Someone who climbs mountains.
Low evergreen shrub of high north temperate regions of Europe and Asia and America bearing red edible berries.
California partridge; slightly larger than the California quail.
California partridge; slightly larger than the California quail.
An unshaved growth of hair on the upper lip.
etymology: Used in English since the 16th century.

definition: A drinking cup with a bar inside the rim to keep a man's mustache out of the drink.
The quantity that can be held in the mouth.
example: He swallowed a mouthful of sea water when he fell in.
etymology: From Middle English mouthful, mouth-full, mouthe full, from Old English *mūþfull, from Proto-West Germanic *munþafull, equivalent to mouth + -ful.

definition: (of personal property as opposed to real estate) can be moved from place to place (especially carried by hand).
example: Easter is a movable holiday.
etymology: From Old French movable. By surface analysis, move + -able.

definition: A barrier that can be moved to allow passage.
A religious holiday that falls on different dates in different years.
Workman employed by a moving company.
example: The movers were very careful with the grand piano.
etymology: From move + -er.

definition: A stairway whose steps move continuously on a circulating belt.
Cut with a blade or mower.
example: Mow the grass.
etymology: From Middle English mowe, from Old French moe (“grimace”), from Frankish *mauwa (“pout, protruding lip”), from Proto-Germanic *mawwō (“muff, sleeve”). Akin to Middle Dutch mouwe (“protruding lip”).

definition: Garden tool for mowing grass on lawns.
example: Moppers and mowers.
etymology: From Middle English mowere, equivalent to mow + -er.

definition: Mild white Italian cheese.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian mozzarella, from mozzare (“to cut off”), from Latin mutilare.

definition: Do random, unplanned work or activities or spend time idly.
example: The old lady is usually mucking about in her little house.

definition: Do random, unplanned work or activities or spend time idly.
example: The old lady is usually mucking about in her little house.

definition: Make a mess of, destroy or ruin.
A laborer who digs ditches.
Having narrow flat sickle-shaped submerged fronds; North America.
A puddle of mud.
example: The children loved a mud puddle.

definition: Being or made softer or less loud or clear.
example: Muffled drums.

definition: Any of several trees of the genus Morus having edible fruit that resembles the blackberry.
Trees or shrubs having a milky juice; in some classifications includes genus Cannabis.

Thick-branched wide-spreading tree of Africa and adjacent southwestern Asia often buttressed with branches rising from near the ground; produces cluster of edible but inferior figs on short leafless twigs; the biblical sycamore.
Any of several trees of the genus Morus having edible fruit that resembles the blackberry.
A worker who drives mules.
etymology: From mule + skinner.

definition: Irish version of burgoo.
example: When we did, nobody was there, but we found two empty sleeping bags and some mulligan in a pot on a stove.
etymology: Attested since the 1930s in the sense “chance to re-take a golf stroke”; probably from the name Mulligan, after a golfer who replayed a stroke. See Wikipedia for more information.

definition: Having many stems.
Having many parts or sides.
example: A multilateral negotiation.
etymology: From multi- + lateral.

definition: Using or knowing more than one language.
example: A multilingual translator.
etymology: From multi- + lingual.

definition: A sign indicating the operation of multiplication.
The number by which a multiplicand is multiplied.
example: In the expression 5 × 7, the "5" is a multiplier.
etymology: From multiply + -er.
