definition: The number by which a multiplicand is multiplied.
Type of onion plant producing small clustered mild-flavored bulbs used as seasoning.
(of liquids) clouded as with sediment.
example: Murky waters.
etymology: From Middle English mirky. Related to Old Norse myrkr, Russian мрак (mrak) and its Slavic cognates. By surface analysis, murk + -y.

definition: Erect Old World perennial with faintly musk-scented foliage and white or pink flowers; adventive in United States.
A musical part (vocal or instrumental) that supports or provides background for other musical parts.
A musical interval of eight tones.
Low annual European herb naturalized in America; similar to alfilaria.
Nocturnal gregarious pig-like wild animals of North America and South America.
Small kangaroo of northeastern Australia.
Large shaggy-coated bovid mammal of Canada and Greenland; intermediate in size and anatomy between an ox and a sheep.
etymology: So called because of the strong odour, or musk, emitted by the males during the rutting season.

definition: Eurasian perennial naturalized in eastern North America having very spiny white cottony foliage and nodding musky crimson flower heads; valuable source of nectar.
etymology: First attested in 1633; named for the scent of its immature flower heads.

definition: Smelling of musk.
Having a part of the body crippled or disabled.
An injury that causes disfigurement or that deprives you of a limb or other important body part.
etymology: Latin mutilatio; compare French mutilation.

definition: Meat from a mature domestic sheep.
etymology: From Middle English motoun, moton, from Old French mouton (“sheep”), from Vulgar Latin moltō, from Gaulish *multon-, from Proto-Celtic *moltos (“ram, wether”). Doublet of mouton.

definition: Large evergreen tree of Tasmania.
A religion based on mystical communion with an ultimate reality.
An aura of heightened value or interest or meaning surrounding a person or thing.
etymology: Borrowed from French mystique (“a mystic”), from Latin mysticus. See also the doublet mystic.

definition: Relating to or having the nature of myth.
example: A novel of almost mythic consequence.
etymology: 1660s; from Latin mȳthicus or Ancient Greek μυθικός (muthikós); equivalent to myth + -ic.

definition: Based on or told of in traditional stories; lacking factual basis or historical validity.
etymology: From mythology + -ical.

definition: Tag the base runner to get them out.
example: As I was going out of the door, a fellow detective came hurriedly in. "Nabbed them," cried he.
etymology: From dialectal nap (“to seize, lay hold of”), probably of North Germanic origin, from Old Swedish nappa (“to pluck, pinch”).

definition: A tortilla chip topped with cheese and chili-pepper and broiled.
etymology: Back-formation from nachos.

definition: A quantity of no importance; thing (object:), singular, negative pronoun; pronoun, thing, singular; quantifier: negative existential.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish nada (“nothing”). Doublet of natal, Natal, née, and Noel.

definition: A cosmetic lacquer that dries quickly and that is applied to the nails to color them or make them shiny.
Being or having an unknown or unnamed source.
example: Corporations responsible to nameless owners.
etymology: From Middle English nameles, equivalent to name + -less.

definition: A person with the same name as another.
example: The statesman Winston Churchill has a namesake, the American novelist Winston Churchill.
etymology: Mid-17th century. Equivalent to name + sake.

definition: A small piece of table linen that is used to wipe the mouth and to cover the lap in order to protect clothing.
etymology: From Middle English napekyn, napkyn, equivalent to nape (“cloth”) + -kin (diminutive suffix).

definition: A circular band used to hold a particular person's napkin.
example: The waiter set out the napkin rings alongside the cutlery.

definition: Not prepared or vigilant.
example: The blow caught him napping.

definition: An exceptional interest in and admiration for yourself.
etymology: From obsolete German Narzissismus (now Narzissmus by haplology), from Narziss (“Narcissus”) + -ism. By surface analysis, Narciss(us) (“character in Greek mythology who became obsessed with his own reflection”) + -ism.

definition: Characteristic of those having an inflated idea of their own importance.
etymology: From narcissist + -ic.

definition: Having a narrow mouth.
Any of the paired sinuses in the bones of the face adjacent to the nasal cavity that are lined with mucous membrane that is continuous with the lining of the nasal cavities.
A device with a flexible bulb that replaces the plunger for instillation or aspiration, used to irrigate an external orifice, such as the auditory canal, or to remove congestion from nasal cavity.
(phonetics) A vowel that is produced with a lowering of the velum so that air escapes both through nose as well as the mouth.
Being born or beginning.
example: The nascent chicks.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin nāscēns, nāscentis, present participle of nāscor (“to be born”). Doublet of naissant.

definition: Very large closely branched South African shrub having forked bright green spines and shiny leaves.
Fanatically patriotic.
etymology: From nationalist + -ic.

definition: Small prostrate or ascending shrub having scarlet flowers and succulent fruit resembling cranberries; sometimes placed in genus Styphelia.
An old name for sulfur.
The event of being born.
etymology: From Middle English nativite, from Anglo-Norman nativite, Middle French nativite, and their source, Latin nātīvitās (“birth”). By surface analysis, native + -ity. See also naïveté.

definition: An advocate of the doctrine that the world can be understood in scientific terms.
etymology: From natural + -ist. Piecewise doublet of naturalista.

definition: Causing or able to cause nausea.
example: A nauseating smell.
etymology: From Latin nauseōsus (“causing nausea”), corresponding synchronically to nausea + -ous.

definition: A military shipyard.
The central area of a church.
etymology: Ultimately from Latin nāvem, singular accusative of nāvis, possibly via a Romance source. Doublet of nef and nau.

definition: A high tight collar.
A common poplar of eastern and central United States; cultivated in United States for its rapid growth and luxuriant foliage and in Europe for timber.
Of plants that are rich in nectar.
(meaning literally ‘born’) used to indicate the maiden or family name of a married woman.
example: Hillary Clinton nee Rodham.
etymology: From French née, feminine of né, past participle of naître, to be born.

definition: Biopsy of deep tissue that is obtained through a hollow needle.
A disease of conifers causing the needles to fall.
Without need.
example: It would needlessly bring badness into the world.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English nedelesly. By surface analysis, needless + -ly.

definition: Extremely wicked.
example: Nefarious schemes.

definition: Capable of being passed or negotiated.
example: A negotiable road.
etymology: From negotiate + -able.

definition: An unconditional order or promise to pay an amount of money.
Someone who negotiates (confers with others in order to reach a settlement).
etymology: Borrowed from Latin negōtiātor (“merchant, banker”), equivalent to negotiate + -or.

definition: Art or architecture based on study of 17th century baroque.
example: Like camp, the neo-baroque of Bartlem's artists address the body as a site of performance and tangible sensation.

definition: Relating to or affecting the infant during the first month after birth.
example: Neonatal care.
etymology: From neo- + natal.

definition: The first 28 days of life.
Extremely irritating to the nerves.
example: Nerve-racking noise.

definition: The anxious feeling you have when you have the jitters.
etymology: From nervous + -ness.

definition: Drawn or pressed close to someone or something for or as if for affection or protection.
example: Saw a number of small houses nestled against the hillside.

definition: A team game that resembles basketball; a soccer ball is to be thrown so that it passes through a ring on the top of a post.
etymology: From net + ball.

definition: Having open interstices or resembling a web.
A net of transparent fabric with a loose open weave.
etymology: From net + -ing.

definition: The configuration of a communication network.
Marketing based on studies of consumers' sensorimotor, cognitive, and affective responses.
A medical specialist in the nervous system and the disorders affecting it.
etymology: From neuro- + -logist.

definition: The branch of medical science that deals with the nervous system.
example: Patient had no neurology.
etymology: From New Latin neurologia. By surface analysis, neuro- + -logy.

definition: A cell that is specialized to conduct nerve impulses.
etymology: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”), doublet of nerve and sinew. By surface analysis, neuro- + -on.

definition: Of or relating to neurons.
etymology: From neuron + -al.

definition: Characteristic of or affected by neurosis.
example: Neurotic disorder.
etymology: Formed of neuro- (“of nerves or the nervous system”) + -otic (“having abnormal condition”). The initial element, in turn, is from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”). Attested from the 17th century.

definition: A term used for any state of depression that is not psychotic.
Make politically neutral and thus inoffensive.
example: The treaty neutralized the small republic.
etymology: From French neutraliser (first attested in 1642). By surface analysis, neutral + -ize.

definition: The rate of flow of neutrons; the number of neutrons passing through a unit area in unit time.
Any new participant in some activity.
Newly discovered.
example: His newfound aggressiveness.
etymology: From Middle English newe founde, equivalent to new + found.

definition: An excerpt cut from a newspaper or magazine.
The staff of a newspaper or the news department of a periodical.
example: Every newspaper editor is criticized by the newsroom.
etymology: From news + room.

definition: The writing point of a pen.
etymology: From a variant of neb, perhaps due to association with nibble.

definition: A cabinet containing an automatic record player; records are played by inserting a coin.
Excellent.
example: A nifty trick for reducing your household energy bill.
etymology: From *nift + -y. First element is of unknown origin. Possibly theatrical slang, as a shortened, altered form of Magnificat. Alternatively, perhaps a special use of US regional niffed (“put off, peeved”).

definition: Not far distant in time or space or degree or circumstances.
example: The end is nigh!
etymology: Inherited from Middle English neygh, from Old English nēah, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhw, from Proto-Germanic *nēhw, from *nēhwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂neḱ- (“to reach”).

definition: Nocturnal or crepuscular herons.
A watchman who works during the night.
A male watchman who works during the night.
etymology: From night + watchman. Cf. Old English nihtweard. By surface analysis, night + watch + man.

definition: The time of day immediately following sunset.
example: They finished before the fall of night.
etymology: From night + fall. Cf. dewfall.

definition: The entertainment available to people seeking nighttime diversion.
example: A futile search for intelligent nightlife.
etymology: From night + life.

definition: Moving quickly and lightly.
example: As nimble as a deer.

definition: The decade from 1890 to 1899.
example: My ideal bracket of temperature ranges from the sixties up to the nineties.

definition: A luminance unit equal to 1 candle per square meter measured perpendicular to the rays from the source.
example: This brightness of this LCD screen is between 900 and 1000 nits.
etymology: From Latin nitēre (“to shine”).

definition: The group -NO3.
A chemical fertilizer containing calcium carbonate and ammonium nitrate.
example: Nitro-chalk is valued for its versatility.

definition: A quantity of no importance; thing (object:), singular, negative pronoun; pronoun, thing, singular; quantifier: negative existential.
etymology: From German nix, colloquial form of nichts (“nothing”). Compare also Dutch niks (“nothing”), informal for niets (“nothing”). More at naught.

definition: Anything that requires little thought.
example: Choosing the older version which was as good as the newer version for half the cost was a no-brainer.
etymology: From no + brain + -er.

definition: A titled peer of the realm.
etymology: From noble + man.

definition: Having branches or flower heads that bend downward.
example: Nodding daffodils.

definition: Widely distributed North American wild onion with white to rose flowers.
A member of a people who have no permanent home but move about according to the seasons.
etymology: From Middle French nomade, from Latin Nomas (“wandering shepherd”), from Ancient Greek νομάς (nomás, “roaming, wandering, esp. to find pasture”), from Ancient Greek νομός (nomós, “pasture”). Compare Numidia.

definition: Migratory.
example: The nomadic habits of the Bedouins.
etymology: From Ancient Greek νομαδικός (nomadikós), equivalent to nomad (“a member of a society or class of herdsmen”) + -ic (forming adjectives).

definition: A system of words used to name things in a particular discipline.
example: Biological nomenclature.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin nōmenclātūra (“a calling by name, list of names”), from nōmen (“name”) + calāre (“call”). Doublet of nomenklatura.

definition: In name only.
example: Nominally he is the boss.
etymology: From nominal + -ly.

definition: An address (usually at a political convention) proposing the name of a candidate to run for election.
example: The nomination was brief and to the point.

definition: An address (usually at a political convention) proposing the name of a candidate to run for election.
example: The nomination was brief and to the point.

definition: Not pertaining to or characteristic of birds.
example: But the results reported here show that important aspects of non-avian theropod locomotion can be experimentally recreated in modern birds.
etymology: From non- + avian.

definition: Cannot be bought or sold.
Not having existence or being or actuality.
example: Chimeras are nonexistent.
etymology: From non- + existent.

definition: Any correlation in which the rates of change of the variables is not constant.
Distortion that occurs when the output signal does not have a linear relation to the input signal.
Abstaining (on principle) from the use of violence.
Peaceful resistance to a government by fasting or refusing to cooperate.
Become normal or return to its normal state.
example: Let us hope that relations with this country will normalize soon.
etymology: From normal + -ize.

definition: Relating to or dealing with norms.
example: Normative discipline.
etymology: From Latin norma + -ative. Compare French normatif.

definition: A part of economics that expresses value or normative judgments about economic fairness or what the outcome of the economy or goals of public policy ought to be.
example: Normative economics, in contrast, becomes arbitrary and unmotivated unless it attributes largely self-interested preferences to people.

definition: Moving toward the north.
example: The northbound lane.
etymology: From north + -bound.

definition: Whiting of the east coast of United States; closely resembles king whiting.
Moving toward the north.
example: The northbound lane.
etymology: From north + -ward.

definition: Having a nose (either literal or metaphoric) especially of a specified kind.
example: Rudolph the red-nosed reindeer.

definition: Someone legally empowered to witness signatures and certify a document's validity and to take depositions.
etymology: From Middle English notarie, from Old French notarie (French notaire), from Latin notārius.

definition: Someone legally empowered to witness signatures and certify a document's validity and to take depositions.
etymology: Anglo-Norman/Law French, on model of notaire publique, hence the unusual order of adjective following noun, instead of idiomatic English *public notary.

definition: Notched like a saw with teeth pointing toward the apex.
A source of materials to nourish the body.
etymology: From Middle English norisshement, from Middle French, from Old French norissement, from norrir, equivalent to nourish + -ment.

definition: A short novel.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian novella. Doublet of novel.

definition: A projecting spout from which a fluid is discharged.
example: The shape of the nozzle prevents the use of aftermarket eartips.
etymology: From Middle English noselle, equivalent to nose + -le (diminutive suffix). Compare typologically Russian сопло (soplo) (<~ сопе́ть (sopétʹ), whence also сопа́тка (sopátka)).

definition: A subtle difference in meaning or opinion or attitude.
example: Without understanding the finer nuances you can't enjoy the humor.
etymology: Borrowed from French nuance (“nuance, shade, hue”). Omitting several steps, from Latin nūbēs. Compare typologically Italian sfumatura (< Latin fūmus).

definition: A nuclear reaction in which a massive nucleus splits into smaller nuclei with the simultaneous release of energy.
The warhead of a missile designed to deliver an atom bomb.
A phosphoric ester of a nucleoside; the basic structural unit of nucleic acids (DNA or RNA).
etymology: From nucleo- (“relating to the nucleus”) + -ide (“chemical suffix”).

definition: A layer of deeply pigmented grey matter in the midbrain; associated with the striate body; is involved in metabolic disturbances associated with Parkinson's disease and with Huntington's disease.
To push against gently.
example: She nudged my elbow when she saw her friend enter the restaurant.

definition: Performing complex and lengthy numerical calculations.
A mathematician specializing in number theory.
Of or relating to or denoting numbers.
example: A numeral adjective.

definition: A registered nurse who has received special training as a midwife.
East Indian tree widely cultivated in the tropics for its aromatic seed; source of two spices: nutmeg and mace.
etymology: From Middle English notemege, notemuge, a partial translation of Medieval Latin nux muga, a variant of Medieval Latin nux muscata (“musky nut”). Compare also Old French nois mugede.

definition: Herb of the Mediterranean region having pungent seeds used like those of caraway.
East Indian tree widely cultivated in the tropics for its aromatic seed; source of two spices: nutmeg and mace.
Shaped like a nutmeg.
Of or providing nourishment.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nūtrītius, from nūtrītus, from nūtrīre.

definition: Women's stockings made from a sheer material (nylon or rayon or silk).
A black plant louse that lives on oaks and dogwoods.
Bright blue-green fern widely distributed especially in damp acid woodlands of temperate Northern Hemisphere.
example: Why say we, that […] to know the vertue of Reubarb, qualitie of Oak ferne, and operation of Polipodie, is only peculiar unto man?

definition: Dutifully complying with the commands or instructions of those in authority.
example: An obedient soldier.
etymology: From Middle English obedient, from Old French obedient, from Latin oboediēns, present active participle of oboediō (“obey”).

definition: North American plant having a spike of two-lipped pink or white flowers.
Causing disapproval or protest.
example: A vulgar and objectionable person.
etymology: From objection + -able.

definition: Judgment based on observable phenomena and uninfluenced by emotions or personal prejudices.
example: Maintain objectivity.
etymology: From objective + -ity.

definition: Force somebody to do something.
example: Your carelessness obliges firmness on my part.
etymology: From Middle English obligen, from Old French obligier, obliger, from Latin obligō, obligāre, from ob- + ligō. Doublet of obligate, taken straight from Latin.

definition: Slanting or inclined in direction or course or position — neither parallel nor perpendicular nor right-angled.
example: The oblique rays of the winter sun.
etymology: From Middle French oblique, from Latin oblīquus (also spelled oblīcus) (“slanting, sideways, indirect, envious”).

definition: An angle that is not a right angle or a multiple of a right angle.
Any grammatical case other than the nominative.
A triangle that contains no right angle.
Reduced to nothingness.
etymology: From obliterate + -ed (suffix forming adjectives; and past tenses and past participles of regular verbs).

definition: The quality of being unclear or abstruse and hard to understand.
example: She was plucked from obscurity to star in a Broadway musical.
etymology: From Middle English obscurite, obscuryte, from Middle French obscurité and its etymon Latin obscūritās. By surface analysis, obscure + -ity.

definition: Capable of being seen or noticed.
example: An observable change in behavior.
etymology: From observe + -able.

definition: The act of observing; taking a patient look.
Paying close attention especially to details.
example: The observant police officer noticed that my tax disk was out-of-date.
etymology: Borrowed from French observant.

definition: Relying on observation or experiment.
etymology: From observation + -al.

definition: Characterized by obsessions and compulsions.
example: Obsessive-compulsive neurosis.

definition: The branch of medicine dealing with childbirth and care of the mother.
etymology: From obstetric.

definition: Hinder or prevent the progress or accomplishment of.
example: They obstructed my progress.
etymology: From Latin past participle stem obstruct- (“blocked up”), from verb obstruere, from ob (“against”) + struere (“pile up, build”).

definition: Capable of being obtained.
example: Savings of up to 50 percent are obtainable.
etymology: From obtain + -able.

definition: Of an angle; between 90 and 180 degrees.
etymology: From Middle English obtuse, from Latin obtūsus (“blunt, dull; obtuse”), past participle of obtundere, from obtundō (“to batter, beat, strike; to blunt, dull”), from ob- (“against”) (see ob-) + tundō (“to beat, strike;

definition: An angle between 90 and 180 degrees.
A simple leaf having a rounded or blunt tip.
Someone who lives at a particular place for a prolonged period or who was born there.
example: I cannot say the same of the current occupant of the position.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French occupant (present participle of occuper) or Latin occupāns, occupantis (present participle of occupō). By surface analysis, occupy + -ant.

definition: A long steep-sided depression in the ocean floor.
Any isomeric saturated hydrocarbon found in petroleum and used as a fuel and solvent.
etymology: From oct- + -ane.

definition: A measure of the antiknock properties of gasoline.
A measure of the antiknock properties of gasoline.
A feast day and the seven days following it.
example: The melody jumps up an octave at the beginning, then later drops back down an octave.
etymology: From Latin octavus (“eighth”). Doublet of octavo, ochava, and oitava.

definition: The organ of sight.
example: One can glimpse the sky through the oculus of the Pantheon in Rome.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin oculus (“eye”). Doublet of occhio.

definition: The right eye.
The left eye.
The act of umpiring.
example: The officiating was excellent.

definition: Many times at short intervals.
example: We often met over a cup of coffee.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English oftentymes. By surface analysis, oftentime + -s. Compare oftentime. Compare also German oftmals, Middle French souventesfois.

definition: A cruel wicked and inhuman person.
example: People are going to think I'm an ogre if I refuse to buy coffee for my little brother!

definition: A specialist in petroleum geology.
A powerful person in the oil business.
Treated with oil.
example: Oiled country roads.

definition: A form of all fours in which a total of seven points is game.
Of or relating to olfaction.
example: Olfactory receptor.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin olfactōrius.

definition: A center in the cerebral hemispheres that governs the sense of smell in lower animals; in humans it seems to mediate complex emotional behavior.
A collective term for numerous olfactory filaments in the nasal mucosa.
The organ of smell and entrance to the respiratory tract; the prominent part of the face of man or other mammals.
The sensation that results when olfactory receptors in the nose are stimulated by particular chemicals in gaseous form.
Any property detected by the olfactory system.
A male government appointee who investigates complaints by private persons against the government.
etymology: Borrowed from Swedish ombudsman (equivalent to ombud (“representative, proxy”) + man), from Old Norse umboðsmaðr.

definition: A sign of something about to happen.
example: He looked for an omen before going into battle.
etymology: From Latin ōmen (“foreboding, omen”).

definition: Prevent from being included or considered or accepted.
etymology: At least by 1422, from late Middle English omitten, borrowed from Latin omittō (“to let go”), from ob- + mittō (“to send”), but also had the connotations “to fail to perform” and “to neglect”.

definition: An anthology of articles on a related subject or an anthology of the works of a single author.
example: This work is an omnibus containing all books in the Remembrance of Earth’s Past series.
etymology: Borrowed from French (voiture) omnibus (“(carriage) for all”), from Latin omnibus (“for all”), dative plural of omnis (“all”).

definition: Moving toward one.
example: Look carefully before pulling out into oncoming traffic.
etymology: From Middle English on comynge, oncomynge, oncoomynge; equivalent to on- + coming (noun).

definition: Bagel flavored with onion.
A sudden and severe onset of trouble.
example: They opened the doors and prepared for the onslaught of holiday shoppers.
etymology: From on- + slaught. Formed after Middle Dutch aenslag, aenslach, equivalent to aen + slag, although slaught corresponds to Middle Dutch slacht; slag is cognate with the English weaving term sley.

definition: A translucent mineral consisting of hydrated silica of variable color; some varieties are used as gemstones.
etymology: In Florio’s A World of Words 1598 as opale, from French opale, from Latin opalus, from Medieval Greek ὀπάλλιος (opállios), from Sanskrit उपल (upala, “gem, stone”), from उपरि (upári, “the upper millstone”).

definition: A milky white translucent or opaque glass.
Of or relating to or produced by the open-hearth process.
example: Open-hearth steel.

definition: Southwestern Asian herb with greyish leaves and white or reddish flowers; source of opium.
Someone addicted to opium.
Taking immediate advantage, often unethically, of any circumstance of possible benefit.
example: The danger now isn't so much from the AIDS virus itself as from opportunistic infections.
etymology: From opportunist + -ic.

definition: A person disposed to take a favorable view of things.
A musical work that has been created.
example: The painter's last opus was a dedication to all things living, in a surprising contrast to all of his prior work.

definition: A consonant sound in speech that is made by allowing air to escape from the mouth, as opposed to the nose.
Contraception achieved by taking oral contraceptive pills.
A contraceptive in the form of a pill containing estrogen and progestin to inhibit ovulation and so prevent conception.
(of drugs) through the mouth rather than through injection; by mouth.
example: He was administered the drug orally.
etymology: From oral + -ly.

definition: Tiny bits of orange peel.
Spiders that spin orb webs; cosmopolitan in distribution.
Of spiders who weave circular webs.
A percussion instrument consisting of a set of graduated metal bars mounted on a frame and played with small hammers.
Any cactus of the genus Epiphyllum having flattened jointed irregularly branching stems and showy tubular flowers.
As an important constituent.
example: The drapery served organically to cover the Madonna.
etymology: From organic + -ally.

definition: Of or relating to an organization.
example: Organizational structure.
etymology: From organisation + -al.

definition: Someone who enlists workers to join a union.
etymology: From organise + -er.

definition: Any act of immoderate indulgence.
example: An orgy of shopping.
etymology: Originally in plural from French orgies, from Latin orgia, from Ancient Greek ὄργια (órgia, “secret rites, mysteries”).

definition: Ornamental Asiatic vine with showy orange-yellow fruit with a scarlet aril; naturalized in North America.
Dark brown cockroach originally from orient now nearly cosmopolitan in distribution.
etymology: From the taxonomic name.

definition: Evergreen tree of the Caucasus and Asia Minor used as an ornamental having pendulous branchlets.
Marked by elaborate rhetoric and elaborated with decorative details.
example: Ornate rhetoric taught out of the rule of Plato.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ōrnātus, perfect passive participle of ōrnō (“to equip, adorn”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of orné.

definition: Of or relating to orthopedics.
example: Orthopedic shoes.

definition: A person who refuses to face reality or recognize the truth (a reference to the popular notion that the ostrich hides from danger by burying its head in the sand).
(of securities) not traded on a stock exchange.
Hardy British hound having long pendulous ears and a thick coarse shaggy coat with an oily undercoat; bred for hunting otters.
Inaccessible and sparsely populated.
etymology: From out + back.

definition: That is going out or leaving.
etymology: From out- + bound.

definition: An unrestrained expression of emotion.
example: The man greeted us with an outburst of invective.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English outbersten, outbresten. Cognate with Dutch uitbarsten (“to erupt; burst out”), German ausbersten (“to burst out; erupt”). By surface analysis, out- + burst.

definition: Excluded from a society.
etymology: From Middle English outcasten, equivalent to out- + cast.

definition: Shout louder than.
etymology: From Middle English outcry, outcri, outcrye, equivalent to out- + cry. The verb is from Middle English outcrien.

definition: The area of a baseball playing field beyond the lines connecting the bases.
example: He hit a long fly ball to the outfield in the gap to left.
etymology: From out- + field.

definition: (baseball) a person who plays in the outfield.
example: The outfielder tracked down the long fly.
etymology: From outfield + -er.

definition: The discharge of a fluid from some container.
etymology: From Middle English outflowen, from late Old English ūtflōwan (attested in the past tense as ūt flēow), equivalent to out- + flow. The noun is derived from the verb.

definition: Contrary to or forbidden by law.
example: An outlaw strike.

definition: Relatively far from a center or middle.
example: Outlying settlements.
etymology: From outlie (Etymology 2) + -ing.

definition: Be or do something to a greater degree.
example: This car outperforms all others in its class.
etymology: From out- + perform.

definition: With respect to the outside.
example: Outwardly, the figure is smooth.
etymology: From Middle English outwardly, outwardli, utwardliche, equivalent to outward + -ly.

definition: The artery that branches from the aorta and supplies blood to the ovaries.
A thermometer that registers the temperature inside an oven.
Excessive crowding.
Excessively elaborate or showily expressed.
example: An over-embellished story of the fish that got away.

definition: Covered with water.
example: An overflowing tub.
etymology: From overflow + -ing.

definition: Excessive heating.
Traveling or passing over land.
example: An overland journey.
etymology: From over + land.

definition: Protective covering consisting, for example, of a layer of boards applied to the studs and joists of a building to strengthen it and serve as a foundation for a weatherproof exterior.
etymology: From Middle English overleyen, from Old English oferleċġan, from Proto-West Germanic *obarlaggjan, from Proto-Germanic *uberlagjaną, equivalent to over- + lay.

definition: Loaded past capacity.
A person who has general authority over others.
example: The various tribal chieftains met each spring to elect an overlord that would lead them in time of war.
etymology: From Middle English oferrlaferrd, orlard, our-lord, ouyr-lord, equivalent to over- + lord.

definition: Too costly for the value.
example: Overpriced items at resort shops.

definition: Having superior power and influence.
example: Our overriding concern is the safety of the children.

definition: Going by something that is moving in order to get in front of it.
In an overt manner.
example: He did it overtly.
etymology: From overt + -ly.

definition: Orchestral music played at the beginning of an opera or oratorio.
example: C. 1612', George Chapman, A Hymne to Hermes the cave's inmost overture.
etymology: From Middle English overture, from Anglo-Norman, Middle French overture, from Old French overture, from Latin apertūra. Doublet of aperture.

definition: Turn from an upright or normal position.
example: The big vase overturned.
etymology: From Middle English overturnen, equivalent to over- + turn. Compare also Middle English overterven (“to overturn”), see terve.

definition: Exploitation to the point of diminishing returns.
etymology: From over- + use.

definition: Overcome, as with emotions or perceptual stimuli.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English overwhelmen, equivalent to over- + whelm.

definition: Taking place in the presence of oxygen.
example: Oxidative glycolysis.
etymology: From oxide + -ative or oxidate + -ive.

definition: Black-and-white shorebird with stout legs and bill; feed on oysters etc.
A small dry usually round cracker.
etymology: Perhaps because originally served with oyster stew or clam chowder, or because their form (a vaguely round "shell" that splits evenly into two parts) was suggestive of the shell of an oyster.

definition: Oysters in cream.
Stuffing made with oysters.
Opposed to war.
etymology: From French pacifiste, equivalent to pacific + -ist.

definition: Softened by the addition of cushions or padding.
Artifact consisting of soft or resilient material used to fill or give shape or protect or add comfort.
example: That magazine is mostly advertisements; the rest is padding.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: A steam vessel propelled by paddle wheels.
A chaplain in one of the military services.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian padre, Spanish padre, or Portuguese padre (“priest”), which are from Latin pater (“father”). Doublet of ayr, faeder, father, pater, and père.

definition: Requiring little hard work or exertion.
example: A painless solution to the problem.
etymology: From Middle English paynles, peynlees, equivalent to pain + -less. Compare West Frisian pynleas (“painless”), Dutch pijnloos (“painless”).

definition: A capsule filled with water-soluble dye used as a projectile in playing the game of paintball.
etymology: From paint + ball.

definition: Freshwater turtles having bright yellow and red markings; common in the eastern United States.
Asiatic plant grown for its cluster of edible white stalks with dark green leaves.
Acceptable to the taste or mind.
example: Palatable food.
etymology: From palate + -able.

definition: A silver-white metallic element of the platinum group that resembles platinum; occurs in some copper and nickel ores; does not tarnish at ordinary temperatures and is used (alloyed with gold) in jewelry.
etymology: The sense of "safeguard" comes from Latin Palladium (the image of Pallas that protected Troy), from Ancient Greek Παλλάδιον (Palládion), from Παλλάς (Pallás), an epithet used before Athena.

definition: The range of colour characteristic of a particular artist or painting or school of art.
etymology: From Middle English paillet, from Anglo-Norman paillete (“bundle of straw”), from Old French paille (“straw, chaff”), from Latin palea (“chaff”).

definition: Moderating pain or sorrow by making it easier to bear.
etymology: From Middle French palliatif, from New Latin *palliātīvus, from Medieval Latin palliō (“to cloak”), from Latin pallium (“a cloak”).

definition: South American tree of dry interior regions of Argentina and Paraguay having resinous heartwood used for incense.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish palo santo.

definition: Densely branched spiny tree of southwestern United States having showy yellow flowers and blue-green bark; sometimes placed in genus Cercidium.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish palo verde (“green stick”).

definition: Capable of being perceived; especially capable of being handled or touched or felt.
example: A barely palpable dust.
etymology: From Middle French palpable and its source, Latin palpābilis, which is from palpō (“to touch softly”) + -bilis.

definition: Loss of the ability to move a body part.
etymology: From pal + -sy.

definition: Batter for making pancakes.
A large elongated exocrine gland located behind the stomach; secretes pancreatic juice and insulin.
etymology: Existing in English since the sixteenth century: from Latin pancreas, from Ancient Greek πάγκρεας (pánkreas), from πᾶν (pân, “all”) (equivalent to English pan-) + κρέας (kréas, “flesh”).

definition: A branch of the splenic artery that supplies the pancreas.
A duct connecting the pancreas with the intestine.
Veins draining the pancreas and emptying into the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
Sheet glass cut in shapes for windows or doors.
etymology: From Middle English pane, pan, from Old French pan, from Latin pannus, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂n- (“fabric”). Doublet of pagne and pannus.

definition: A sudden sharp feeling.
example: Pangs of regret.
etymology: The origin of the noun is uncertain; it is possibly derived from Middle English *pange, perhaps an altered form of prange, prōnge (“affliction, agony, pain;

definition: As from an altitude or distance.
example: A panoramic view.
etymology: From panorama + -ic.

definition: Gunsight (a telescopic device for an artillery piece) that can be rotated horizontally in a full circle.
A situation or topic as if viewed from an altitude or distance.
The noise made by a short puff of steam (as from an engine).
example: To commemorate our 50th anniversary we've rolled out a new pant with our signature blue and white seams.
etymology: From Middle English panten, whence also English dialectal pank.

definition: The leg of a pair of trousers.
All the gods of a religion.
etymology: From Pantheon (“a Roman temple to the gods later used as a church”), c. 1300.

definition: A performance using gestures and body movements without words.
etymology: First appears c. 1606, from Latin pantomīmus, from Ancient Greek παντόμιμος (pantómimos), from πᾶς (pâs, “each, all”) + μιμέομαι (miméomai, “to mimic”). The verbal form first appears c. 1768.

definition: A small storeroom for storing foods or wines.
etymology: From Middle English panetrie, from Old French paneterie, related to Latin panis (“bread”).

definition: Shrubby Asiatic tree having bark (tapa) that resembles cloth; grown as a shade tree in Europe and America; male flowers are pendulous catkins and female are urn-shaped followed by small orange-red aggregate berries.
A short moral story (often with animal characters).
example: In the New Testament the parables told by Jesus Christ convey His message, as in "The parable of the prodigal son".
etymology: From Middle English parable, from Old French parable, parabole, from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ, “comparison”). Doublet of parabola, parole, and palaver.

definition: An ideal instance; a perfect embodiment of a concept.
example: In the novel, Constanza is a paragon of virtue who would never compromise her reputation.

definition: Only one line can be drawn through a point parallel to another line.
A person trained to assist medical professionals and to give emergency medical treatment.
etymology: From para- + medic.

definition: Of or relating to a group of civilians organized to function like or to assist a military unit.
etymology: From para- + military.

definition: A group of civilians organized in a military fashion (especially to operate in place of or to assist regular army troops).
A group of civilians organized in a military fashion (especially to operate in place of or to assist regular army troops).
Rewording for the purpose of clarification.
example: Close paraphrase.
etymology: From Middle French paraphrase, from Latin paraphrasis, from Ancient Greek παράφρασις (paráphrasis), equivalent to para- + phrase. Doublet of paraphrasis.

definition: Worm that is parasitic on the intestines of vertebrates especially roundworms and tapeworms and flukes.
A superior paper resembling sheepskin.
A large area of land preserved in its natural state as public property.
etymology: From park + land.

definition: Reception room in an inn or club where visitors can be received.
A passenger car for day travel; you pay extra fare for individual chairs.
A game suitable for playing in a parlor.
A small grand piano.
A private religious school run by a church or parish.
A young salmon up to 2 years old.
etymology: Compare Scottish Gaelic bradan (“salmon”).

definition: Root vegetable common in central and eastern European cuisine, where it is used in soups and stews, or simply eaten raw, as a snack (similar to carrots).
Have some of the qualities or attributes of something.
example: Will you partake of some food?
etymology: Back-formation from Middle English part-takinge, part-takynge (“a sharing; partaking”), a calque of Latin particeps (“participating”); equivalent to part + take. Compare take part.

definition: Be active in.
Affording the opportunity for individual participation.
example: Participatory democracy.
etymology: From participate + -ory.

definition: Composed of distinct particles.
example: Particulate air pollution.
etymology: From Latin particulāt-, past participial stem (compare the verbal suffix -ate) of particulō (“to particularize”), from particula (“particle”) + -ō (verbal suffix).

definition: A small discrete mass of solid or liquid matter that remains individually dispersed in gas or liquid emissions (usually considered to be an atmospheric pollutant).
A stream of atomic or subatomic particles that may be charged positively (e.g. alpha particles) or negatively (e.g. beta particles) or not at all (e.g. neutrons).
Flesh of either quail or grouse.
example: On the first day of Christmas, my true love sent to me a partridge in a pear tree.

definition: Tropical American plant having leaflets somewhat sensitive to the touch; sometimes placed in genus Cassia.
Any of several types of commercially grown celery having green stalks.
A civil or military authority in Turkey or Egypt.
etymology: From Ottoman Turkish پاشا (pāšā) (Turkish paşa);

definition: A person who passes by casually or by chance.
example: A passer of counterfeit banknotes.
etymology: From pass + -er.

definition: A person who passes by casually or by chance.
etymology: From passer + by. Compare bystander.

definition: In a passive manner.
example: He listened passively.
etymology: From passive + -ly.

definition: Affixed or as if affixed with glue or paste.
example: Pieces of pasted paper.

definition: Having pale delicate colors.
A diversion that occupies one's time and thoughts (usually pleasantly).
example: Sailing is her favorite pastime.
etymology: From earlier passtime, pass-time, from Middle English passe tyme, passetyme, calque of Middle French passetemps.

definition: Mended usually clumsily by covering a hole with a patch.
example: Patched jeans.

definition: A paternity leave is a parental leave that a father can take after the birth of his child.
example: Don't worry Petunia, I'll take a paternity leave to help you take care of Dudley.
etymology: From paternity + leave, modelled after maternity leave.

definition: A lawsuit filed to determine the father of a child born out of wedlock (and to provide for the support of the child once paternity is determined).

A test based on blood groups to determine whether a particular man could be the biological father of a particular child; negative results prove he was not the father but positive results show only that he could be.
The fallacy of attributing human feelings to inanimate objects; ‘the friendly sun’ is an example of the pathetic fallacy.
etymology: Coined by British cultural critic John Ruskin in 1856 in his work Modern Painters.

definition: Someone who can find paths through unexplored territory.
Any disease-producing agent (especially a virus or bacterium or other microorganism).
etymology: From patho- + -gen. Second element ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“lineage”) through Ancient Greek γένος (génos, “birth”)

definition: A doctor who specializes in medical diagnosis.
etymology: From pathology + -ist.

definition: Characteristic of a form of social organization in which the male is the family head and title is traced through the male line.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin patriarchālis, from patriarcha + -ālis. Sychronically analyzable as patriarch + -al.

definition: A cross with two crossbars.
A form of social organization in which a male is the family head and title is traced through the male line.
etymology: From Latin patriarchia, from Medieval Greek πατριαρχία (patriarkhía), from Koine Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “patriarch”), from πατρία (patría) and ἄρχω (árkhō). By surface analysis, patri- + -archy.

definition: A series with a definite pattern of advance.
A setting with precious stones so closely set that no metal shows.
A person who pays money for something.
example: The company is the largest tax payer in the region.
etymology: From pay + -er (“subject of action”).

definition: A proportion in relation to a whole (which is usually the amount per hundred); ten percent.
Of or relating to the preservation of peace between hostile groups by international military forces.
example: A peacekeeping force.
etymology: From peace + keeping, after keep the peace.

definition: The activity of keeping the peace by military forces (especially when international military forces enforce a truce between hostile groups or nations).
The activity of keeping the peace by military forces (especially when international military forces enforce a truce between hostile groups or nations).
A period of time during which there is no war.
etymology: From peace + time.

definition: A disease of trees bearing drupes.
Brittle containing peanuts.
A disease blackening the leaves of pear and apple trees.
Erect and almost thornless American hawthorn with somewhat pear-shaped berries.
A fishery where they fish for pearl oysters.
Wet spongy ground of decomposing vegetation; has poorer drainage than a swamp; soil is unfit for cultivation but can be cut and dried and used for fuel.
etymology: From peat + bog.

definition: Any of various pale or ashy mosses of the genus Sphagnum whose decomposed remains form peat.
Of or relating to pedagogy.
example: Pedagogical significance.
etymology: From pedagogic + -al.

definition: The principles and methods of instruction.
etymology: From Middle French pédagogie, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγία (paidagōgía). By surface analysis, ped- (“child”) + -agogy.

definition: The act of selling goods for a living.
A specialist in the care of babies.
etymology: From pediatric + -ian.

definition: Loss of bits of outer skin by peeling or shedding or coming off in scales.
example: She flavored the broth with vegetable peelings.

definition: Fastened by pegs.
example: The pegged-down branches of the plant will take root.

definition: An acronym for pedestrian light control; a pedestrian crossing with traffic lights that are controlled by pedestrians.
etymology: Short for pedestrian light-controlled crossing.

definition: A small rounded mass of a substance.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English pelote, pelet, from Old French pelote (“small ball”), from Vulgar Latin *pilotta, diminutive of Latin pila (“ball”). Doublet of pelota.

definition: The space bounded by the bones of the pelvis and containing the pelvic viscera.
Either of a pair of fins attached to the pelvic girdle in fishes that help control the direction of movement; correspond to hind limbs of a land vertebrate.
The writing point of a pen.
Remorse for your past conduct.
etymology: From Middle English penaunce, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French peneance, from Latin paenitentia (“repentance, penitence”). Doublet of penitence.

definition: A strong liking.
example: The Irish have a penchant for blarney.

definition: A clock regulated by a pendulum.
Any of various antibiotics obtained from Penicillium molds (or produced synthetically) and used in the treatment of various infections and diseases.
Used for punishment or reform of criminals or wrongdoers.
example: Penitentiary institutions.

definition: Second last.
example: The author inadvertently reveals the murderer in the penultimate chapter.
etymology: From Latin paenultimus (“penultimate”) + -ate (adjective-forming suffix), from paene (“almost”) + ultimus (“last”). Equivalent to pene- + ultimate. Compare French pénultième.

definition: A shaker with a perforated top for sprinkling ground pepper.
Evergreen shrub or small tree whose foliage is conspicuously blotched with red and yellow and having small black fruits.
Herb with downy leaves and small purple or white flowers that yields a pungent oil used as a flavoring.
A candy flavored with peppermint oil.
Red gum tree of Tasmania.
Oil from the peppermint plant used as flavoring.
A pork and beef sausage (or a thin slice of this sausage).
example: Yo, Tony, gimme a slice of pepperoni and a coke.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian peperoni (“bell peppers”), the plural of peperone (“bell pepper”).

definition: By the year; every year (usually with reference to a sum of money paid or received).
example: He earned $100,000 per annum.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin per annum, English from the 16th century.

definition: A daily allowance for living expenses (especially while traveling in connection with your job).
etymology: From Latin per + diem (“day”).

definition: (statistics) any of the 99 numbered points that divide an ordered set of scores into 100 parts each of which contains one-hundredth of the total.
example: She is highly intelligent—she has an IQ in the top percentile.
etymology: Coined by Francis Galton in 1885, from percent + -ile.

definition: Perennial climber of central and southern Europe having purple or pink or white flowers; naturalized in North America.
Having a hole cut through.
example: A perforated eardrum.

definition: Fraught with danger.
example: A perilous voyage across the Atlantic in a small boat.
etymology: From Middle English perilous, from Old French perilleus, equivalent to peril + -ous, from the noun peril, or from Latin perīculōsus. Doublet of periculous.

definition: Happening or recurring at regular intervals.
example: The periodic appearance of the seventeen-year locust.
etymology: From period + -ical.

definition: An incidental benefit awarded for certain types of employment (especially if it is regarded as a right).
example: Free coffee is one of the perks of the job.
etymology: Clipping of perquisite.

definition: Gain or regain energy.
A series of waves in the hair made by applying heat and chemicals.
etymology: Short for permanent.

definition: That may be permitted especially as according to rule.
example: Permissible behavior in school.
etymology: From Middle English permyssyble, from Old French permissible, from Medieval Latin permissibilis.

definition: A viscous liquid with strong oxidizing properties; a powerful bleaching agent; also used (in aqueous solutions) as a mild disinfectant and (in strong concentrations) as an oxidant in rocket fuels.
etymology: From per- + oxide.

definition: A blond whose hair is bleached with peroxide.
Everlastingly; for all time.
example: Rays … streaming perpetually from the sun.
etymology: From Middle English perpetuelly; equivalent to perpetual + -ly.

definition: Cause to continue or prevail.
example: Perpetuate a myth.
etymology: From earlier preparat (see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).

definition: Full of difficulty or confusion or bewilderment.
example: Perplexed language.

definition: In a persistent manner.
example: He was asking questions, unavoidable questions, persistently ….
etymology: From persistent + -ly.

definition: A personal attractiveness or interestingness that enables you to influence others.
A lightweight consumer electronic device that looks like a hand-held computer but instead performs specific tasks; can serve as a diary or a personal database or a telephone or an alarm clock etc.
A pronoun expressing a distinction of person.
Made for or directed or adjusted to a particular individual.
example: Personalized luggage.

definition: Marked by a disposition to oppose and contradict.
example: Took perverse satisfaction in foiling her plans.
etymology: From Middle English perverse, pervers, from Old French pervers, from Latin perversum (“thoroughly turned”), past participle of pervertere, from per- (“thoroughly”) + vertere (“to turn”).

definition: The part of the leg of a human being below the ankle joint.
etymology: From Latin pēs (“foot”). Doublet of foot, pie (“Spanish unit of length”), and pous.

definition: Causing irritation or annoyance.
example: A pesky mosquito.
etymology: Possibly from pesty. Compare similar alteration between nasty and nasky.

definition: The basic unit of money in Uruguay; equal to 100 centesimos.
Toxic condition resulting from ingesting or inhaling a pesticide.
Someone left in charge of pets while their owners are away from home.
Part of the perianth that is usually brightly colored.
Resembling a petal.
A member of the lower middle class.
Epilepsy characterized by paroxysmal attacks of brief clouding of consciousness (and possibly other abnormalities).
example: She has been suffering from petit mal since childhood.
etymology: Borrowed from French petit mal (literally “little illness”).

definition: Gauge that indicates the amount of gasoline left in the gasoline tank of a vehicle.
A specialist in petroleum geology.
A collection of docile animals for children to pet and feed.
A member of a petit jury.
Waxy white nearly leafless plant with stems in clusters and racemes of white flowers; northwestern United States to northern California and east to Idaho.
Small red ant of warm regions; a common household pest.
The science or study of drugs: their preparation and properties and uses and effects.
etymology: From pharmaco- + -logy.

definition: Large long-tailed gallinaceous bird native to the Old World but introduced elsewhere.
An index of the relation between any two sets of scores that can both be represented on ordered binary dimensions (e.g., male-female).
Generous in assistance to the poor.
example: Philanthropic contributions.
etymology: From French philanthropique.

definition: Voluntary promotion of human welfare.
Someone who makes charitable donations intended to increase human well-being.
etymology: From philanthropy + -ist; compare French philanthrope.

definition: Composing or characteristic of an orchestral group.
example: Philharmonic players.
etymology: From French philharmonique; from Italian filarmonico. By surface analysis, phil- + harmonic.

definition: The pitch used to tune instruments for concert performances; usually assigns 440 Hz to the A above middle C.
An anxiety disorder characterized by extreme and irrational fear of simple things or social situations.
example: Phobic disorder is a general term for all phobias.
etymology: First attested in c. 1790, from words ending in -phobia, ultimately from Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”). Compare ism, from -ism, itis, from -itis, and ana, from -ana.

definition: Of or relating to speech sounds.
example: Phonetic transcription.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin phōnēticus, from Ancient Greek φωνητῐκός (phōnētĭkós). By surface analysis, phone + -etic.

definition: An articulatory or acoustic property of speech sounds.
A written character used in phonetic transcription to represent a particular speech sound.
Producing a voltage when exposed to radiant energy (especially light).
etymology: From photo- + voltaic.

definition: A cell that converts solar energy into electrical energy.

Keeping a safe space between yourself and other people, and avoiding crowds, in order to slow the spread of infectious diseases. Large-scale measures include canceling group events or closing schools, workplaces and public spaces.
A situation is physically impossible if its description is inconsistent with physical laws (i.e. with the laws of Nature).
The appearance of the network.
example: The physical topologies of local area networks include the bus, the ring and the star.

definition: Perennial herb of East Indies to Polynesia and Australia; cultivated for its large edible root yielding Otaheite arrowroot starch.
An accordion with a right-hand keyboard.
A sonata for piano.
A public square with room for pedestrians.
etymology: From Italian piazza. Doublet of piatza, place, platz, and plaza.

definition: A small flute; pitched an octave above the standard flute.
etymology: From Italian piccolo (“small”).

definition: A fence made of upright pickets.
Relish of chopped (usually sweet) pickles.
(used of foods) preserved in a pickling liquid.
Herring preserved in a pickling liquid (usually brine or vinegar).
Pertaining to or consisting of pictures.
example: Pictorial perspective.
etymology: From Latin pictōrius (“of painting”) + -al, from pictor (“painter”).

definition: Illustrations used to decorate or explain a text.
Having sections or patches colored differently and usually brightly.
example: Pied daisies.
etymology: From archaic pie (“magpie”), from Old French pie, from Latin pica. Compare typologically Polish srokaty < sroka.

definition: A gentle slope leading from the base of a mountain to a region of flat land.
etymology: From Piedmont, ultimately from Italian piemonte (“foot of a mountain”); cognate with French piémont.

definition: Righteousness by virtue of being pious.
example: Colleen's piety led her to make sacrifices that most people would not have made.
etymology: From Middle English piete, borrowed from Middle French pieté, from Latin pietās. See also the doublets pietà and pity. By surface analysis, pious + -ety.

definition: Any of several pike-like fishes of the perch family.
Any of several pike-like fishes of the perch family.
etymology: From pike + perch.

definition: A large pile driving device.
The guidance of ships or airplanes from place to place.
A game played on a sloping board; the object is to propel marbles against pins or into pockets.
etymology: From pin + ball.

definition: A game played on a sloping board; the object is to propel marbles against pins or into pockets.
Game equipment on which pinball is played.
example: In Britain they call a pinball machine a ‘pin table’.

definition: Sounding as if the nose were pinched.
Fern of Florida and West Indies and Central America with rhizome densely clad in grown hairs.
Of a color tinged with pink.
A mutual promise of a couple not to date anyone else; on college campuses it was once signaled by the giving of a fraternity pin.
A spotted or calico horse or pony.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish pinto (“painted, mottled”).

definition: Mottled or spotted bean of southwestern United States; usually dried.
etymology: From Spanish pinto (“painted”), named for its mottled skin.

definition: Usually small round bread that can open into a pocket for filling.
etymology: From Greek πίτα (píta, “pie”), more at pizza. Doublet of pide and pizza.

definition: Total absence of light.
A long-handled hand tool with sharp widely spaced prongs for lifting and pitching hay.
example: The city council was facing the pitchforks once the public had realized what the new ordinance entailed.
etymology: From Middle English pichfork, pycchefork, pychforke, pikeforke, pikkforke, pic-forcke, equivalent to pitch (verb) + fork (i.e. "a fork used for pitching or throwing material, like hay").

definition: Pitted with cell-like cavities (as a honeycomb).
The formation of small pits in a surface as a consequence of corrosion.
example: Test pittings were carried out prior to the main excavation.

definition: (folklore) fairies that are somewhat mischievous.
etymology: Uncertain; 17thC, originally in the folklore of southwest England; perhaps diminutive of dialectal Swedish pysk (“fairy”), though the transmission of a Swedish dialect term to southwest Britain is unexplained;

definition: That part of the ovary of a flowering plant where the ovules form.
(of a body of water) free from disturbance by heavy waves.
example: A ribbon of sand between the angry sea and the placid bay.
etymology: Borrowed from French placide, from Latin placidus (“peaceful, calm, placid”), from placeō (“please, satisfy”).

definition: A piece of writing that has been copied from someone else and is presented as being your own work.
example: Even if it's not illegal, plagiarism is usually frowned upon.
etymology: From plagiary + -ism.

definition: Involving or having two dimensions.
example: A planar projection of a three-dimensional object is its projection onto a plane.
etymology: From Late Latin plānārius (“relating to a plane”), derived from Latin plānus (“flat”, “level”), equivalent to plane + -ar, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”).

definition: A mixer consisting of a bowl and an agitator that is rapidly moved around the bowl to mix its contents.
example: With the ability to mix a wide variety of ingredients, planetary mixers are more versatile than their spiral counterparts.

definition: A nebula that was once thought to be a star with its planets but is now thought to be a very hot star surrounded by an expanding envelope of ionized gases that emit a fluorescent glow because of intense radiation from the star.
etymology: Coined by William Herschel because of their apparent resemblance to the planet Uranus.

definition: The aggregate of small plant and animal organisms that float or drift in great numbers in fresh or salt water.
The owner or manager of a plantation.
etymology: From plant + -er.

definition: Bandage consisting of a firm covering (often made of plaster of Paris) that immobilizes broken bones while they heal.
(of hair) made smooth by applying a sticky or glossy substance.
example: Black hair plastered with pomade.

definition: A map showing planned or actual features of an area (streets and building lots etc.).
etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English plat, platte (“flat part of a sword;

definition: A thin coating of metal deposited on a surface.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Thermometer that measures temperature by changes in the resistance of a spiral of platinum wire.
Free from physical desire.
example: Platonic love.
etymology: Variant of Platonic, which see. The sense “non-sexual” dates to the 17th century in English, and to the 15th century in Latin; see platonic love for details.

definition: Plaything consisting of a small model of a house that children can play inside of.
etymology: From Middle English *pleyhous, possibly continuing Old English pleġhūs (“playhouse, theatre”). By surface analysis, play + house. Compare Dutch speelhuis, German Spielhaus.

definition: Time for play or diversion.
example: The school bell rings to mark the end of playtime.
etymology: From play + time.

definition: Affording satisfaction or pleasure.
example: Full of happiness and pleasurable excitement.
etymology: From pleasure + -able.

definition: A volunteer who records (usually by telephone) contributions pledged in a fund drive.
Full in all respects.
example: A plenary session of the legislature.
etymology: From Middle English plenarie, plenarye, from Late Latin plēnārius, from Latin plēnus (“full”).

definition: Extreme excess.
example: The menu offers a plethora of cuisines from around the world.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin plēthōra, from Ancient Greek πληθώρα (plēthṓra, “fullness, satiety”), from πλήθω (plḗthō, “to be full”) + -η (-ē, nominal suffix).

definition: A horse used to pull a plow.
Continue moving forward.
example: We could stop for a coffee, or plough on to the hotel.

definition: To break and turn over earth especially with a plow.
example: Farmer Jones plowed his east field last week.

definition: Proceed (with a plan of action).
A horse used to pull a plow.
An opening remark intended to secure an advantage for the speaker.
example: The free T-shirt is really a ploy to get you inside to see their sales pitch.
etymology: Possibly from a shortened form of employ or deploy. Or from earlier ploye, from Middle English, borrowed from Middle French ployer (compare modern plier), from Latin plicāre.

definition: Pull or pull out sharply.
example: Pluck the flowers off the bush.
etymology: From Middle English plucken, plukken, plockien, from Old English pluccian, ploccian (“to pluck, pull away, tear”), also Old English plyċċan ("to pluck, pull, snatch;

definition: Pluck or pull at with the fingers.
Of a stringed instrument; sounded with the fingers or a plectrum.
A stiff flour pudding steamed or boiled usually and containing e.g. currants and raisins and citron.
Rip off; ask an unreasonable price.
example: He plumes himself on his skill.
etymology: From Late Middle English plum, plume (“feather;

definition: A reedlike grass of the genus Erianthus having large plumes.
Herb of China and Japan widely cultivated for its plumelike panicles of creamy white flowers.
Of a plant tipped with a plume.
Drop sharply.
example: Her cheeks have plumped.
etymology: From Middle English plump, plompe, a borrowing from Middle Dutch plomp or Middle Low German plump. Cognate with Saterland Frisian plump (“plump”).

definition: Drop heavily.
Be behind; approve of.
example: He plumped for the Labor Party.

definition: Arrive suddenly and unannounced.
example: He plumped in on a Sunday morning.

definition: Depart suddenly.
example: He plumped out of the house.

definition: Make fuller by shaking.
example: Please plump up the pillows.

definition: Take illegally; of intellectual property.
example: This writer plundered from famous authors.
etymology: Recorded since 1632 during the Thirty Years War, native British use since the Cromwellian Civil War.

definition: Men's baggy knickers hanging below the knees; formerly worn for sports (especially golf).
A steel or beryllium sphere containing plutonium 239 that triggers nuclear fission when compressed by explosives.
A steel or beryllium sphere containing plutonium 239 that triggers nuclear fission when compressed by explosives.
Give what is desired or needed, especially support, food or sustenance.
example: To ply someone with questions or solicitations.
etymology: From Middle English pleit, plit, plite (“a fold, pleat, wrinkle; braid, strand in a braided cord, ply”), from Anglo-Norman pli, plei, pleit, and Middle French pli, ploy, ply (“a fold, pleat; joint in armour;

definition: Of or relating to or using air (or a similar gas).
example: Pneumatic drill.
etymology: From Latin pneumaticus, from Ancient Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikós, “relating to wind or air”), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, air, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “to blow, breath”).

definition: A power drill powered by compressed air.
A hammer driven by compressed air.
A tire made of reinforced rubber and filled with compressed air; used on motor vehicles and bicycles etc.
Cooking in simmering liquid.
A small battleship built to conform with treaty limitations on tonnage and armament (from 1925 to 1930).
A flask that holds spirits.
A handkerchief that is carried in a pocket.
A poet who is unofficially regarded as holding an honorary position in a particular group or region.
example: She is the poet laureate of all lyricists.

definition: Be motionless, in suspension.
example: The bird poised for a few moments before it attacked.
etymology: From Middle English poys, poyse, from Anglo-Norman pois, Middle French pois (“weight”) and Anglo-Norman poise, Middle French poise (“measure of weight”), from Latin pendere (“to weigh, ponder, think”). Doublet of peise.

definition: Large branching biennial herb native to Eurasia and Africa and adventive in North America having large fernlike leaves and white flowers; usually found in damp habitats; all parts extremely poisonous.
A hat tied under the chin.
A relation between two opposite attributes or tendencies.
example: He viewed it as a balanced polarity between good and evil.

definition: A female member of a police force.
A dissenter from political orthodoxy.
The opinion you hold with respect to political questions.
Music performed for dancing the polka.
etymology: Via French and German from Czech polka, variant of půlka (“half”) as in "half-step"; see půl (“half”).

definition: Design consisting of a pattern of regularly spaced circular spots.
etymology: First use appears in the US c. 1857 in the publication Godey's Lady's Book. Named after the polka dance, which was popular at the time (1840–1890).

definition: Someone who conducts surveys of public opinion.
example: A pollster conducts public opinion polls.

definition: A tree with limbs cut back to promote a more bushy growth of foliage.
example: And at this place there was a long, straight causeway, with two long rows of pollard willows, one upon either hand.
etymology: From Middle English poll (“head”) + the pejorative suffix -ard (“person characterized by or associated with something, often in a negative way”). The suffix has the same meaning as in drunkard and coward.

definition: Lean white flesh of North Atlantic fish; similar to codfish.
etymology: From Middle English [Term?], perhaps from Scots podlok.

definition: A quick-drying resilient synthetic fiber consisting primarily of polyester.
The condition or practice of having more than one spouse at a time.
example: Are there countries where polygamy is legal for both men and women?
etymology: Recorded since 1591, from Late Latin polygamia, from Ancient Greek πολυγαμία (polugamía), itself from πολύγαμος (polúgamos, “married to many”), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + γάμος (gámos, “marriage”).

definition: A closed plane figure bounded by straight sides.
example: Meronyms: angle, side, cathetus, leg, hypotenuse; see also Thesaurus:polygon.
etymology: From Ancient Greek πολύγωνον (polúgōnon), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + γωνία (gōnía, “angle”), equivalent to poly- + -gon.

definition: A technical school offering instruction in many industrial arts and applied sciences.
etymology: First attested in 1805. From French polytechnique, from the École polytechnique, engineering school founded 1794 in Paris;

definition: A technical school offering instruction in many industrial arts and applied sciences.
Puffed up with vanity.
example: A pompous speech.

definition: Wood of a deciduous conifer of the genus Taxodium, native to North America.
Long-legged bug that skims about on the surface of water.
Deeply or seriously thoughtful.
A hair style that draws the hair back so that it hangs down in back of the head like a pony's tail.
etymology: From pony + tail.

definition: An intelligent dog with a heavy curly solid-colored coat that is usually clipped; an old breed sometimes trained as sporting dogs or as performing dogs.
etymology: From German Pudel, a shortened form of Pudelhund, a compound of Hund (“dog”) and the German Low German term Pudel, Pūdel (“puddle”), from the onomatopoeic term pudeln (“to splash about”).

definition: An intelligent dog with a heavy curly solid-colored coat that is usually clipped; an old breed sometimes trained as sporting dogs or as performing dogs.
Soft light-colored non-durable wood of the poplar.
etymology: From Middle English popler, from Anglo-Norman popler and Old French poplier (compare French peuplier), from Latin pōpulus, with a suffix later added.

definition: Any of numerous trees of north temperate regions having light soft wood and flowers borne in catkins.
Among the people.
example: This topic was popularly discussed.
etymology: From popular + -ly.

definition: Woody pore fungi; any fungus of the family Polyporaceae or family Boletaceae having the spore-bearing surface within tubes or pores; the fruiting bodies are usually woody at maturity and persistent.
Woody pore fungi; any fungus of the family Polyporaceae or family Boletaceae having the spore-bearing surface within tubes or pores; the fruiting bodies are usually woody at maturity and persistent.
Soft food made by boiling oatmeal or other meal or legumes in water or milk until thick.
example: Eat your porridge while it's hot!
etymology: Variant of pottage (“thick soup or stew”), influenced by porray (“stew of leeks”). The "prison sentence" sense comes from the British tradition of serving prisoners porridge for breakfast.

definition: A watchman on a wharf.
The cost of carrying or transporting.
etymology: From Middle English portage, borrowed from Middle French portage, from Old French portage, from Early Medieval Latin portāticum. By surface analysis, port (“to carry”) + -age.

definition: Of or relating to or determined by position.
etymology: From position + -al.

definition: A temporary police force.
etymology: Ellipsis of posse comitatus.

definition: Serving to express or indicate possession.
example: Possessive pronouns.
etymology: From Middle French possessif, from Latin possessivus (“of or pertaining to possession”), from possessiō (“possessing”), from possidēre (“to possess”). By surface analysis, possess + -ive.

definition: The case expressing ownership.
Discussion of an event after it has occurred.
A code of letters and digits added to a postal address to aid in the sorting of mail.
etymology: From post + code.

definition: Of or relating to study or research that is done after work for the doctoral degree has been completed.
etymology: From post- + doctoral.

definition: A man who delivers the mail.
etymology: From post + -man.

definition: The person in charge of a post office.
etymology: From post + master.

definition: The official in charge of the national postal service.
Of or relating to postmodernism.
example: Postmodernist architecture.
etymology: From post- + modern.

definition: Time during which some action is awaited.
example: The lawyer asked for a postponement in the trial so he could spend more time preparing before it began.
etymology: From postpone + -ment.

definition: A white crystalline double sulfate of aluminum: the potassium double sulfate of aluminum.
A white salt (K2CO3) that is basic in solution; used to make glass and cleansing agents.
Salt of potassium (KCl) (trade names K-Dur 20, Kaochlor and K-lor and Klorvess and K-lyte); taken in tablet form to treat potassium deficiency.
A poisonous salt (KCN) used in electroplating and in photography.
(KNO3) used especially as a fertilizer and explosive.
A blight of potatoes.
Large Australasian evergreen fern with an edible rhizome sometimes used as a vegetable by indigenous people.
Toilet consisting of a small seat used by young children.
(of children) trained to use the toilet.
Container for carrying gunpowder; made of the hollow horn of an animal.
A potentially explosive state.
example: Powder keg of Europe (term describing the unstable state of the Balkans before World War I).

definition: Dried ground gingerroot.
A substance such that one to three tablespoons dissolved in a glass of warm water is a homemade emetic.
A lawn mower powered by a gasoline motor.
In a powerful manner.
example: The federal government replaced the powerfully pro-settler Sir Godfrey Huggins with the even tougher and more determined ex-trade unionist.
etymology: From powerful + -ly.

definition: A common venereal disease caused by the treponema pallidum spirochete; symptoms change through progressive stages; can be congenital (transmitted through the placenta).
example: A pox on all their houses.
etymology: From the plural of Middle English pocke. See also pock. The curse sense involves metonymy: wishing a literal pox upon someone is the original form of pox-relevant curse, and the word pox itself also came to mean curse.

definition: An imperial decree that becomes part of the fundamental law of the land.
Brown mottled North American grouse of western prairies.
Orchid of boggy or wet lands of north central United States having racemes of very fragrant creamy or greenish white flowers.
Similar to the common sunflower with slender usually branching stems common in central United States.
(Judaism) a shawl with a ritually knotted fringe at each corner; worn by Jews at morning prayer.
The common mantis.
etymology: Mantis from Ancient Greek μάντις (mántis). Named "praying mantis" for their stance, with the forelegs held together in a way that resembles a person praying.

definition: Keep from happening or arising; make impossible.
example: Your role in the projects precludes your involvement in the competitive project.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin praeclūdere.

definition: In a predictable manner or to a predictable degree.
example: Predictably, he did not like the news.
etymology: From predictable + -ly.

definition: Someone who makes predictions of the future (usually on the basis of special knowledge).
example: The rainfall in April is a predictor for the number of mosquitoes in May.
etymology: From predict + -or.

definition: A variable that can be used to predict the value of another variable (as in statistical regression).
A chief officer or chief magistrate.
example: The prefect of Paris police.
etymology: From Middle English prefect and prefecte, from Old French prefect (Mod. French préfet), from Latin praefectus (“one placed in charge, overseer, director, prefect”), from praeficere (“to place in charge”).

definition: The district administered by a prefect (as in France or Japan or the Roman Empire).
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French préfecture, from Latin praefectūra. Equivalent to prefect + -ure.

definition: Manifesting partiality.
example: Preferential tariff rates.
etymology: From Medieval Latin preferentia + -al.

definition: An affix that is added in front of the word.
example: In the UK, a number with an 0800 prefix is a toll-free number.

definition: A parenthesis-free notation for forming mathematical expressions in which each operator precedes its operands.
Emanating from a person's emotions and prejudices.
A first draft of a prospectus; must be clearly marked to indicate that parts may be changed in the final prospectus.
example: Because some portions of the cover page are printed in red ink a preliminary prospectus is sometimes called a red herring.

definition: Occurring or existing before birth.
example: The prenatal period.
etymology: From pre- + natal.

definition: Any of the diagnostic procedures used to determine whether a fetus has a genetic abnormality.
Works for an expert to learn a trade.
etymology: An old (Middle English) apheretic form of apprentice.

definition: So unreasonable as to invite derision.
example: A preposterous attempt to turn back the pages of history.
