etymology: From Latin praeposterus (“with the hinder part before, reversed, inverted, perverted”), from prae (“before”) + posterus (“coming after”).

definition: Required as a prior condition or course of study.
example: The prerequisite warm-up to the match was ignored.
etymology: From pre- + requisite.

definition: A right reserved exclusively by a particular person or group (especially a hereditary or official right).
example: Suffrage was the prerogative of white adult males.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman prerogative (noun), from Latin praerogātīva (“previous verdict; claim, privilege”), noun use of the feminine singular of praerogātīvus (“having first vote; privileged”).

definition: An excerpt cut from a newspaper or magazine.
Gauge for measuring and indicating fluid pressure.
An assumption that is taken for granted.
example: The presumption is that an event has taken place.
etymology: From pre- + Latin sūmptus + -ion, from Middle English presumpcioun, presumption, from Old French presumption and its etymon Latin praesūmptiō.

definition: The act of giving a false appearance.
example: His conformity was only pretending.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French pretensse, from Late Latin praetēnsus, past participle of Latin praetendō (“to pretend”), from prae- (“before”) + tendō (“to stretch”); see pretend.

definition: Making claim to or creating an appearance of (often undeserved) importance or distinction.
example: A pretentious country house.
etymology: From French prétentieux, from prétention, from Latin praetēnsus (“false or hypocritical profession”), past participle of praetendō. Note that pretentious is spelled with a ‘t’, unlike related pretense, pretension.

definition: Capable of being prevented.
example: Conscious of preventable human suffering.
etymology: From prevent + -able.

definition: Remedy that prevents or slows the course of an illness or disease.
example: The doctor recommended several preventatives.
etymology: From prevent + -ative.

definition: Very irritable.
example: He became prickly and spiteful.
etymology: From prickle + -y.

definition: Any of a number of trees or shrubs of the genus Zanthoxylum having spiny branches.
Obstruction of the sweat ducts during high heat and humidity.
etymology: 1730-40, Americanism.

definition: One of the main flight feathers projecting along the outer edge of a bird's wing.
The first stage; characterized by a chancre at the site of infection.
A senior clergyman and dignitary.
example: Primates range from lemurs to gorillas.
etymology: First attested in 1876. From French primate, from the substantivization of Latin prīmās, prīmātis (“one of the first, chief, excellent, noble”), same as Etymology 2.

definition: An agent that is the cause of all things but does not itself have a cause.
etymology: Originally in translation of Latin primum mobile.

definition: (usually followed by ‘to’ or ‘for’) on the point of or strongly disposed.
example: Primed for a fight.

definition: Having existed from the beginning; in an earliest or original stage or state.
example: Primordial matter.
etymology: From the Latin prīmōrdiālis (“of the beginning”). Compare primordium and -al.

definition: A prince who is the husband of a reigning female sovereign.
etymology: Calque of French prince consort.

definition: Based on or manifesting objectively defined standards of rightness or morality.
example: Principled pragmatism and unprincipled expediency.
etymology: From principle + -ed.

definition: Religious residence in a monastery governed by a prior or a convent governed by a prioress.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman priorie.

definition: Changing something from state to private ownership or control.
etymology: From privatise + -ation.

definition: A mathematician who specializes in probability theory.
A court having jurisdiction over the probate of wills and the administration of estates.
Diligent and thorough in inquiry or investigation.
example: A probing inquiry.

definition: Someone who supervises (an examination).
etymology: Inherited from Middle English procatour, procutour, contraction of procuratour; compare proxy. Doublet of procurator and procurer.

definition: Get by special effort.
example: He procured extra cigarettes even though they were rationed.
etymology: From Middle English procuren, from Old French procurer, from Late Latin prōcūrāre (“to manage, administer”), from prō (“on behalf of”) + cūrō (“to care for”).

definition: Professing to be qualified.
example: A professed philosopher.

definition: Someone who sells stock shares at a profit.
Making the profit as great as possible.
example: The profit-maximizing price.

definition: The immediate descendants of a person.
example: I treasure this five-generation photograph of my great-great grandmother and her progeny.
etymology: From Middle English progenie, from Old French progenie, from Latin prōgeniēs, from prōgignō (“beget”).

definition: A steroid hormone (trade name Lipo-Lutin) produced in the ovary; prepares and maintains the uterus for pregnancy.
etymology: From pro- + Latin gestāre (“to bear, to carry”) + English -one.

definition: An introduction to a play.
etymology: From Middle English prologue, prologe, from Old French prologue, from Latin prologus, from Ancient Greek πρόλογος (prólogos). Equivalent to pro- + -logue.

definition: Lengthen in time; cause to be or last longer.
example: We prolonged our stay.
etymology: Either a back-formation from prolongation, or from Old French prolonguer or porloignier, from Latin prōlongō, from prō + longō. Doublet of purloin.

definition: A formal ball held for a school class toward the end of the academic year.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French promenade, from promener (“to walk”).

definition: A deck at the top of a passenger ship.
A function word that is used in place of a noun or noun phrase.
Transmit from one generation to the next.
example: Propagate these characteristics.
etymology: First attested in 1535; from Latin prōpāgātus, perfect passive participle of prōpāgō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Participial usage up until Early Modern English.

definition: Colorless gas found in natural gas and petroleum; used as a fuel.
etymology: From clipping of propionic acid + -ane, from French propionique, from Ancient Greek πρό (pró) + πίων (píōn, “fat”). Analyzable as prop- + -ane, borrowing or calque of German Propan.

definition: Cause to move forward with force.
example: Steam propels this ship.
etymology: From Middle English propellen (“drive out, expel”), from Latin propellō, from pro- (“forward”) and pellō (“to push, to move”).

definition: An inclination to do something.
example: He has a propensity for lengthy discussions of certain favorite topics.
etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin prōpensitās. By surface analysis, propense (“inclined, disposed”) + -ity.

definition: Foretelling events as if by supernatural intervention.
example: Prophetic writings.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French prophétique, from Latin prophēticus, from Ancient Greek προφητικός (prophētikós), equivalent to prophet + -ic.

definition: A person who pleads for a cause or propounds an idea.
etymology: From Latin prōpōnēns, present participle of prōpōnō (“to put forward; propose”).

definition: Being in due proportion.
example: Proportionate representation of a minority group.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōportiōnātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, proportion + -ate.

definition: A formal written offer to sell securities (filed with the SEC) that sets forth a plan for a (proposed) business enterprise.
example: A prospectus should contain the facts that an investor needs to make an informed decision.
etymology: From French prospectus (“a prospectus”), borrowed from Latin prospectus. Doublet of prospect and prospekt.

definition: Of or relating to prosthetics.
example: Prosthetic leg/arm.
etymology: From New Latin prostheticus, from Ancient Greek προσθετικός (prosthetikós, “adding; repletive;

definition: Corrective consisting of a replacement for a part of the body.
A steep artificial slope in front of a fortification.
A person who dissents from some established policy.
example: The protesters thronged Trafalgar Square and sang anti-war songs.
etymology: From protest + -er.

definition: Indicating the first or earliest or original.
etymology: From the prefix proto-.

definition: A collider that collides beams of protons and antiprotons.
Extending out above or beyond a surface or boundary.
example: His protruding ribs.

definition: Where something originated or was nurtured in its early existence.
example: Many supermarkets display the provenance of their food products.
etymology: Borrowed from French provenance (“origin”), from Middle French provenant, present participle of provenir (“come forth, arise”), from Latin provenio (“to come forth”).

definition: A condensed but memorable saying embodying some important fact of experience that is taken as true by many people.
etymology: From Old French proverbe, from Latin proverbium.

definition: Of or relating to or resembling or expressed in a proverb.
example: He kicked the proverbial bucket.
etymology: From Latin prōverbiālis, equivalent to proverb + -ial

definition: Unfriendly behavior that causes anger or resentment.
example: When it's time to check for provocation, ask the patient about what makes their chief complaint better or worse.
etymology: From Middle English provocacioun, from Old French provocacion, from Late Latin prōvocātiō, prōvocātiōnem, from Latin prōvocō. By surface analysis, provoke + -ation. Doublet of provokatsiya.

definition: A high-ranking university administrator.
etymology: From Middle English, from late Old English prōfost, prāfost, from Late Latin prōpositus, variant of Latin praepositus (“[one] placed in command”). In some senses, via Anglo-Norman provolt;

definition: A military court for trying people charged with minor offenses in an occupied area.
A detachment under the command of a provost marshall.
The supervisor of the military police.
Situated nearest to point of attachment or origin.
example: The proximal end of a bone.

definition: Discretion in practical affairs.
etymology: From Middle English prudence (“discretion; foresight; knowledge; intelligence, wisdom; act of good judgment;

definition: Arising from or characterized by prudence especially in business matters.
example: He abstained partly for prudential reasons.
etymology: From Latin prudentia + -al.

definition: Something that has been pruned off of a plant.
etymology: From prune + -ing.

definition: A long-handled pruning saw with a curved blade at the end and sometimes a clipper; used to prune small trees.
A knife with a curved or hooked blade.
A handsaw used for pruning trees.
To move or force, especially in an effort to get something open.
example: Raccoons managed to pry the lid off the garbage pail.
etymology: The noun is probably a back-formation from prise, prize (“tool for levering, lever”), construed as the plural of pry.

definition: A heavy iron lever with one end forged into a wedge.
A fictitious name used when the person performs a particular social role.
example: The Reverend Charles Lutwidge Dodgson wrote "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland" under the pseudonym Lewis Carroll.
etymology: Borrowed from French pseudonyme (“pseudonymous”, adjective), from Latin pseudonymus (adjective), from Ancient Greek ψευδώνυμος (pseudṓnumos, adjective). By surface analysis, pseudo- + -onym.

definition: A set of techniques for exploring underlying motives and a method of treating various mental disorders; based on the theories of Sigmund Freud.
example: His physician recommended psychoanalysis.
etymology: From international scientific vocabulary, after German Psychoanalyse. By surface analysis, psycho- + analysis.

definition: Any severe mental disorder in which contact with reality is lost or highly distorted.
etymology: From psych- + -osis. Not descended from Ancient Greek ψύχωσις (psúkhōsis, “animation, principle of life”), which is a piecewise cognate.

definition: Relating or near the pubis.
example: Pubic bones.
etymology: From pubis + -ic.

definition: One of the three sections of the hipbone; together these two bones form the front of the pelvis.
Hair growing in the pubic area.
An official who inflicts capital punishment in pursuit of a warrant.
A company that moves the possessions of a family or business from one site to another.
Someone who publicizes.
etymology: Borrowed from French publiciste, equivalent to public + -ist.

definition: Made known; especially made widely known.
A communal village built by Indians in the southwestern United States.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish pueblo, from Latin populus. Doublet of people.

definition: Being puffed out; used of hair style or clothing.
example: Puffy breath.
etymology: From puff + -y.

definition: Small compact smooth-coated breed of Asiatic origin having a tightly curled tail and broad flat wrinkled muzzle.
etymology: Origin unknown, possibly related to West Flemish pugge (“(adjective) small; (noun) short person; pet name derived from the first name Pugge”);

definition: A short nose; flattened and turned up at the end.
Small compact smooth-coated breed of Asiatic origin having a tightly curled tail and broad flat wrinkled muzzle.
Having the flat wrinkled face of a pug dog.
Having a blunt nose.
example: A pug-nosed boy with freckles.

definition: Involving the lungs with progressive wasting of the body.
A platform raised above the surrounding level to give prominence to the person on it.
example: He seems like too timid a man to fill the pulpit at such a large church.
etymology: From Middle English pulpit, from Old French pulpite and Latin pulpitum (“platform”). Doublet of pulpitum and polypus. Piecewise doublet of polypod.

definition: Modulation that imposes a signal on a train of pulses.
Large American feline resembling a lion.
Pierce with a pointed object; make a hole into.
example: Puncture a tire.

definition: Someone who has been admitted to membership in a scholarly field.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindi पंडित (paṇḍit) / Urdu پنڈت (panḍit), from Sanskrit पण्डित (paṇḍita, “scholar, learned man, teacher, philosopher”). Doublet of pandit.

definition: Someone who propels a boat with a pole.
etymology: From punt (“a kind of boat”) + -er.

definition: A temporary condition of torment or suffering.
example: A purgatory of drug abuse.
etymology: From Middle English purgatorie, from Old French purgatore, purgatorie, from Latin purgātōrium (“cleansing”). Cognate to English purge.

definition: Remove impurities from, increase the concentration of, and separate through the process of distillation.
example: Purify the water.
etymology: From Middle English purifien, purifyen, from Old French purifier, purifiier, from Latin pūrificō, pūrificāre, from pūrus (“pure; clean”).

definition: Variety of European beech with shining purple or copper-colored leaves.
Tufted locoweed of southwestern United States having purple or pink to white flowers.
Of lavender tinged with purple.
Of a color tinged with purple.
Of a color tinged with purple.
Serving as or indicating the existence of a purpose or goal.
etymology: From purpose + -ful.

definition: In a purposeful manner.
example: He caught the motorcycles in the full glare of his headlights, braked and slipped purposefully out of the car.
etymology: From purposeful + -ly.

definition: A seine designed to be set by two boats around a school of fish and then closed at the bottom by means of a line.
A fluid product of inflammation.
example: Pus was seeping out of the wound.
etymology: From Middle English pus (15th c.), a borrowing from Latin pus (“pus”). Widely displaced quitter and atter in this sense.

definition: Marked by aggressive ambition and energy and initiative.
etymology: From push + -y.

definition: Not clear to the understanding.
European grass spreading rapidly by creeping rhizomes; naturalized in North America as a weed.
Having four units or components.
example: Quadruple rhythm has four beats per measure.
etymology: From Middle English quadruple, from Latin quadruplus. Can be analyzed as quadri- + -ple.

definition: A time signature indicating four beats to the bar.
Flesh of quail; suitable for roasting or broiling if young; otherwise must be braised.
etymology: From Middle English quaylen, from Middle Dutch queilen, quēlen, from Old Dutch *quelan, from Proto-West Germanic *kwelan, from Proto-Germanic *kwelaną (“to suffer”). Doublet of queal.

definition: Anticipate with dread or anxiety.
Spiny shrub with silvery-scurfy foliage of alkaline plains of southwestern United States and Mexico.
Spiny shrub with silvery-scurfy foliage of alkaline plains of southwestern United States and Mexico.
One who quakes and trembles with (or as with) fear.
Use as a quantifier.
etymology: From Medieval Latin quantifico (introduced by Sir William Hamilton in logic).

definition: (physics) hypothetical truly fundamental particle in mesons and baryons; there are supposed to be six flavors of quarks (and their antiquarks), which come in pairs; each has an electric charge of +2/3 or -1/3.
example: Quarks have not been observed directly but theoretical predictions based on their existence have been confirmed experimentally.
etymology: Etymology 1 sense 1 (“subatomic particle”) was coined by the American physicist Murray Gell-Mann (1929–2019) in 1963, apparently an arbitrary word.

definition: Fresh unripened cheese of a smooth texture made from pasteurized milk, a starter, and rennet.
A United States liquid unit equal to 32 fluid ounces; four quarts equal one gallon.
etymology: From Middle English quart, quarte, from Old French quarte, carte, from Latin quartus (“one-fourth”). Cognate with Spanish cuarto (“quarter; room, quarters”).

definition: An army officer who provides clothing and subsistence for troops.
etymology: From Middle English quartermayster, quartermaistre, equivalent to quarter + master. Perhaps reinforced by and merged with Dutch kwartiermeester, kwartier-meester. Compare German Quartiermeister, French quartier-maître.

definition: A staff officer in charge of supplies for a whole army.
The wife of a reigning king.
Suppress or crush completely.
example: To quell grief.
etymology: From Middle English quellen, from Old English cwellan (“to kill”), from Proto-West Germanic *kwalljan, from Proto-Germanic *kwaljaną (“to make die; kill”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH-.

definition: Pen made from a bird's feather.
example: He picked up his quill and wrote a poem.

definition: Any of the larger wing or tail feathers of a bird.
Pen made from a bird's feather.
Representing the perfect example of a class or quality.
etymology: PIE word *pénkʷe From quintessence + -al.

definition: A strange attitude or habit.
example: The car steers cleanly, but the gearshift has a few quirks.
etymology: First attested in the 1540s. Of uncertain origin.

definition: A gathering of the minimal number of members of an organization to conduct business.
example: We can discuss the issue tonight but cannot vote until we have a quorum.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English quorum (c.

definition: A hole in the ground as a nest made by wild rabbits.
A hutch for rabbits.
Of or infected by rabies.
example: A rabid dog or fox.
etymology: From the Latin rabidus, from rabiō (“to rave”).

definition: An acute viral disease of the nervous system of warm-blooded animals (usually transmitted by the bite of a rabid animal); rabies is fatal if the virus reaches the brain.
A course over which races are run.
etymology: From race + course.

definition: A course over which races are run.
etymology: From race + track.

definition: Causing great physical or mental suffering.
Branch of the brachial artery beginning below the elbow and extending down the forearm around the wrist and into the palm.
etymology: Radial here means “of or pertaining to the radius” (one of the bones of the arm).

definition: The property of symmetry about an axis.
example: The starfish illustrates radial symmetry.

definition: The amount of electromagnetic radiation leaving or arriving at a point on a surface.
etymology: From radiant + -ance.

definition: The rate of flow of radiant energy (electromagnetic waves).
Diverging from a common point.
A flexible hose between the radiator and the engine block.
Astronomical telescope that picks up electromagnetic radiations in the radio-frequency range from extraterrestrial sources.
The branch of medical science dealing with the medical use of X-rays or other penetrating radiation.
etymology: From radio- + -logy.

definition: (medicine) the treatment of disease (especially cancer) by exposure to a radioactive substance.
etymology: From radio- + therapy.

definition: Equipment used to treat diseases with x-rays or radioactivity.
A lottery in which the prizes are goods rather than money.
example: He entered a raffle to win a lifetime supply of toothpaste, but he did not win.

definition: Dispose of in a lottery.
example: We raffled off a trip to the Bahamas.

definition: Being or dressed in clothes that are worn or torn.
example: Clothes as ragged as a scarecrow's.
etymology: From Middle English ragged, from North Germanic. Compare with Old Norse rǫgvaðr (“tufted”) and Norwegian ragget (“shaggy”).

definition: Common perennial native to Europe and western Asia having usually pink flowers with ragged petals.
etymology: From ragged + robin, probably because of the untidy appearance of its petals.

definition: Gauge consisting of an instrument to measure the quantity of precipitation.
Pacific coast fish.
Drops of fresh water that fall as precipitation from clouds.
etymology: From Middle English reinwater, from Old English reġnwæter, equivalent to rain + water. Cognate with West Frisian reinwetter, Dutch regenwater, German Regenwasser, Swedish regnvatten.

definition: A doughnut made light with yeast rather than baking powder.
Dried grape.
etymology: From Middle English raysyn, borrowed from Anglo-Norman reysin (“grape, raisin”), from Late Latin racīmus, from Latin racēmus. Possibly a distant cognate of Persian رز (raz, “vine”). Doublet of raceme.

definition: Bread containing raisins.
The act of mobilizing for a common purpose.
example: The bell was a signal for the rallying of the whole neighborhood.

definition: A slogan used to rally support for a cause.
A point or principle on which scattered or opposing groups can come together.
Spreading out in different directions or distributed irregularly.
A person who owns or operates a ranch.
etymology: From ranch + -er.

definition: A loud bombastic declamation expressed with strong emotion.
etymology: From rant + -ing.

definition: A relationship of mutual understanding or trust and agreement between people.
example: He always tried to maintain a rapport with his customers.
etymology: Borrowed from French rapport. Doublet of report.

definition: A deceitful and unreliable scoundrel.
example: That little rascal bit me!

definition: Any of several breeds of terrier developed to catch rats.
etymology: Named for its talent and avidity for flushing and catching rats.

definition: Move by degrees in one direction only.
example: A ratcheting lopping tool.

definition: Toothed wheel held in place by a pawl or detent and turned by a lever.
Making something valid by formally ratifying or confirming it.
example: The ratification of the treaty.
etymology: From Middle French ratification, from Medieval Latin ratificatio.

definition: The food allowance for one day (especially for service personnel).
example: The rations should be nutritionally balanced.
etymology: From French ration. Doublet of reason and ratio.

definition: A card certifying the bearer's right to purchase rationed goods.
Distribute in rations, as in the army.
example: Cigarettes are rationed.

definition: In a rational manner.
example: We must act rationally.
etymology: From rational + -ly.

definition: The act of rationing.
example: During the war the government imposed rationing of food and gasoline.

definition: Thrown into a state of agitated confusion; (‘rattled’ is an informal term).
Extraordinarily good or great; used especially as intensifiers.
example: Had a rattling conversation about politics.

etymology: From Middle English rower, rowere, roware, equivalent to row + -er. Cognate with Dutch roeier (“rower”), Danish roer (“rower”), Norwegian roer (“rower”). Compare also Old English rōwend (“rower”).

definition: Stag with antlers of 12 or more branches.
Boa of grasslands and woodlands of western North America; looks and feels like rubber with tail and head of similar shape.
European freshwater fish resembling the roach.

definition: Implement for beating dust out of carpets.
A sling made with rum.
A steak cut from the rump.
A concluding summary (as in presenting a case before a law court).

definition: Any character from an ancient Germanic alphabet used in Scandinavia from the 3rd century to the Middle Ages.
example: Each rune had its own magical significance.
etymology: Borrowed from Old Norse rún, which is from Proto-Germanic *rūnō (“letter, literature, secret”), which is borrowed either from Proto-Celtic *rūnā or from the same source as it;

definition: A crosspiece between the legs of a chair.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Hairy trailing or prostrate western Australian vine with bright scarlet-pink flowers.
An error in logic or arithmetic that must be detected at run time.
The basic unit of money in Sri Lanka; equal to 100 cents.
A deceptive maneuver (especially to avoid capture).
etymology: From Middle English rūse (“evasive movements of a pursued animal; circuitous course taken by a hunter to pursue a game animal”), from Old French rëuse, ruse (“evasive movements of a pursued animal;

definition: Antioxidant that inhibits the formation of rust.
A groove or furrow (especially one in soft earth caused by wheels).
example: Early in Wicked Game, Steve goes into his first-ever rut.
etymology: From Middle English rutte (noun) and rutten (verb), from Old French rut (“noise, roar, bellowing”), from Latin rugītus, from rugīre (“to roar”).

A portable power saw with a reciprocating blade; can be used with a variety of blades depending on the application and kind of cut; generally have a plate that rides on the surface that is being cut.
Medium-sized five-needled pine of southwestern California having long cylindrical cones.
A fencing sword with a v-shaped blade and a slightly curved handle.
etymology: Borrowed from French sabre, from German Säbel, from Polish szabla, from Hungarian szablya. Cognate with Danish sabel, Russian са́бля (sáblja), Serbo-Croatian сабља, Sicilian sciàbbula.

definition: Coarse fabric used for bags or sacks.
example: The farmer grabbed a handful of sacking and rubbed down the cow.

definition: Used in or connected with a sacrifice.
example: Sacrificial lamb.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin sacrificiālis (“sacrificial”), from sacrificium (“sacrifice”), from sacrificus (“sacrificial”), from sacrificō (“sacrifice”), from sacer (“sacred, holy”) + faciō (“do, make”).

definition: Large grouse of sagebrush regions of North America.
Formerly a term of respect for important white Europeans in colonial India; used after the name.
etymology: From Hindustani صاحب / साहिब (sāhib, “lord”), from Classical Persian صاحب (sāhib), from Arabic صَاحِب (ṣāḥib, “companion”).

definition: A warship that was powered by sails and equipped with many heavy guns; not built after the middle of the 19th century.
A deep bow; a Muslim form of salutation.
etymology: From Arabic سَلَام (salām, “peace”). Doublet of shalom, a borrowing from Hebrew.

definition: The second pillar of Islam is prayer; a prescribed liturgy performed five times a day (preferably in a mosque) and oriented toward Mecca.
etymology: Borrowed from Malay salah.

definition: Having a quality that thrusts itself into attention.

Rod-shaped Gram-negative enterobacteria; cause typhoid fever and food poisoning; can be used as a bioweapon.

definition: A shaker with a perforated top for sprinkling salt.
Water containing salts.
example: The water in the ocean is all saltwater.
etymology: From Middle English saltwater, salte water, equivalent to salt + water.

Large west African tree having large palmately lobed leaves and axillary cymose panicles of small white flowers and one-winged seeds; yields soft white to pale yellow wood.
etymology: Borrowed from Brazilian Portuguese samba, possibly borrowed from Kongo semba. Doublet of semba.

definition: An observation station that is set up to make sample observations of something.
etymology: From Old French essamplaire, from Latin exemplāris. Doublet of exemplar.

definition: The quality of being holy.
etymology: From Middle English sanctity, from Old French sanctete, from Latin sānctitās.

definition: Very small silvery eellike schooling fishes that burrow into sandy beaches.
etymology: From Middle English sandeel, sandell, sandel, equivalent to sand + eel. Cognate with German Sandaal (“sand eel”), Danish sandål (“sand eel”).

A framework that holds the panes of a window in the window frame.

definition: A strong cord connecting a sash weight to a sliding sash.
A strong cord connecting a sash weight to a sliding sash.
A lock attached to the sashes of a double hung window that can fix both in the shut position.
A counterweight for a sliding sash.
A window with (usually two) sashes that slide vertically to let in air.
etymology: Compound of sash + window.

definition: Improperly forward or bold.
etymology: A modification of saucy, equivalent to sass + -y, originally used in American English. First attested in 1799, but in common usage only as of the mid-19th century.

definition: Flat stitches worked so closely as to resemble satin.
Reddish-brown wood and lumber from heartwood of the sweet gum tree used to make furniture.
A weave in which the filling and warp threads intersect in such a way as to give a smooth compact surface with no distinguishable twill line.
A deep pan with a handle; used for stewing or boiling.

definition: Something with a round shape resembling a flat circular plate.
etymology: From Middle English saucer, from Old French saussier (and feminine saussiere; hence modern French saucier m, saucière f).

definition: Having large round wide-open eyes.
Having a concave shape like a saucer.
Any of several aromatic herbs or subshrubs of the genus Satureja having spikes of flowers attractive to bees.
etymology: From the Middle English savory, savourie, from Old French savouré, from Old French savourer, from Late Latin sapōrāre, from Latin sapor (“taste, flavour”), from sapiō, sapere (“taste of, have a flavour of”).

Notched like a saw with teeth pointing toward the apex.

definition: A system of scaffolds.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English scaffaldyng, skaffaldyng, equivalent to scaffold + -ing.

etymology: (1646) From French sécrétion, from Latin sēcrētiō, sēcrētiōnem.

definition: A doctrine that rejects religion and religious considerations.

definition: Requiring sitting or little activity.

etymology: From Middle French sédentaire, from Latin sedentārius (“sitting”), from sedeō (“to sit, to be seated”).

definition: Resembling or containing or formed by the accumulation of sediment.

Rock formed from consolidated clay sediments.

etymology: From Old French sedicion, from Latin sēditiō (“sedition, discord”), from sēd- (“apart”) (an alternative form of sē-) + itiō (“going”).

The duty of serving as a sentry.

etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Eruptions along a nerve path often accompanied by severe neuralgia.
etymology: From Latin cingulus, variant of cingulum (“girdle”), translating Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē), ζωστήρ (zōstḗr).

definition: Someone who ships goods.
example: The shipper should have paid for insurance on the package, because it was damaged when it arrived.
etymology: Either formed anew from ship + -er or borrowed from Middle Low German schipper; compare skipper and Old English sċipere (“sailor”). Piecewise doublet of skipper (“captain, sailor”).

definition: Ruin utterly.
example: You have shipwrecked my career.
etymology: From Middle English schipwrak, from Old English sċipwræc (“jetsam”), equivalent to ship + wrack.

definition: A shipwrecked person.
A reflex motion caused by cold or fear or excitement.
example: A shiver went up my spine.
etymology: Origin uncertain, perhaps an alteration of chavel, or a frequentive of sheaf.

definition: Vibrating slightly and irregularly; as e.g. with fear or cold or like the leaves of an aspen in a breeze.
example: Sparkling light from the shivering crystals of the chandelier.

definition: To a shocking degree.
example: Teachers were shockingly underpaid.
etymology: From shocking + -ly.

definition: Made of inferior workmanship and materials.
example: Do not settle for shoddy knives if you are serious about cooking.
etymology: * Unknown, but possibly from shoad (“loose stone and rubble; fragments”), equivalent to shoad + -y; or possibly from the Arabic word for reuse. Shoad was of inferior quality for building.

definition: A person who makes or repairs shoes.
etymology: From Middle English shomaker, equivalent to shoe + maker. Compare Dutch schoenmaker, German Schuhmacher, Danish skomager.

definition: Someone who visits stores in search of articles to buy.
Having a blunt nose.
Of plants having relatively short stalks.
Having a short stem.
Fat such as butter or lard used in baked goods.
The property of being an amount by which something is less than expected or required.
example: Due to a shortfall in revenue, we will have to make some cuts.
etymology: Deverbal from fall short. By surface analysis, short + fall.

definition: Written in abbreviated or symbolic form.
example: Shorthand notes.
etymology: The noun is derived from short + hand (“handwriting; style of penmanship”). The verb is derived from the noun.

definition: A list of applicants winnowed from a longer list who have been deemed suitable and from which the successful person will be chosen.
(baseball) the person who plays the shortstop position.
example: The shortstop ranged deep into the hole to make the stop.
etymology: From short + stop.

definition: An act so striking or impressive that the show must be delayed until the audience quiets down.
An area where merchandise (such as cars) can be displayed.
example: In Britain a showroom is called a ‘salesroom’.
etymology: From show + room. Verb sense circa 2011.

definition: Shell containing lead pellets that explodes in flight.
example: The dog ate my sandwich, and there was shrapnel all over the place from him tearing open the bag.
etymology: From Shrapnel.

definition: Marked by practical hardheaded intelligence.
example: He was too shrewd to go along with them on a road that could lead only to their overthrow.
etymology: From Middle English schrewed (“depraved; wicked”, literally “accursed”), from schrewen (“to curse;

definition: A line that suspends the harness from the canopy of a parachute.
etymology: From Middle English shroud, from Old English sċrūd, from Proto-Germanic *skrūdą (“shroud, dress, attire”). Compare Proto-Germanic *skrūdijaną (“to shroud”).

definition: A low woody perennial plant usually having several major stems.
etymology: From Middle English schrub, schrob, (also unassibilated as scrub), from Old English *sċrob (in placenames) and sċrybb (“a shrub; shrubbery; underbrush”); akin to Norwegian skrubbe (“the dwarf cornel tree”).

definition: An almost pleasurable sensation of fright.
example: Seeing the spider under his pillow gave John a shudder.

definition: Walking with a slow dragging motion without lifting your feet.
Avoid and stay away from deliberately; stay clear of.
example: Acrophobes shun mountaineering.

definition: A defeat in a game where one side fails to score.
example: A shutout is a reverse strike: the union complained and the workers wanted to work, but management was opposed.
etymology: Deverbal from shut out.

definition: An edge tool for cutting grass or crops; has a curved blade and a short handle.
etymology: From Middle English sikel (also assibilated in sichel), from Old English sicol, siċel, from Proto-West Germanic *sikilu, itself borrowed from Latin sēcula (“sickle”) or sīcīlis (“sickle”).

definition: An abnormal red blood cell that has a crescent shape and an abnormal form of hemoglobin.
One of the long curved tail feathers of a rooster.
Curved like a sickle.
Unhealthy looking.
example: A sickly child.
etymology: From Middle English seekly, sekely, siklich, sekeliche, equivalent to sick + -ly. Possibly a modification of Old English sīcle (“sickly”) and/or derived from Old Norse sjúkligr (“sickly”).

definition: One of the longitudinal beams running along either side of a railway vehicle, onto which the bodywork is mounted, in passenger-carrying vehicles usually forming the side or the base of the floor.
(law) a courtroom conference between the lawyers and the judge that is held out of the jury's hearing.
example: The tables in the sidebar can be used to determine “average” height and weight, and to provide a slight random variation if desired.
etymology: From side + bar.

definition: A close friend who accompanies their buddies in their activities.
etymology: From side + kick, which in the late 19th and early 20th century was a slang term for the front side pocket of a pair of trousers, known as the pocket safest from theft.

definition: Examine in order to test suitability.
etymology: From Middle English sive, syfe, from Old English sife, from Proto-West Germanic *sibi (“sieve”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyp-, *seyb- (“to pour, sieve, strain, run, drip”).

definition: Separate or remove.
Move as if through a sieve.
example: The soldiers sifted through the woods.
etymology: From Middle English syften, from Old English siftan, from Proto-West Germanic *siftijan.

definition: Going about to look at places of interest.
example: Sightseeing is a frequent reason to visit San Francisco.
etymology: From sight + seeing.

definition: Signs collectively (especially commercial signs or posters).
example: There will be signage displayed at each post.
etymology: From sign + -age.

definition: Denote or connote.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English signifien, from Old French signifier, from Latin significare.

definition: A porous form of silica that is highly absorbent.
Any of a large class of siloxanes that are unusually stable over a wide range of temperatures; used in lubricants and adhesives and coatings and synthetic rubber and electrical insulation.
A polymeric silicone compound.
A twilled silk fabric used mostly for lining parts of gentlemen's coats.
Large tree of Australasia.
Medium to tall fast-growing tree with orange flowers and feathery bipinnate leaves silky-hairy beneath; eastern Australia.
Small shrubby tree of western North America (Alaska to Oregon).
Having hair that resembles silk.
etymology: From silky + haired.

definition: Structural member consisting of a continuous horizontal timber forming the lowest member of a framework or supporting structure.
example: She looked out the window resting her elbows on the window sill.
etymology: Compare sile.

definition: Large tree native to eastern Europe and Asia Minor having leaves with white tomentum on the under side; widely cultivated as an ornamental.
A nitrate used in making photographic emulsions; also used in medicine as a cautery and as a topical antibacterial agent.
A solder that contains silver.
A dull silvery whiting of southern Atlantic and Gulf Coasts of the United States.
Tableware made of silver or silver plate or pewter or stainless steel.
etymology: From silver + -ware.

definition: Resembling or reminiscent of silver.
example: A soft silvern voice.
etymology: From Middle English silvery, sylvyry; equivalent to silver + -y.

definition: Of something having a color that is a light shiny blue.
Of something having a color that is a light shiny green.
Of a white that resembles silver.
etymology: From silvery + white.

definition: Any phobia (other than agoraphobia) associated with relatively simple well-defined stimuli.
The curve of y=sin x.
Without a date fixed (as of an adjournment).
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Latin sine diē (literally “without a day”).

definition: A wave whose waveform resembles a sine curve.
(of clothing) closing with a narrow overlap and fastened with a single row of buttons.
example: A single-breasted jacket.

definition: Without assistance.
example: I built this house single-handedly.
etymology: From single-handed + -ly.

definition: Univalve.
A single object (as distinguished from a pair).
etymology: From single + -ton, probably following the model of simpleton.

definition: A headache resulting from congestion or infection in the paranasal sinuses.
An organism (person or animal) that sits.
example: It's always such a pain to get a sitter on short notice.
etymology: From Middle English sitter, sittere, syttare, equivalent to sit + -er.

definition: The rider sits still in the saddle.
A person who is at least six feet tall.
etymology: From six + footer.

definition: Fairly large in size.
Any glutinous material used to fill pores in surfaces or to stiffen fabrics.
Hot enough to burn with or as if with a hissing sound.
example: A sizzling steak.

definition: A board with wheels that is ridden in a standing or crouching position and propelled by foot.
etymology: From skate + board. The foot-treadable skateboard sense (noun sense 1) came first (mid-20th century). The vehicle chassis sense (noun sense 2) was named for its resemblance thereto (late 20th or early 21st century).

definition: The sport of skating on a skateboard.
Giving only major points; lacking completeness.
example: A sketchy account.
etymology: From sketch + -y. Extension of "brief, imperfect, unfinished" notion.

definition: Having an oblique or slanting direction or position.
example: The picture was skew.
etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English skeuen, skewe, skewen (“to run at an angle or obliquely;

definition: Having an oblique or slanting direction or position.
A crash helmet.
Someone who skis.
example: A professional skier.
etymology: From ski + -er.

definition: A pan used for frying foods.
etymology: From Old French escuëlette, diminutive of escuëlle (“a porringer”), (French écuelle), from Vulgar Latin scutella, diminutive of scutra, scuta (“tray, dish”). Compare scuttle (“basket”).

definition: Usually cooked in a skillet over an open fire: especially cornbread with ham bits and sometimes Irish soda bread.
Batter baked atop a layer of sweetened fruit then turned upside down so fruit is on top.
Clingfish with typical skillet shape.
Having or showing knowledge and skill and aptitude.
example: A lesser-known but no less skillful composer.
etymology: From Middle English skilful, skylfull, scelvol, equivalent to skill + -ful.

definition: Travel on the surface of water.
example: Skimming stones.

definition: Milk from which the cream has been skimmed.
example: We like to drink skim milk instead so as to consume fewer calories.

definition: Remove from the surface.
example: Skim cream from the surface of milk.

definition: Read superficially.
The act of removing floating material from the surface of a liquid.
example: Aluminium skimmings.
etymology: From skim + -ing.

definition: A minor short-term fight.
example: Three people were arrested after a skirmish in a bar.
etymology: From Middle English skirmish (as a verb), from Old French escarmouche (“skirmish”), from Italian scaramuccia, earlier schermugio. Doublet of escarmouche, Scaramouche, and Scaramucci.

definition: A man who is aggressive in making amorous advances to women.
A short theatrical episode.
etymology: Origin uncertain. Perhaps from Old Norse skjúta (“to shoot, dart, move quickly”), variant of skjóta. Compare flytja (“to move”).

definition: Stocky shaggy-coated North American carnivorous mammal.
Performing acrobatics in free fall before pulling the ripcord of a parachute.
A very tall building with many stories.
Patterned by having color applied with sweeping strokes.
example: Brown iris … slashed with yellow.

definition: As if striking with slashing blows.
example: His slashing demon-ridden cadenza.
etymology: From slash + -ing.

definition: Of cloth; thin and loosely woven.
example: The coat has a sleazy lining.
etymology: Origin obscure. Possibly a corruption of silesia. Silesia was formerly the most important location of Germany’s weaving industry.

definition: A vehicle mounted on runners and pulled by horses or dogs; for transportation over snow.
example: The child zoomed down the hill on his sled.

definition: A dog trained to draw a sled usually in a team.
Transport in a sleigh.
etymology: From Middle English slegge, from Old English sleċġ (“sledgehammer; mallet”), from Proto-Germanic *slagjǭ.

definition: A dog trained to draw a sled usually in a team.
Apnea that occurs during sleep.
A soporific drug in the form of a pill (or tablet or capsule).
Experiencing or accompanied by sleeplessness.
example: Lay sleepless all night.
etymology: From Middle English slepeles, from Old English slǣplēas; equivalent to sleep + -less.

definition: Someone who cannot sleep.
Having a slim body.
Having slender wings.
A golf shot that curves to the right for a right-handed golfer.
example: He took lessons to cure his slicing.

definition: A person who slips or slides because of loss of traction.
example: The closer had a wicked slider that was almost unhittable.
etymology: From slide + -er. The meaning "small hamburger" was originally used to describe onion-steamed small burgers at White Castle restaurants, formerly spelt "Slyder".

definition: A retractable fin keel used on sailboats to prevent drifting to leeward.
A mushroom of the genus Amanita.
Covered with or resembling slime.
example: A slimy substance covered the rocks.
etymology: From Middle English slymy, slimi, either derived from the Old English noun slīm or an unattested *slīmiġ, replacing Old English slipiġ (“slippy, slimy”). Equivalent to slime + -y.

definition: Low footwear that can be slipped on and off easily; usually worn indoors.
example: Get out of bed, put on your slippers, and come downstairs.
etymology: From Middle English slypper, equivalent to slip + -er.

definition: Any of several tropical American shrubby succulent plants resembling cacti but having foot-shaped bracts.
Shaped in the form of a slipper.
North American elm having rough leaves that are red when opening; yields a hard wood.
Having an oblique or slanted direction.
example: A sloping roof.

definition: Common coarse-haired long-snouted bear of south-central Asia.
Necrotic tissue; a mortified or gangrenous part or mass.
example: That is the slough of a rattler; we must be careful.
etymology: From Middle English slogh, slugh, slouh, from Proto-Germanic *sluk-, perhaps related to *sleupaną (“to slip, sneak”) (compare Gothic 𐍃𐌻𐌹𐌿𐍀𐌰𐌽 (sliupan)). Akin to Middle Low German slô (“sheath, skin on a hoof”).

definition: North American cordgrass having leaves with dry membranous margins and glumes with long awns.
Discard as undesirable.
example: The candidate sloughed off his former campaign workers.

definition: The act of slowing down or falling behind.
etymology: Deverbal from slow down.

definition: Most slowly.
The precipitate produced by sewage treatment.
etymology: From Middle English slugge, sluche (“mud, mire”), probably an alteration of Middle English sliche, slicche ("mud, slush, tar";

definition: A cutting implement used to cut leading (spacing between lines) and slugs (thicker pieces of lead to provide support to set type forms).
A natural and periodic state of rest during which consciousness of the world is suspended.
example: Calm as a child in dreamless slumber.

definition: An overnight party of girls who dress in nightclothes and pass the night talking.
Play smoothly or legato.
example: The pianist slurred the most beautiful passage in the sonata.
etymology: From Middle English sloor (“thin or fluid mud”). The ultimate origin is uncertain, but perhaps related to a group of words derived from Proto-Germanic *slūm- (“loose, slack, flabby”), such as slumber.

definition: Treat hurriedly or avoid dealing with properly.
The act of smacking something; a blow delivered with an open hand.
example: Children who received regular smackings.

definition: Small red-fruited trailing cranberry of Arctic and cool regions of the Northern Hemisphere.
The longest part of the alimentary canal; where digestion is completed.
etymology: From small + intestine, perhaps a partial calque of Middle English smaltharm, smaleþarm, from Old English smælþearme (“lower gut, small intestine”, literally “small tharm”).

definition: Of stocks of companies with a market capitalization of less than one billion dollars.
Having small teeth.
The virus that causes smallpox in humans; can be used as a bioweapon.
A pungent preparation of ammonium carbonate and perfume; sniffed as a stimulant to relieve faintness.
A smile expressing smugness or scorn instead of pleasure.
etymology: From Middle English smirken, from Old English smearcian (“to smile”), corresponding to smerian + -cian (English -k; compare talk and stalk from, respectively, tell and steal).

definition: (used in combination) affected by something overwhelming.
example: Conscience-smitten.
etymology: From Middle English smiten, from Old English smiten, ġesmiten, from Proto-Germanic *smitanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *smītaną (“to hurl; fling”), equivalent to smite + -en (past participle ending).

definition: Air pollution by a mixture of smoke and fog.
etymology: Blend of smoke + fog.

definition: Eel cured by smoking.
Mackerel cured by smoking.
A smoky yellow or brown quartz.
Having a smooth shell.
Having a smooth, fine-grained structure.
Home appliance consisting of a flat metal base that is heated and used to smooth cloth.
A small plane for finish work.
Held in check with difficulty.
example: A smothered cough.

definition: Import or export without paying customs duties.
example: She smuggled cigarettes across the border.

definition: Distributed or sold illicitly.
Tropical fern widespread in Old World; naturalized in Jamaica and Florida.
Predatory tropical fishes with jutting jaws and strong teeth.
A brim that can be turned up and down on opposite sides.
(football) the person who plays center on the line of scrimmage and snaps the ball to the quarterback.
example: A snapper-up of bargains.
etymology: From snap + -er.

definition: Able to right itself when on its back by flipping into the air with a clicking sound.
Apt to speak irritably.
example: A snappish tone of voice.
etymology: From snap + -y.

definition: A small drum with two heads and a snare stretched across the lower head.
A canvas shoe with a pliable rubber sole.
example: Spectator I have just left the right worshipful and his myrmidons about a sneaker of five gallons!
etymology: From sneak + -er. The shoes sense is a reference to the quietness of the shoes.

definition: A symptom consisting of the involuntary expulsion of air from the nose.
Hunt or shoot snipe.
example: I am the type who is liable to snipe you With two seconds left to go, whoa.
etymology: From Middle English snipe, snype (“a type of bird”), from Old Norse snípa, as in mýrisnípa (“moor snipe”). Akin to Norwegian snipe.

definition: An elaborate practical joke in which the unsuspecting victim hunts a snipe and is typically left in the dark holding a bag and waiting for the snipe to run into it.
example: In the South a snipe hunt is practically a rite of passage.
etymology: * snipe + hunt * Although snipe are an actual family of birds, a snipe hunt was originally a quest for an imaginary creature whose description varies.

definition: A small piece of anything (especially a piece that has been snipped off).
example: From the snippet I heard of their rehearsal, they sound pretty good.
etymology: From snip + -et. Compare snippock.

definition: Take by theft.
example: Someone snitched my wallet!
etymology: Origin uncertain. Perhaps an alteration of Middle English snacche (“a trap, snare”), snacchen (“to seize (prey)”, whence modern English snatch). Compare also Middle English snik snak (“a sudden blow, snap”).

definition: Fool or dupe.
example: He was snookered by the con-man's smooth talk.

definition: Game equipment consisting of a heavy table on which pool is played.
White Arctic bunting.
A light brief snowfall and gust of wind (or something resembling that).
A board that resembles a broad ski or a small surfboard; used in a standing position to slide down snow-covered slopes.
etymology: From snow + board.

definition: The act of sliding down a snow-covered slope while standing on a snowboard.
Precipitation falling from clouds in the form of ice crystals.
example: There has been snowfall every day this week.
etymology: By surface analysis, snow + fall. Cognate with Dutch sneeuwval, German Schneefall, Old Norse snjófall, snæfall (whence Danish snefald, Norwegian snøfall, and Swedish snöfall).

definition: A figure of a person made of packed snow.
Slender fringed orchid of eastern North America having white flowers.
The charred portion of a candlewick.
etymology: Late Middle English, from Middle Dutch snuffen (“to snuff, sniff, snuffle”). Related to Dutch snuiven (“to sniff”), Middle Low German snûve (“pose, head-cold”), German Schnupfen (“head-cold”).

definition: Pass from physical life and lose all bodily attributes and functions necessary to sustain life.
A person who uses snuff.
Snuff colored; of a greyish to yellowish brown.
Dark yellowish brown.
Dark yellowish brown.
Offering safety; well protected or concealed.
example: A snug harbor.
etymology: From dialectal English snug (“tight, handsome”), perhaps from Old Norse snøggr, from Proto-Germanic *snawwuz (“short, quick, fast”).

definition: Move or arrange oneself in a comfortable and cozy position.
example: The children snuggled into their sleeping bags.
etymology: From snug + -le (frequentative suffix).

definition: Dispenser of liquid soap.
Rise rapidly.
example: The dollar soared against the yen.

definition: An anthropologist who studies such cultural phenomena as kinship systems.

Keeping a safe space between yourself and other people, and avoiding crowds, in order to slow the spread of infectious diseases. Large-scale measures include canceling group events or closing schools, workplaces and public spaces.
Someone who drinks liquor repeatedly in small quantities.
Any phobia (other than agoraphobia) associated with situations in which you are subject to criticism by others (as fear of eating in public or public speaking etc.).
A disputant who advocates reform.
The action of establishing on a socialist basis.
example: The socialization of medical services.
etymology: From socialize + -ation or social + -ization.

definition: Take part in social activities; interact with others.
example: He never socializes with his colleagues.
etymology: From social + -ize.

definition: A social scientist who studies the institutions and development of human society.
etymology: From sociology + -ist.

definition: Someone with a sociopathic personality; a person with an antisocial personality disorder (‘psychopath’ was once widely used but has now been superseded by ‘sociopath’).
etymology: From socio- + -path. First use appears c. 1914.

definition: A wrench with a handle onto which sockets of different sizes can be fitted.
A sodium salt of carbonic acid; used in making soap powders and glass and paper.
A white poisonous salt (NaCN) used in electroplating.
A colorless crystalline salt of sodium (NaF) used in fluoridation of water and to prevent tooth decay.
(NaNO3) used especially as a fertilizer and explosive.
A solid white bitter salt used in manufacturing glass and paper and dyes and pharmaceuticals.
Solder that melts at a relatively low temperature.
(of a bullet) made of soft material that expands on impact.
Repair with soft-solder.
Toned down.
Having a softening or soothing effect especially to the skin.
etymology: From Middle English softenynge, softynand, equivalent to soften + -ing.

definition: (of soil) soft and watery.
example: A soggy film.
etymology: From sog + -y.

definition: An alloy (usually of lead and tin) used when melted to join two metal surfaces.
In a grave and sedate manner.
example: The judge sat there solemnly.
etymology: From solemn + -ly.

definition: Make a solicitation or entreaty for something; request urgently or persistently.
example: Henry IV solicited the Pope for a divorce.
etymology: From Middle English soliciten, solliciten, from Old French soliciter, solliciter, borrowed from Latin sollicitō (“stir, disturb;

definition: An entreaty addressed to someone of superior status.
example: A solicitation to the king for relief.
etymology: From Middle French sollicitation, from Latin sollicitātiō.

definition: A tax imposed by the government in special circumstances, intended to provide funding towards theoretically solidifying projects.
example: Up to €972 (€1,944 for married couples) annual income tax, no solidarity surcharge is levied.

definition: Changed into a solid mass.
As an undiversified whole.
example: The unions voted solidly for Roosevelt.
etymology: From solid + -ly.

definition: A gem (usually a diamond) in a setting by itself.
etymology: Borrowed from French solitaire, ultimately from Latin sōlitārius. Doublet of solitary.

definition: A musician who performs a solo.
etymology: From solo + -ist.

definition: Either of the two times of the year when the sun is at its greatest distance from the celestial equator.
etymology: From Middle English solstice, from Old French solstice, from Latin sōlstitium.

definition: The basic unit of money in Uzbekistan.
etymology: From Kyrgyz сом (som) and Uzbek сўм (soʻm) (Cyrillic) / soʻm (Roman), both of which come from the Turkic root *som ("pure [gold]").

definition: Lacking brightness or color; dull.
example: Children in somber brown clothes.

definition: In or at or to some place.
example: We can't find the damned thing, but it must be someplace.
etymology: From some + place.

definition: A musical composition of 3 or 4 movements of contrasting forms.
etymology: From Italian sonata, from the feminine past participle of sonare (modern suonare), from Latin sonāre (“to make sound”). Doublet of sounded.

definition: The form of a movement, which consists of exposition and development and recapitulation.
A black colloidal substance consisting wholly or principally of amorphous carbon and used to make pigments and ink.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English soot, soote, sote, sot, from Old English sōt, from Proto-Germanic *sōtą (“soot”), from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”).

definition: A very dark black.
Of the black color of soot.
Give moral or emotional strength to.
One who practices magic or sorcery.
The belief in magical spells that harness occult forces or evil spirits to produce unnatural effects in the world.
example: The tale is full of magic and sorcery.
etymology: From Middle English sorcery, borrowed from Middle French sorcerie, ultimately derived from Latin sors (“fate”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”). Cognate with serō, seriēs, sermō. Compare also French sorcier.

definition: To a great extent.
example: I missed him sorely.
etymology: From Middle English sorely, from Old English sārlīċ (adjective), sārlīċe (adverb); equivalent to sore + -ly.

definition: A pain that is felt (as when the area is touched).
example: The salve made the soreness go away, but with the aches gone I suddenly noticed my other pains.
etymology: From Middle English sornes, sornesse, sarnesse, from Old English sārnes (“bodily pain; mental pain, affliction, grief”), from Proto-West Germanic *sairanassī, equivalent to sore + -ness.

definition: Full of or expressing deep emotion.
example: Soulful eyes.
etymology: From soul + -ful (adjective suffix).

definition: Moving toward the south.
example: A southbound train.
etymology: From south + -bound.

definition: Wood of a common cypress of southeastern United States having trunk expanded at base; found in coastal swamps and flooding river bottoms.
Evergreen tree of southern United States having large stiff glossy leaves and huge white sweet-smelling flowers.
Moving toward the south.
example: A southbound train.
etymology: From south + -ward.

definition: A uniformly warty stocky toad of washes and streams of semiarid southwestern United States.
Any of several Old World coarse prickly-leaved shrubs and subshrubs having milky juice and yellow flowers; widely naturalized; often noxious weeds in cultivated soil.
A source of oil; used for forage and soil improvement and as food.
etymology: From soy + bean.

definition: Meal made from soybeans.
Soybeans bought or sold at an agreed price for delivery at a specified future date.
Meal made from soybeans.
A milk substitute containing soybean flour and water; used in some infant formulas and in making tofu.
Oil from soya beans.

Erect bushy hairy annual herb having trifoliate leaves and purple to pink flowers; extensively cultivated for food and forage and soil improvement but especially for its nutritious oil-rich seeds; native to Asia.
A slap with the flat of the hand.
example: To have a quick spank.
etymology: Uncertain. Possibly imitative, or perhaps a special use of Etymology 2 (below) in the sense of a horse stamping its foot against the ground.

definition: Furnish with spars.
etymology: From Middle English sparren (“to dart out;

example: Don't just sit there on your tod.

The system of tones used in a particular language or dialect of a tone language.

East Asian fern having fronds shaped like tongues; sometimes placed in genus Cyclophorus.
An expression that is difficult to articulate clearly.

Epilepsy in which the body is rigid during the seizure.
A film made by photographing a series of cartoon drawings to give the illusion of movement when projected in rapid sequence.

definition: Having teeth especially of a certain number or type; often used in combination.

A hypothetical quark with a charge of +2/3 and a mass more than 100,000 times that of an electron.
Loss of sensation confined to the skin or mucous surfaces (as when benzocaine or Lidocaine is applied to the surface).
Concerned with topography.
example: A topographical engineer.

Topographic study of a given place (especially the history of the place as indicated by its topography).
example: Greenland's topology has been shaped by the glaciers of the ice age.
etymology: From Late Latin topologia, from By surface analysis, topo- (“place”) + -logy (“study of, a branch of knowledge”).

definition: A worker who makes or adds the top to something.
example: In his latest standup set, his topper is a callback to the dog bowl story.
etymology: From Middle English toppor, equivalent to top + -er.

definition: Experiencing intense pain especially mental pain.
example: A small tormented schoolboy.

definition: Converter for transmitting and amplifying torque (especially by hydraulic means).
A wrench that has a gauge that indicates the amount of torque being applied.
(law) any wrongdoing for which an action for damages may be brought.
etymology: From Middle English tort (“(uncountable) wrong; (countable) an injury, a wrong”), from Old French tort (“misdeed, wrong”) (modern French tort (“an error, wrong;

definition: A small piece of tortilla.
Extremely painful.
A small amount (especially of a drink).
example: A tot of rum.

example: As soon as Debbie can tot up the scores, we'll know who won.

definition: Characterized by a government in which the political authority exercises absolute and centralized control.
example: A totalitarian regime crushes all autonomous institutions in its drive to seize the human soul.
etymology: From Italian totalitario (“complete, absolute, totalitarian”) + -an. Equivalent to totality + -arian.

definition: A government that subordinates the individual to the state and strictly controls all aspects of life by coercive measures.
A clan or tribe identified by their kinship to a common totemic object.
etymology: Borrowed from Ojibwe (o)doodem(an).

definition: A tribal emblem consisting of a pillar carved and painted with totemic figures; erected by Indian tribes of the northwest Pacific coast.
example: The teacher's pet was fairly high on the class totem pole.

definition: A computer display that enables the user to interact with the computer by touching areas on the screen.
Quick to take offense.

etymology: A variant of earlier tetchy (“cranky, easily annoyed, difficult to handle”), under influence from some senses of touch (“affect, disturb”) and simulating touch + -y.

definition: A sporting competition in which contestants play a series of games to decide the winner.
example: By a knight of ghostes & shadowes, I sumon’d am to Tourney. ten leagues beyond the wide worlds end.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman turnei, from Old French tornei (“tournament”), from tornoier (“to joust, tilt”).

definition: Someone who buys tickets to an event in order to resell them at a profit.
example: Be careful of the ticket touts outside the arena; they are famed for selling counterfeits.
etymology: Probably from French tout (“all”).

definition: An assemblage of parts or details (as in a work of art) considered as forming a whole.
etymology: From French tout ensemble, literally "all together".

definition: The branch of pharmacology that deals with the nature and effects and treatments of poisons.
etymology: From French toxicologie, equivalent to toxico- + -logy.

definition: The breed of very small poodles.
A small active dog.
A set of nonsensical syllables used while humming a refrain.
An investigator who is employed to find missing persons or missing goods.

A government order imposing a trade barrier.
On a steam locomotive, an axle connecting a coupled pair of unpowered wheels located behind the driving wheels.

definition: (of a body of water) free from disturbance by heavy waves.
example: A lake of tranquil blue water reflecting a tranquil blue sky.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French tranquille, from Latin tranquillus, from trāns- + the root of quiēs (“rest, quiet, peace”), ultimately from *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest”).

definition: Crossing the Atlantic Ocean.
example: Transatlantic flight.
etymology: From trans- + Atlantic.

definition: Be greater in scope or size than some standard.
example: We cannot transcend what we refuse to face.
etymology: From Middle English transcenden, from Old French transcender, from Latin transcendō (“to climb over, step over, surpass, transcend”), from trans (“over”) + scandō (“to climb”); see scan; compare ascend, descend.

definition: Existing outside of or not in accordance with nature.
example: Find transcendental motives for sublunary action.
etymology: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin transcendentālis + English -al (suffix meaning of or relating to forming adjectives; and forming nouns, especially of verbal action).

definition: An irrational number that is not algebraic.
Recorded for broadcast.
example: A transcribed announcement.

definition: Capable of being moved or conveyed from one place to another.

A semiconductor device capable of amplification.

definition: Of or relating to uniform movement without rotation.
example: Translational medicine.

definition: Allowing light to pass through diffusely.
example: Translucent amber.
etymology: From Latin trānslūcentem, accusative of trānslūcēns, present participle of trānslūcēre.

definition: A material having the property of admitting light diffusely; a partly transparent material.
Involving or operating in several nations or nationalities.
example: Transnational terrorist networks.

definition: An operation moving an organ from one organism (the donor) to another (the recipient).
example: He had a kidney transplant.

definition: Characterized by feeling or showing fond affection for.

(of a stream) flowing into a larger stream.

definition: Language used in a figurative or nonliteral sense.

Cosmetic surgery of the abdomen to remove wrinkles and tighten the skin over the stomach.
Characterized by unrest or disorder or insubordination.

definition: A vast treeless plain in the Arctic regions where the subsoil is permanently frozen.
etymology: Borrowed from Russian ту́ндра (túndra), borrowed from Kildin Sami тӯндрэ (tūndre), from Proto-Sami *tuontër (“a kind of mountain in Lapland”).

Swan that nests in tundra regions of the New and Old Worlds.

The craft of composing type and printing from it.

definition: A small guitar having four strings.
etymology: Borrowed from Hawaiian ʻukulele, from ʻuku (“flea”) + lele (“jump, jumping”).

definition: A circumscribed inflammatory and often suppurating lesion on the skin or an internal mucous surface resulting in necrosis of tissue.

definition: A diet of foods that are not irritating.
Having frequencies above those of audible sound.
etymology: From ultra- + sonic.

definition: A device used to examine an internal bodily structure by the use of ultrasonic waves, esp for the diagnosis of abnormality in a fetus.

definition: Relating to or resembling the umbilicus.

example: If you take it to court, you're the guy who screams at the ump ’cause they don't like the call at the plate.

definition: Without warning or announcement.

definition: Not endowed with authority.

definition: A natural and unavoidable catastrophe that interrupts the expected course of events.
Being or thrown out of equilibrium.
example: Unbalanced reporting.

definition: Hard to defeat.
example: An unbeatable ball team.
etymology: From un- + beat + -able. Beatable is a back-formation.

definition: Impossible to break especially under ordinary usage.
example: Unbreakable plastic dinnerwear.
etymology: From un- + break + -able.

definition: Marked by continuous or uninterrupted extension in space or time or sequence.
example: Cars in an unbroken procession.
etymology: From Middle English unbroken, from Old English unġebrocen (“unbroken”), equivalent to un- + broken. Cognate with Dutch ongebroken (“unbroken”), German Low German unbroken (“unbroken”), German ungebrochen (“unbroken”).

definition: Not subject to censorship.
example: Uncensored news reports.
etymology: From un- + censored.

definition: (of unknown regions) not yet surveyed or investigated.
example: Uncharted seas.
etymology: From un- + charted. Piecewise doublet of uncarded.

definition: Not restrained or controlled.
example: An unchecked temper.
etymology: From un- + checked.

definition: Soiled or likely to soil with dirt or grime.
example: Wore an unclean shirt.
etymology: From Middle English unclene, from Old English unclǣne, equivalent to un- + clean.

definition: In physical discomfort.
example: She lay on the couch, her body uncomfortably twisted.
etymology: From uncomfortable + -ly or un- + comfortably.

definition: Not making concessions.
example: Took an uncompromising stance in the peace talks.
etymology: From un- + compromising.

definition: Not subject to a condition.
example: He accepted the offer unconditionally.
etymology: From unconditional + -ly.

definition: Not finally established or settled.
example: An unconfirmed letter of credit.
etymology: From un- + confirmed.

definition: Without awareness.
example: She jumped up unconsciously when he entered the room.
etymology: From un- + consciously, and more rarely, from unconscious + -ly.

definition: Difficult to solve or alleviate.
example: Uncontrollable pain.
etymology: From un- + controllable.

definition: Not being under control; out of control.
example: The greatest uncontrolled health problem is AIDS.
etymology: From un- + controlled.

Not bearing a date.

definition: Not brought to a conclusion; subject to further thought.
example: Our position on this bill is still undecided.
etymology: From Middle English undecided, equivalent to un- + decided.

definition: Not precisely limited, determined, or distinguished.
example: An undefined term.
etymology: From un- + defined.

definition: To an undeniable degree or in an undeniable manner.
example: She is undeniably the most gifted student in the class.
etymology: From undeniable + -ly, equivalent to un- + deny + -ably.

definition: The material removed by a cut made underneath.

definition: The lower side of anything.

definition: Exhibiting restrained good taste.

definition: Not perceived or discerned.

etymology: From un- + detected.

definition: Not developed, mature, or fully formulated.

etymology: From un- + developed.

definition: Not discovered.

etymology: From un- + discovered.

definition: Not parted by conflict of opinion.
example: Presented an undivided front.

The interest in property owned by tenants whereby each tenant has an equal right to enjoy the entire property.

definition: Not having a good education.
etymology: From un- + educated.

definition: An ignorant person.
In an unambiguous manner.

definition: Not true to duty or obligation or promises.

definition: Not encouraging or approving or pleasing.

Not anticipated.

definition: Not excusable.

definition: Emotions experienced when not in a state of well-being.

definition: Not injured or harmed.

definition: Affected with madness or insanity.

definition: Not hallowed or consecrated.

definition: Dressed in a uniform.

definition: A condition in which everything is regular and unvarying.

definition: Become one.

definition: Combining into a single unit.
