In a unilateral manner; by means of one part or party.
example: They worked out an agreement unilaterally.
etymology: From unilateral + -ly.

definition: Totally unlikely.
etymology: From un- + imagine + -able.

definition: Not important.
example: A relatively unimportant feature of the system.
etymology: From un- + important.

definition: Not having inhabitants; not lived in.
example: An uninhabited island.
etymology: From un- + inhabited.

definition: Not covered by insurance.
example: An uninsured motorist.
etymology: From un- + insured.

definition: Done or made or performed with purpose and intent.
example: Near-synonyms: incidental; see also Thesaurus:accidental, Thesaurus:unintentional.
etymology: From un- + intentional.

definition: Without intention; in an unintentional manner.
example: She hit him unintentionally.
etymology: From unintentional + -ly or un- + intentionally.

definition: Not having or showing interest.
example: An uninterested spectator.
etymology: From un- + interested.

definition: The quality of being one of a kind.
etymology: From unique + -ness.

definition: Relating to or characterized by or aiming toward unity.
example: The unitary principles of nationalism.
etymology: From unit + -ary.

definition: Lacking justification or authorization.
example: The unjustified killing of an innocent.
etymology: From un- + justified.

definition: Without knowledge or intention.
etymology: From unknowing + -ly.

definition: Not conforming to the law.
example: They were unlawfully married.
etymology: From unlawful + -ly or un- + lawfully.

definition: Lacking official approval.
etymology: From un- + licensed.

definition: Remove (cargo, people, etc.) from and leave.
example: Unload the cargo.
etymology: From un- + load.

definition: The labor of taking a load of something off of or out of a vehicle or ship or container etc.
Not having an identifying mark.
example: Unmarked cards.
etymology: From un- + marked.

definition: Of the remaining member of a pair.
example: Unmatched socks.

definition: Clearly evident to the mind.
example: His opposition to slavery was unmistakable.
etymology: From un- + mistake + -able.

definition: Independent in behavior or thought.
etymology: From un- + orthodox.

definition: Remove from its packing.
example: Unpack the presents.
etymology: From Middle English unpakken, equivalent to un- + pack. Compare Saterland Frisian uutpakje (“to unpack”), West Frisian útpakke (“to unpack”), Dutch uitpakken (“to unpack”), German auspacken (“to unpack”).

definition: Radically distinctive and without equal.
example: Unparalleled athletic ability.
etymology: From un- + paralleled.

definition: Without apparent forethought or prompting or planning.
example: An unplanned economy.
etymology: From un- + planned.

definition: Not producing or capable of producing.
example: Elimination of high-cost or unproductive industries.
etymology: From un- + productive.

definition: Not limited or restricted.
example: An unqualified denial.
etymology: From un- + qualified.

definition: Without question.
example: Fred Winter is unquestionably the jockey to follow.
etymology: From unquestionable + -ly or un- + question + -ably.

definition: Become or cause to become undone by separating the fibers or threads of.
example: Unravel the thread.
etymology: PIE word *h₂énti From un- (suffix denoting the inverse of the specified action) + ravel. cognates * Dutch ontrafelen (“to unravel”)

definition: (of animals) not recorded with or certified by an official breed association.
example: Unregistered dairy cattle.
etymology: From un- + registered.

definition: Not regulated; not subject to rule or discipline.
example: Unregulated off-shore fishing.
etymology: From un- + regulated.

definition: Not (or not yet) made available for distribution or publication.
example: Someone leaked the unreleased announcement.
etymology: From un- + released.

definition: Noisy and lacking in restraint or discipline.
example: An unruly class.

definition: Not giving satisfaction.
example: Shops should take back unsatisfactory goods.
etymology: From un- + satisfactory.

definition: Without scruples or principles.
example: Unscrupulous politicos who would be happy to sell … their country in order to gain power.
etymology: From un- + scrupulous.

definition: Not firmly fastened or secured.
example: An unsecured Internet connection.
etymology: From un- + secured.

definition: The ability of a customer to obtain goods or services before payment, based on the trust that payment will be made in the future.
Still in doubt.
example: An unsettled issue.

definition: Lacking a signature.
example: The message was typewritten and unsigned.
etymology: From un- + signed.

definition: Not having or showing or requiring special skill or proficiency.
example: Unskilled in the art of rhetoric.
etymology: From un- + skilled.

definition: A person who lacks technical training.
Not requested or sought.
example: Unsolicited junk mail.

definition: Defying expression or description.
example: Unspeakable happiness.
etymology: From Middle English unspekable, equivalent to un- + speakable.

definition: Expressed without speech.
example: Unspoken grief.
etymology: From un- + spoken.

definition: An accusation that is understood without needing to be spoken.
Not suspicious.
example: Deceiving the unsuspecting public.
etymology: From un- + suspecting.

definition: (of theories etc.) incapable of being defended or justified.
example: The theory of cold fusion was untenable.
etymology: From un- + tenable.

definition: Badly timed.
example: An untimely remark.
etymology: From Middle English untymely (also earlier untimliche), equivalent to un- + timely. First attested in the early 13th century. Compare Middle Danish utimelig, Old English untídlic (“unseasonable”).

definition: Not of the nobility.
example: Untitled civilians.
etymology: From un- + titled.

definition: Beyond the reach of criticism or attack or impeachment.
example: For the first time criticism was directed at a hitherto untouchable target.
etymology: From un- + touchable.

definition: Not disciplined or conditioned or made adept by training.
example: An untrained voice.
etymology: From un- + trained.

definition: Remove the veil from.
example: Women must not unveil themselves in public in some religious societies.
etymology: From Middle English *unveilen (suggested by past participle unveiled, vnueylyd (“unveiled”)). Equivalent to un- + veil.

definition: Putting on display for the first time.
example: He attended the unveiling of the statue.

definition: Incapable of being justified or explained.
etymology: From un- + warranted.

definition: Marked by firm determination or resolution; not shakable.
example: Unwavering loyalty.
etymology: From un- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + wavering (“being in doubt, indecisive”).

definition: Not welcome; not giving pleasure or received with pleasure.
example: Unwelcome publicity.
etymology: From Middle English unwelcome, unwelcum; equivalent to un- + welcome.

definition: Someone who gets in (to a party) without an invitation or without paying.
A person who for some reason is not wanted or welcome.
Somewhat ill or prone to illness.
example: Is unwell and can't come to work.
etymology: From un- + well.

definition: The trait of being unwilling.
example: His unwillingness to cooperate vetoed every proposal I made.
etymology: From unwilling + -ness.

definition: Reverse the winding or twisting of.
example: Unwind a ball of yarn.
etymology: From Middle English unwinden, from Old English unwindan (“to unwind; unwrap”), from Proto-Germanic *andawindaną (“to unwind”); equivalent to un- + wind (“to coil”). Cognate with Dutch ontwinden (“to unwind”).

definition: Showing or resulting from lack of judgment or wisdom.
example: An unwise investor is soon impoverished.
etymology: From Middle English unwis, from Old English unwīs (“unwise, foolish, ignorant, uninformed, insane”), equivalent to un- + wise.

definition: Without knowledge or intention.
example: He unwittingly deleted the references.

definition: Lacking in value or merit.
example: Dispel a student whose conduct is deemed unworthy.
etymology: From Middle English unworthy, equivalent to un- + worthy.

definition: Based on custom rather than documentation.
example: An unwritten law.
etymology: From Middle English unwriten, from Old English unwriten, unġewriten (“unwritten”), equivalent to un- + written.

definition: Law based on customary behavior.
A stable quark with an electric charge of +2/3 and a mass 607 times that of an electron.
Activity involved in maintaining something in good working order.
example: I would enjoy having a swimming pool, but I don't want to deal with the upkeep.
etymology: From up + keep.

definition: Used of high or hilly country.
etymology: From Middle English upland, from Old English ūpland (“the country”); equivalent to up- + land. The word as an adjective developed in Middle English.

definition: Native tropical American plant now cultivated in the United States yielding short-staple cotton.
A large subgenre of trance music, named for the feeling which listeners claim to get (often described as a ‘rush’).
The condition of being urbanized.
etymology: From urbanize + -ation.

definition: A calculus formed in the kidney.
A large vase that usually has a pedestal or feet.
etymology: From Middle English urne, from Old French urne, from Latin urna (“vessel”). Doublet of urna.

definition: An urn-shaped discomycete with a nearly black interior.
Having a concave shape like an urn.
The quality of being able to provide good service.
etymology: From usable + -ity or use + -ability.

definition: Of or involving the uterus.
example: Uterine cancer.
etymology: From Middle French utérin, from Latin uterinus (“pertaining to the womb; born of the same mother”), from Latin uterus (“womb”). Related to English uterus. By surface analysis, uter- + -ine.

definition: Either of a pair of tubes conducting the egg from the ovary to the uterus.
Made useful.
Having a useful function.
example: Utilitarian steel tables.
etymology: From utility + -arian. Coined by English philosopher Jeremy Bentham as early as 1781, and popularized by his student John Stuart Mill, who mistakenly attributed the term to John Galt.

definition: Of or pertaining to or resembling a utopia.
example: A Utopian novel.
etymology: From utopia + -an.

definition: Socialism achieved by voluntary sacrifice.
Communicated in words.
example: Frequently uttered sentiments.

definition: Leave (a job, post, or position) voluntarily.
example: She vacated the position when she got pregnant.

definition: Flask with double walls separated by vacuum; used to maintain substances at high or low temperatures.
A gauge for indicating negative atmospheric pressure.
A manservant who acts as a personal attendant to their employer.
A service provided (at a club or restaurant or airport etc.) whereby a patron leaves a car at the entrance and an attendant parks and retrieves it.
The qualities of a hero or heroine; exceptional or heroic courage when facing danger (especially in battle).
example: He received a medal for valor.

definition: Mechanical device attached to an elevated structure; rotates freely to show the direction of the wind.
A climbing orchid bearing a podlike fruit yielding vanilla beans; widely cultivated from Florida southward throughout tropical America.
Smelling of vanilla.
An electronic cigarette, that produces a nicotine containing vapor.
example: I won't buy a vape anytime soon because one may cost up to $20.
etymology: Clipping of vaporize.

definition: Liquid for use in electronic cigarettes.
Consumption of a vaporized nicotine solution.
example: He went vaping with me last night.

definition: A visible suspension in the air of particles of some substance.
A room that can be filled with steam in which people bathe; ‘vapour bath’ is a British term.
The density of a gas relative to the density of hydrogen.

A stoppage in a pipeline caused by gas bubbles (especially a stoppage that develops in hot weather in an internal-combustion engine when fuel in the gas line boils and forms bubbles that block the flow of gasoline to the carburetor).
The pressure exerted by a vapor; often understood to mean saturated vapor pressure (the vapor pressure of a vapor in contact with its liquid form).
In diverse ways.
example: The alternatives that are variously represented by the participants.
etymology: From various + -ly.

definition: Large tree native to southeastern Asia; the nuts yield oil used in varnishes; nut kernels strung together are used locally as candles.
A tube in which a body fluid circulates.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin vās (“vessel”) around 1645 through 1655. Doublet of vase.

definition: An artificial blood vessel, used in a surgical procedure performed to redirect blood flow in a region of the body.
Having a hemispherical vault or dome.
Cut of veal suitable for roasting.
The analysis of a vector field.
Turn sharply; change direction abruptly.
example: The motorbike veered to the right.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle Dutch vieren (“to slacken”).

definition: In a vehement manner.
example: He vehemently denied the accusations against him.
etymology: From vehement + -ly.

definition: Of or relating to or intended for (motor) vehicles.
example: Vehicular traffic.
etymology: From Late Latin vehiculāris. By surface analysis, vehicle + -ar.

definition: The aggregation of vehicles coming and going in a particular locality.
An accusation that is understood without needing to be spoken.
Smooth and soft to sight or hearing or touch or taste.
Coating consisting of a thin layer of superior wood glued to a base of inferior wood.
Disposed to seek revenge or intended for revenge.
example: His chains now broken, the prisoner turned a vengeful eye toward his former captors.
etymology: From venge + -ful.

definition: Extremely poisonous or injurious; producing venom.
example: Venomous snakes.
etymology: From Middle English venymous, from Old French venimos, composed of venim (“venom”) + -os (adjective-forming suffix). Synchronically analysable as venom + -ous. Compare Modern French venimeux.

definition: The act of venting.
Toward or on or near the belly (front of a primate or lower surface of a lower animal).
example: The ventral aspect of the human body.
etymology: From French ventral, from Latin ventrālis, from venter (“belly, abdomen”); by surface analysis, ventr- + -al.

definition: One of the two roots of a spinal nerve that passes ventrally from the spinal cord and that consists of motor fibers.
One of the two roots of a spinal nerve that passes ventrally from the spinal cord and that consists of motor fibers.
In precisely the same words used by a writer or speaker.
example: Repeated their dialog verbatim.
etymology: Attested in English since 1481 (therefore considered a Middle English derivation by some): from Medieval Latin verbātim (“word for word”), from Latin verbum (“word”) + -ātim (adverbial suffix).

definition: A dark green impure marble.
Serving to support or corroborate.
Often used as intensifiers.
example: He's a veritable swine.
etymology: From verity + -able, from Middle French veritable, from Old French veritable, from Latin veritabilis.

definition: A characteristic language of a particular group (as among thieves).
A genre of art and outdoor constructions made by untrained artists who do not recognize themselves as artists.
Thoroughly acquainted through study or experience.
The point of intersection of lines or the point opposite the base of a figure.
example: The mountain’s vertex was covered in snow.
etymology: Late Middle English, borrowed from Latin vertex (“whirl, eddy; top, crown, peak, summit”). Doublet of vortex.

definition: A reeling sensation; a feeling that you are about to fall.
A doctor who practices veterinary medicine.
etymology: From Latin veterīnārius (“cattle doctor”) + -an, from veterīnae (“beasts of burden, draught-”), probably from vehō (“to convey, draw”), or from vetus (“old”). By surface analysis, veterinary + -an.

definition: A small bottle that contains a drug (especially a sealed sterile container for injection by needle).
etymology: From Middle English vial, viole, a variant of fiole, phiole, phial (“small bowl or cup for liquids, etc.; flask”) [and other forms]: see further at phial. Doublet of phiale.

definition: Shake, quiver, or throb; move back and forth rapidly, usually in an uncontrolled manner.
example: To vibrate a sword or a staff.
etymology: The adjective (then also used as a participle) is first attested in 1420, in Middle English, the verb in 1620;

definition: A mechanical device that vibrates.
example: A reed is the vibrator that produces the sound.
etymology: From New Latin vibrātor, from Latin vibrō (“to vibrate”). By surface analysis, vibrate + -or.

definition: One ranking below or serving in the place of a chairman.
Governor of a country or province who rules as the representative of his or her king or sovereign.
example: Ireland was governed by a Viceroy representing the English King/Queen when it was part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.
etymology: From Middle French vice-roy, from vice- + roy (“king”). Compare viscount.

definition: (of persons) taken advantage of.
A video recording made on magnetic tape.
etymology: From video + tape, a trademark of the media company Ampex.

definition: A period of sleeplessness.
example: His dog kept vigil outside the hospital for eight days while he was recovering from an accident.
etymology: From Middle English vigile (“a devotional watching”), from Old French vigile, from Latin vigilia (“wakefulness, watch”), from vigil (“awake”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵ- (“to be strong, lively, awake”).

definition: A candle lighted by a worshiper in a church.
A candle lighted by a worshiper in a church.
The process of paying close and continuous attention.
example: Vigilance is especially susceptible to fatigue.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French vigilance, from Latin vigilantia.

definition: A volunteer committee to maintain order where an efficient legal system does not exist.
A male member of a vigilance committee.
A female member of a vigilance committee.
Forceful exertion.
Minute eelworm that feeds on organisms that cause fermentation in e.g. vinegar.
A colorless liquid unsaturated nitrile made from propene.
Smelling of violets.
Of something that is tinged with violet.
Of something that is tinged with violet.
A musician who plays the violin.
etymology: From violin + -ist.

definition: Morally excellent.
example: Successful communities need strong, selfless leaders and a virtuous people.
etymology: From Middle English vertuous, borrowed from Anglo-Norman vertuous, vertous, ultimately from Late Latin virtuōsus, from Latin virtūs. By surface analysis, virtue + -ous.

definition: Resistance of a liquid to shear forces (and hence to flow).
etymology: From Middle French viscosité, from Old French viscosité, from Medieval Latin viscositas; analysable as viscous + -ity.

definition: (in various countries) a son or younger brother or a count.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman viscounte, from Medieval Latin vicecomes, from Latin vice + comes. Equivalent to vice- + count. Doublet of vicecomes and vicomte.

definition: A male important or distinguished visitor.
The particular occupation for which you are trained.
example: Nursing is a vocation that many people find horrendous.
etymology: From Middle English vocacioun, from Old French vocation, from Latin vocātiō.

definition: Martini made with vodka rather than gin.
The act of adjusting an organ pipe (or wind instrument) so that it conforms to the standards of tone and pitch and color.
etymology: From voice + -ing.

definition: A game in which two teams hit an inflated ball over a high net using their hands.
Give personal assurance; guarantee.
example: Will he vouch for me?
etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English vouchen (“to call, summon; to provide; to make available, proffer;

definition: The repetition of similar vowels in the stressed syllables of successive words.
The sound made by the vibration of vocal folds modified by the resonance of the vocal tract.
etymology: From Latin vōx (“voice”). Doublet of voice.

definition: Walking with your feet in shallow water.
etymology: From wade + -ing.

definition: Any of many long-legged birds that wade in water in search of food.
etymology: From wading + bird.

definition: A shallow pool for children.
A small adhesive disk of paste; used to seal letters.
etymology: From Middle English wafre, from Anglo-Norman wafre, waufre (Old French gaufre), from a Germanic source. Compare Middle Low German wāfel, Middle Dutch wafel (“honeycomb”), West Flemish wafer. See also waffle.

definition: Resembling a thin crisp wafer.
Very thin.
example: Wafer-thin sheets of metal.

definition: A witty amusing person who makes jokes.
example: The wag of my dog's tail expresses happiness.
etymology: From Middle English waggen, probably from Old English wagian (“to wag, wave, shake”) with reinforcement from Old Norse vaga (“to wag, waddle”); both from Proto-Germanic *wagōną (“to wag”). Related to English way.

definition: A traditional Thai greeting where the hands are placed together in a prayer-like position.
example: Among Thais, there are strict rules of hierarchy that dictate how and when the wai should be given.
etymology: Borrowed from Thai ไหว้ (wâi, “a gesture of thanks”).

definition: Vocally expressing grief or sorrow or resembling such expression.
example: Wailing mourners.
etymology: From wail + -ing.

definition: A wagon maker.
etymology: From unattested Middle English *waynwrighte, from Old English wæġnwyrhta, corresponding to wain + wright.

definition: Do without or cease to hold or adhere to.
example: If you waive the right to be silent, anything you say can be used against you in a court of law.
etymology: From Middle English weyven (“to wave, waver”), from Old Norse veifa (“to wave, swing”) (Norwegian veiva), from Proto-Germanic *waibijaną.

definition: A path set aside for walking.
etymology: From walk + way.

definition: A disease of English walnut trees.
Someone who leads a wandering unsettled life.
etymology: From Middle English wanderere, wandrere, wanderare, equivalent to wander + -er.

definition: (of the Moon) pertaining to the period during which the visible surface of the moon decreases.
example: After full moon comes the waning moon.
etymology: From Middle English waninge, alteration of earlier waniand, waniende, from Old English waniende, from Proto-Germanic *wanōndz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *wanōną (“to wane”), equivalent to wane + -ing.

definition: A yell intended to rally a group of soldiers in battle.
The front part of a guided missile or rocket or torpedo that carries the nuclear or explosive charge or the chemical or biological agents.
etymology: From war + head, originally to distinguish a live war head of a torpedo from an inert exercise head. Piecewise doublet of war chief.

definition: Supreme military leader exercising civil power in a region especially one accountable to nobody when the central government is weak.
etymology: From war + lord.

definition: In a hearty manner.
example: We welcomed her warmly.
etymology: From warm + -ly.

definition: Conspicuous coloration or markings of an animal serving to warn off predators.
Engaged in war.
example: Belligerent (or warring) nations.
etymology: From Middle English werrynge. By surface analysis, war + -ing.

definition: A government ship that is available for waging war.
etymology: From war + ship.

definition: An uninhabited wilderness that is worthless for cultivation.
example: The trackless wastes of the desert.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English wast lond, modification of earlier weste lond, from Old English weste land (“wasteland”); equivalent to waste + land.

definition: A guardian or defender against theft or illegal practices or waste.
example: She is the global watchdog for human rights abuses.
etymology: From watch + dog.

definition: A close observer; someone who looks at something (such as an exhibition of some kind).
example: Sky watchers discovered a new star.
etymology: From Middle English wacchere, wachere, wacher, equivalent to watch + -er.

definition: Engaged in or accustomed to close observation.
example: The teacher kept a watchful eye on her pupils during the school trip.
etymology: From Middle English waccheful, equivalent to watch + -ful. Compare West Frisian waaks (“watchful”), Dutch waaks, waakzaam (“watchful”), German wachsam (“watchful”), Swedish vaksam (“watchful”).

definition: A male guard who keeps watch.
Blister containing a nonpurulent clear watery content.
Chute with flowing water down which toboggans and inner tubes and people slide into a pool.
A faucet for drawing water from a pipe or cask.
Gauge for indicating the level of water in e.g. a tank or boiler or reservoir.
Hickory of southern United States having many narrow leaflets and rather bitter nuts.
Honey locust of swamps and bottomlands of southern United States having short oval pods; yields dark heavy wood.
Aquatic fern of tropical America often used in aquariums.
Water in a vaporous form diffused in the atmosphere but below boiling temperature.
Grown in Australasia and Polynesia for its large root with fine edible white flesh.
A painting produced with watercolors.
etymology: From water + color.

definition: An African melon.
A navigable body of water.
etymology: From Middle English waterwey, from Old English wæterweġ (“waterway”), from Proto-West Germanic *watarweg, equivalent to water + way.

definition: Filled with water.
example: Watery soil.
etymology: From Middle English watery, wattry, from Old English wæteriġ (“watery”), from Proto-West Germanic *watarīg. Equivalent to water + -y.

definition: With eyes full of tears.
(of hair) having waves.
example: She had long wavy hair.
etymology: From wave + -y.

definition: Writing implement consisting of a colored stick of composition wax used for writing and drawing.
Any shrub or small tree of the genus Myrica with aromatic foliage and small wax-coated berries.
Treated with wax.
example: Waxed floors.

definition: The application of wax to a surface.
Resistant to guidance or discipline.
example: Wayward behavior.
etymology: Shortening of away + -ward.

definition: Having a weak stem.
Lacking bodily or muscular strength or vitality.
etymology: From Old English wāclīċe (“weakly”), equivalent to weak + -ly (adjectival suffix); compare Old English wāclīċ (“weak; ignoble; mean”), and Old Norse veikligr (“weakly; sick”);

definition: A person who wears or carries or displays something as a body covering or accessory.
example: The wearer of the crown.
etymology: From Middle English werer, werere, equivalent to wear + -er.

definition: Worn by exposure to the weather.
example: A house of weathered shingles.

definition: Variety of European beech with pendulous limbs.
Medium-sized spruce of California and Oregon having pendulous branches.
Willow with long drooping branches and slender leaves native to China; widely cultivated as an ornamental.
Bodybuilding by exercise that involves lifting weights.
etymology: From weight + lifting.

definition: In a weird manner.
example: She was dressed weirdly.
etymology: From weird + -ly.

definition: Having good branches.
Having tasteful clothing and being scrupulously neat.
Provided with artificial light.
example: A well-lighted stairwell.

definition: Of good upbringing.
example: A well-mannered gentleman always allows others first.
etymology: Compare Middle English wel ymanerede, wel y-manerit.

definition: (of actions or states) slightly short of or not quite accomplished; all but.
example: The recording is well-nigh perfect.
etymology: From Middle English wel-neigh (“physically close to; near in time to; almost, nearly;

definition: Moving toward the west.
example: Westbound pioneers.
etymology: From west + -bound.

definition: Of wind; from the west.
example: A westerly wind.
etymology: From Middle English westerli, from wester + -ly.

definition: Small or medium irregularly branched tree of the Pacific coast of North America; yields fine hard close-grained wood.
Of the western part of a city.
example: He lives in upper westside Manhattan.
etymology: From west + side.

definition: A low area where the land is saturated with water.
etymology: From wet + land. Cognate with West Frisian wetlân.

definition: Miscellaneous curios.
example: At the lexicography club, we welcome all discussion of words and whatnot.
etymology: From what + not.

definition: Small roundworm parasitic on wheat.
Embryo of the wheat kernel; removed before milling and eaten as a source of vitamins.
Propelling something on wheels.
example: The wheelings of birds in the sky.

definition: From what place, source, or cause.
example: Whence came I?
etymology: From Middle English whennes, from Old English hwanon (with adverbial genitive -s), related to hwonne (whence when). Analyzable as when + -s.

definition: The serum or watery part of milk that is separated from the curd in making cheese.
etymology: Onomatopoeic, variation on wahey.

definition: Perceive by inhaling through the nose.
etymology: The noun is possibly: * partly a variant of Middle English wef, weffe (“bad smell, stench, stink; exhalation; vapour;

definition: Determined by chance or impulse or whim rather than by necessity or reason.
example: The victim of whimsical persecutions.
etymology: From whimsy + -ical.

definition: An injury to the neck (the cervical vertebrae) resulting from rapid acceleration or deceleration (as in an automobile accident).
example: Tonal whiplash.
etymology: From whip + lash.

definition: An injury to the neck (the cervical vertebrae) resulting from rapid acceleration or deceleration (as in an automobile accident).
A more or less vertical column of air whirling around itself as it moves over the surface of the Earth.
example: Once he got that new scooter he turned into a whirlwind and damaged all the flowers.
etymology: From Middle English whirlewind, whirlewynde, equivalent to whirl + wind. Compare Middle Dutch wervelwint, Old Norse hvirfilvindr.

definition: Move somewhere quickly.
example: The President was whisked away in his limo.
etymology: From Middle English whisk, borrowed from Old Norse visk, from Proto-Germanic *wiskaz, *wiskō (“bundle of hay, wisp”), from Proto-Indo-European *weys-.

definition: Take away quickly and suddenly.
Move by very quickly.
Brush or wipe off lightly.
A jug that contains whiskey.
An informant who exposes wrongdoing within an organization in the hope of stopping it.
example: The law gives little protection to whistleblowers who feel the public has a right to know what is going on.
